findings.claim: LangGraph is maintained, MIT-licensed, and on the 1.x line. LangGraph 1.0 and LangChain 1.0 shipped on 2025-10-22 with a promise of 'no breaking changes until 2.0', and PyPI lists 1.2.12 (2026-09-21) as the latest release.
findings.relevance: A stable graph runtime with a written API-stability promise is a low-risk base for the commander's control flow.
findings.correction: No correction. The blog is dated 2025-10-22 and says 'no breaking changes until 2.0'. PyPI shows 1.2.12 released 2026-09-21 under MIT, and the GitHub release tag langgraph==1.2.12 carries the same date. The 1.0 date is also confirmed by a third-party Medium article.

findings.claim: In LangGraph, each node or agent can use a different LLM. LangChain's own multi-agent post says 'Each agent could even be powered by a separate fine-tuned LLM', and init_chat_model takes 'provider:model' strings for OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Bedrock, Azure, HuggingFace and OpenRouter.
findings.relevance: Supports binding each white-box reviewer sub-agent to a different provider, which is the goal of reducing single-model bias.
findings.correction: Small nuance. The API reference confirms the 'provider:model' format (e.g. 'openai:gpt-5.5') is equivalent to passing model_provider=. The docs' own examples for Bedrock ('bedrock_converse'), HuggingFace and OpenRouter use the model_provider kwarg rather than a colon string, but both forms work. The quote 'Each agent could even be powered by a separate fine-tuned LLM!' is exact. All sources are from LangChain.

findings.claim: LangGraph covers supervisor and hierarchical-team patterns, where the supervisor is 'an agent whose tools are other agents'.
findings.relevance: This maps directly onto the commander/dispatcher topology.
findings.correction: Add a caveat. The langgraph-supervisor README now says 'We now recommend using the supervisor pattern directly via tools rather than this library for most use cases.' So plan on a hand-built tool-calling supervisor, not the create_supervisor library.

findings.claim: LangGraph's human-in-the-loop uses interrupt(), which requires a checkpointer, and resumes with Command(resume=...). The docs warn that code before an interrupt re-runs on resume, so side effects placed before it should be idempotent.
findings.relevance: Human approval gates are possible (for example, sign-off on the threat model before black-box tests are generated), but test-execution nodes must be designed to be idempotent.
findings.correction: No correction. The API reference says 'you must enable a checkpointer' and 'The graph resumes from the start of the node, re-executing all logic.' The guide says side effects before interrupt 'should (ideally) be idempotent'. Both sources are LangChain's own; no third-party source was checked.

findings.claim: LangGraph persistence uses checkpointers keyed by thread_id: InMemorySaver (lost on restart), SqliteSaver, and PostgresSaver/AsyncPostgresSaver. These support conversation continuity, human-in-the-loop, time travel and fault tolerance.
findings.relevance: Lets long white-box then black-box pipelines survive crashes and be replayed for audit.
findings.correction: No correction. The langgraph-checkpoint-postgres package (3.1.2, 2026-08-07) documents PostgresSaver and AsyncPostgresSaver with configurable.thread_id.

findings.claim: AutoGen is in maintenance mode: 'It will not receive new features or enhancements and is community managed going forward.' Microsoft Agent Framework is named as its successor. The last autogen-agentchat PyPI release is 0.7.5 (2025-09-30), under the MIT license.
findings.relevance: Do not build a new toolkit on AutoGen. Use Microsoft Agent Framework if you want the Microsoft stack.
findings.correction: Small nuance. The repo is dual-licensed: MIT for code and CC-BY-4.0 for docs. The autogen-agentchat package itself is MIT.

findings.claim: Microsoft Agent Framework (MAF) reached 1.0 GA for .NET and Python on 2026-04-03. It is MIT-licensed, and PyPI shows agent-framework 1.19.0 (2026-09-18); the Go SDK is in public preview.
findings.relevance: MAF is an actively maintained, production-stable option with an explicit multi-agent workflow engine.
findings.correction: Small nuances. PyPI dates agent-framework 1.0.0 to 2026-04-02, while the GA blog is dated 2026-04-03, likely a time-zone difference. The Go SDK lives in a separate repo (microsoft/agent-framework-go), and Learn says it is in public preview without declarative agents, RAG, CodeAct or functional workflows. The .NET line is at dotnet-1.22.0 (2026-09-18).

findings.claim: MAF's 1.0 announcement lists first-party connectors for Microsoft Foundry, Azure OpenAI, OpenAI, Anthropic Claude, Amazon Bedrock, Google Gemini and Ollama. Each Agent takes its own chat client, so different agents can use different providers.
findings.relevance: Supports mixing Claude, OpenAI and open models per sub-agent. Nemotron would go through an OpenAI-compatible or Ollama path, which I did not test.
findings.correction: No correction. The blog lists exactly 'Microsoft Foundry, Azure OpenAI, OpenAI, Anthropic Claude, Amazon Bedrock, Google Gemini and Ollama'. Learn's Python sample builds Agent(client=FoundryChatClient(...)), so each agent gets its own client. Both sources are Microsoft's; the Visual Studio Magazine article returned 403 and could not be checked.

findings.claim: MAF workflows support sequential, concurrent, handoff, group chat and Magentic-One orchestration, with checkpointing and human-in-the-loop approvals via request/response ports. Pending human requests are saved in checkpoints and re-emitted when a run is restored.
findings.relevance: Gives the commander durable pause and resume at gates, for example after threat modeling.
findings.correction: Small nuance. In Python, HITL uses ctx.request_info() with @response_handler; RequestPort is the .NET and Go construct. Learn says 'pending requests are also saved as part of the checkpoint state... re-emitted as RequestInfoEvent objects.' Python file and Cosmos checkpoint stores use restricted pickle, and Learn warns never to load checkpoints from untrusted sources.

findings.claim: MAF has built-in MCP client support and A2A protocol support for agent collaboration across runtimes.
findings.relevance: Tools such as SAST scanners and test runners can be exposed over MCP, and remote agents can be reached over A2A.
findings.correction: Small nuance. At the 1.0 announcement the blog said 'A2A 1.0 support coming soon'. A2A v1 support was later announced for .NET, and Python has an agent_framework.a2a.A2AAgent class. All sources are Microsoft's.

findings.claim: CrewAI is maintained and MIT-licensed, with frequent releases (1.15.22 on 2026-09-16). It is a standalone framework, not built on LangChain.
findings.relevance: A viable higher-level option. The fast release cadence means version pinning matters.
findings.correction: No correction. PyPI and GitHub releases show 1.15.22 on 2026-09-16, with roughly weekly releases. Wikipedia, an independent source, confirms MIT and 'independent of LangChain'.

findings.claim: CrewAI sets the LLM per agent (Agent(llm=LLM(model='provider/model-id')) or YAML). OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Azure, Bedrock and Snowflake Cortex are native; all other providers, including Nvidia NIM, Ollama and OpenRouter, go through LiteLLM.
findings.relevance: Per-agent cross-provider assignment is first-class, and Nemotron can be reached through the NIM route.
findings.correction: Small nuance. LiteLLM-backed providers need the extra install `crewai[litellm]`. Only CrewAI's own docs were checked, with no independent source; this matters given LiteLLM's March 2026 supply-chain incident (claim 31).

findings.claim: CrewAI's hierarchical process requires a manager_llm or manager_agent. The manager handles 'planning, delegation, and validation' and assigns tasks to agents rather than having them pre-assigned.
findings.relevance: This is a built-in commander pattern, though LLM-driven delegation is less deterministic than an explicit graph.
findings.correction: No correction. The docs say 'Tasks are not pre-assigned; the manager allocates tasks to agents based on their capabilities, reviews outputs, and assesses task completion.' Only CrewAI's own docs were checked.

findings.claim: CrewAI Flows provide state persistence with @persist (SQLite by default), resume or fork by state ID, and a @human_feedback decorator that pauses a flow for human input.
findings.relevance: Covers checkpointing and human approval gates for the pipeline stages.
findings.correction: Small nuances. Resume uses kickoff(inputs={'id': uuid}); fork uses kickoff(restore_from_state_id=uuid), which assigns a new state.id. @human_feedback needs CrewAI 1.8.0 or later. Only CrewAI's own docs were checked.

findings.claim: CrewAI turns on anonymous telemetry by default, collecting things like agent roles, tool names and LLM settings. It can be disabled with CREWAI_DISABLE_TELEMETRY=true.
findings.relevance: A security-testing toolkit that handles proprietary code should turn telemetry off by default.
findings.correction: Small addition. OTEL_SDK_DISABLED=true also disables it, but that turns off all OpenTelemetry, not just CrewAI's. The GitHub README mentions only OTEL_SDK_DISABLED. The 1.15.21 release notes add telemetry for checkpoint runtime and CLI usage. The share_crew opt-in sends more detailed data.

findings.claim: OpenAI Agents SDK (Python) is MIT-licensed and still pre-1.0: PyPI shows 0.22.3 on 2026-09-17. It supports handoffs, agents-as-tools, guardrails, tracing and MCP.
findings.relevance: Actively maintained, but a 0.x version means breaking changes can still arrive, so pin versions.
findings.correction: No correction. There is no 1.0 release yet. GitHub releases confirm v0.22.3 is the latest.

findings.claim: The OpenAI Agents SDK allows a different model per agent and non-OpenAI providers through OpenAI-compatible clients or beta LiteLLM/any-llm adapters. The docs warn that tracing fails without an OpenAI key, many providers lack the Responses API, some lack structured outputs, and hosted tools are OpenAI-only.
findings.relevance: Cross-provider sub-agents work, but with real feature loss. Use Chat Completions and a non-OpenAI tracing processor for mixed fleets.
findings.correction: Small nuance. The docs say trace upload to OpenAI fails without an OpenAI key, and you can disable tracing or use another trace processor. The tools page says hosted tools are offered 'when using the OpenAIResponsesModel'. Tool search and programmatic tool calling are 'available only with OpenAI Responses models.' Both LiteLLM and any-llm are 'best-effort, beta'.

findings.claim: OpenAI Agents SDK human-in-the-loop marks tools with needs_approval. The run pauses with interruptions and is serialized to RunState (to_json/from_json) for approval and later resume, and the docs warn to deserialize only snapshots from trusted storage. Sessions include SQLite, Redis, SQLAlchemy, MongoDB, Dapr and an EncryptedSession wrapper.
findings.relevance: Supports approval gates and state that persists across processes.
findings.correction: No correction. to_string()/from_string() also exist. The docs add that 'a schema check or a tool-call fingerprint does not authenticate a snapshot.' Other sessions include OpenAIConversationsSession, AsyncSQLiteSession and AdvancedSQLiteSession. Only OpenAI's own docs were checked.

findings.claim: Claude Agent SDK (Python and TypeScript) runs Claude Code as a library and provides subagents, hooks, MCP, permissions and sessions. The Python package is MIT-licensed per PyPI and its LICENSE file (0.2.158 on 2026-09-23), but the docs say use is governed by Anthropic's Commercial Terms of Service.
findings.relevance: A strong harness for agents that need file access, shell and approvals. Licensing is dual: MIT code plus commercial usage terms.
findings.correction: Small nuance. The docs say use is governed by the Commercial Terms 'except to the extent a specific component or dependency is covered by a different license as indicated in that component's LICENSE file'. The package bundles a native Claude Code binary. Third-party products may not offer claude.ai login or rate limits unless previously approved, so use API keys.

findings.claim: Claude Agent SDK subagents each have their own prompt, tools, MCP servers, permissionMode and model. The model field takes aliases (opus, sonnet, haiku, inherit) or a full model ID, and nesting, concurrency and spend can be capped (default depth 3, 20 concurrent subagents, optional max_budget_usd).
findings.relevance: Fits the commander design well: tool-restricted, read-only reviewer subagents with cost limits.
findings.correction: Small additions. The alias list also includes 'fable'. Depth and concurrency are set with the env vars CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_SUBAGENT_SPAWN_DEPTH and CLAUDE_CODE_MAX_CONCURRENT_SUBAGENTS; the spend cap has no default. These limits apply from TypeScript SDK v0.3.219 and Python SDK v0.2.127, and earlier versions differ.

findings.claim: Claude Agent SDK cannot bind subagents to non-Claude models. Anthropic's docs say it 'doesn't support routing Claude Code to non-Claude models through any gateway'; supported backends are the Anthropic API, Bedrock, Claude Platform on AWS, Google Cloud's Agent Platform (Vertex) and Microsoft Foundry.
findings.relevance: Hard limitation: to get GPT or Nemotron reviewers under a Claude Agent SDK commander, the other models must be called as tools (for example, an MCP server wrapping LiteLLM). This is my own architectural inference, not a documented feature.
findings.correction: No correction. The exact sentence is 'Anthropic doesn't endorse, maintain, or audit third-party gateway products, and doesn't support routing Claude Code to non-Claude models through any gateway.' The quickstart lists CLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK, CLAUDE_CODE_USE_ANTHROPIC_AWS, CLAUDE_CODE_USE_VERTEX and CLAUDE_CODE_USE_FOUNDRY. To use Nemotron or GPT, a non-Claude reviewer needs a separate runtime, such as LangGraph or MAF plus LiteLLM.

findings.claim: Claude Agent SDK approvals run through a fixed pipeline: hooks, deny rules, ask rules, permission mode, allow rules, then the canUseTool callback. Modes are default, dontAsk, acceptEdits, bypassPermissions, plan and auto, and a subagent never gets bypassPermissions unless the parent session has it.
findings.relevance: Fine-grained human-in-the-loop and least-privilege controls for sub-agents running tests against the user's own staging systems.
findings.correction: Small nuance. The bypassPermissions rule for subagents requires Claude Code v2.1.267 or later. Subagents inherit the parent's mode unless their own permissionMode is set and the parent is in default, dontAsk or plan. In bypassPermissions, allowed_tools does not restrict anything; use disallowed_tools or hooks to block tools.

findings.claim: Claude Agent SDK sessions are stored as local JSONL transcripts that can be continued, resumed by ID or forked. A SessionStore adapter is needed to resume across hosts, and file checkpointing is separate from conversation state.
findings.relevance: State persistence exists, but CI or ephemeral runners need a shared session store or explicit state handoff.
findings.correction: Small nuance. Transcripts are stored under ~/.claude/projects/<encoded-cwd>/*.jsonl. A SessionStore adapter is one option for cross-host resume; you can also copy the .jsonl file or pass results into a fresh session. 'Sessions persist the conversation, not the filesystem.'

findings.claim: Google ADK (Python) is Apache-2.0-licensed and on the 2.x line (google-adk 2.9.2 on 2026-09-18). ADK 2.0 added a graph-based Workflow Runtime and reached GA on 2026-05-19 (Python), 2026-06-30 (Go) and 2026-08-21 (TypeScript), with breaking changes from 1.x.
findings.relevance: Actively maintained, but the recent major version bump means fewer battle-tested examples.
findings.correction: Small additions. Java 2.0 is not GA yet. The 1.x line still gets patches (v1.39.1 on 2026-08-27). PyPI notes breaking changes to 'the agent API, event model, and session schema.' All sources are Google's.

findings.claim: ADK is 'optimized for Gemini' but model-agnostic. Non-Gemini models plug in through connector wrappers such as LiteLlm, Anthropic, Ollama, vLLM and Apigee, passed as the model parameter of each LlmAgent.
findings.relevance: Per-agent cross-provider assignment works because each LlmAgent takes its own model object, but the docs imply this rather than stating it outright.
findings.correction: No correction. LiteRT-LM is also listed. The docs say you 'instantiate a specific wrapper class, such as ApigeeLlm or LiteLlm, and pass this object as the model parameter to your LlmAgent.'

findings.claim: ADK supports coordinator/dispatcher patterns (a parent agent with sub_agents, or AgentTool), ParallelAgent fan-out/gather, and a human-in-the-loop pattern for high-stakes actions.
findings.relevance: The commander pattern and parallel multi-model review are supported directly.
findings.correction: No correction. The guide lists 8 patterns: Sequential, Coordinator/Dispatcher, Parallel Fan-Out/Gather, Hierarchical Decomposition (uses AgentTool), Generator and Critic, Iterative Refinement, Human-in-the-Loop and Composite. ADK 2.0 adds graph, dynamic and collaborative workflows.

findings.claim: ADK human-in-the-loop uses tool confirmation (require_confirmation=True or requestConfirmation). The confirmation docs say DatabaseSessionService and VertexAiSessionService are not supported by this feature, even though DatabaseSessionService is the persistent SQL session store.
findings.relevance: Tension between persistent approvals and durable storage. Check whether ADK 2.0 graph human-input nodes remove this limit.
findings.correction: Small additions. The feature is marked experimental. TypeScript uses requestConfirmation() inside execute; Kotlin uses @Tool(requireConfirmation = true). With a persistent SQL store, durable approval gates need a custom mechanism.

findings.claim: ADK can expose agents over A2A and consume remote ones with RemoteA2aAgent in Python, Go and Java, and also supports MCP tools.
findings.relevance: Makes it possible to split a black-box test agent into a separate A2A service.
findings.correction: Three corrections. A2A in ADK is marked 'Experimental'. The class name differs by language: RemoteA2aAgent in Python, remoteagent.NewA2A(...) in Go, RemoteA2AAgent in Java; Kotlin can also consume. TypeScript is not listed for A2A. MCP tool support is confirmed.

findings.claim: LiteLLM is a Python SDK and self-hostable proxy/gateway for 100+ providers with an OpenAI-compatible interface, cost tracking, budgets, fallbacks, load balancing, guardrails, an MCP gateway and A2A support. The core is MIT and enterprise features are under a separate commercial license; PyPI shows 1.102.1 on 2026-09-23.
findings.relevance: The most common neutral routing layer for binding sub-agents to Claude, OpenAI, Nemotron and others, and it keeps provider keys server-side.
findings.correction: Small nuance. The LICENSE says content in 'enterprise/' is under a separate enterprise license and everything else is MIT. PyPI also shows backport patches (1.101.1, 1.100.2) on the same day as 1.102.1, so pin exact versions.

findings.claim: LiteLLM routes to NVIDIA NIM with the nvidia_nim/ prefix and NVIDIA_NIM_API_KEY, using https://integrate.api.nvidia.com/v1 as the default base URL. Nemotron models are listed.
findings.relevance: A concrete route for the Nemotron reviewer requested by the user. The model IDs listed in LiteLLM docs may lag behind NVIDIA's current catalog.
findings.correction: Small nuances. The LiteLLM doc lists older Nemotron IDs (e.g. nvidia/nemotron-4-340b-instruct) and says all NIM models are supported. The NVIDIA page confirms nvidia/nemotron-3-super-120b-a12b (released 2026-03-11) on the same base URL. That model uses the NVIDIA Nemotron Open Model License, and trial use falls under the NVIDIA API Trial Terms.

findings.claim: litellm 1.82.7 and 1.82.8 on PyPI were malicious on 2026-03-24 (live about 40 minutes), carrying a credential stealer after CI credentials were compromised through a Trivy dependency. LiteLLM says its official proxy Docker image was not affected and advises pinning to 1.82.6 or earlier or 1.83.0+ and rotating secrets.
findings.relevance: The toolkit's own supply chain is an attack surface: pin hashes, prefer vetted images, and isolate provider credentials from the code under test.
findings.correction: No correction. LiteLLM says the packages were live from 10:39 UTC for about 40 minutes. Datadog, an independent source, ties it to the TeamPCP campaign after an earlier Trivy compromise (2026-03-19). Data was exfiltrated to models.litellm.cloud, and LiteLLM advises checking for litellm_init.pth. 1.82.7 and 1.82.8 no longer appear in PyPI's release list.

findings.claim: OpenRouter is a hosted, closed-source SaaS offering an OpenAI-compatible API to hundreds of models. Provider routing controls include order, allow_fallbacks, only, ignore, sort, data_collection='deny' and zdr=true.
findings.relevance: The quickest way to reach many vendors, including Nemotron, with one key, but it adds a third party to the path of the user's source code.
findings.correction: Small nuance. 'Closed-source' is inferred: the OpenRouterTeam GitHub org publishes SDKs, examples and tools but no routing-platform repo. There are more routing fields: require_parameters, quantizations and max_price.

findings.claim: OpenRouter says it has its own zero-data-retention policy (prompts are not kept unless you opt in to logging) and can enforce ZDR provider routing globally or per request. That enforcement does not cover plugins and tools, and endpoints with unknown policies are assumed to retain and train on data.
findings.relevance: Toolkit configs should set zdr/data_collection=deny when sending proprietary code to white-box reviewers.
findings.correction: Small nuance. ZDR can also be set per model group. In-memory prompt caching is not counted as retention. This is OpenRouter's self-description; no independent audit was found.

findings.claim: MCP was donated to the Agentic AI Foundation, a Linux Foundation directed fund co-founded by Anthropic, Block and OpenAI, on 2025-12-09. Governance by the existing maintainers stayed in place.
findings.relevance: MCP is a vendor-neutral standard, suitable as the tool layer (scanners, test runners, repo access) shared by all sub-agents regardless of their LLM.
findings.correction: Small nuance. The LF press release (2025-12-09) confirms the co-founders and the founding projects MCP, goose and AGENTS.md, but does not use the words 'directed fund'. That wording comes from Anthropic's announcement and the MCP blog.

findings.claim: The current MCP specification is 2026-07-28. It makes the protocol stateless (no initialize handshake or Mcp-Session-Id), adds a required server/discover call, moves tasks into an extension, and deprecates Roots, Sampling and Logging.
findings.relevance: New MCP tool servers in the toolkit should target 2026-07-28 while staying compatible with 2025-11-25 clients, since framework SDK support may lag.
findings.correction: Wording fix. server/discover is mandatory for servers to implement, but optional for clients to call. Other changes include MRTR replacing server-initiated requests, subscriptions/listen, removal of ping and SSE resumability, and deprecation of Dynamic Client Registration in favour of Client ID Metadata Documents. Deprecated features stay for at least 12 months. Only the MCP project's own pages were checked.

findings.claim: The MCP security best-practices document covers confused deputy, token passthrough (forbidden), SSRF, state-handle hijacking, local MCP server compromise, OAuth URL validation and scope minimization. It recommends sandboxing local servers and least-privilege scopes.
findings.relevance: The harness's own MCP tool servers must follow these rules. They also give ready-made threat-model categories when the app under test uses MCP.
findings.correction: No correction. It also covers stdio transport security in proxy setups, mix-up attacks, localhost redirect URI impersonation and CIMD trust policies. It says 'MCP servers MUST NOT accept any tokens that were not explicitly issued for the MCP server.'

findings.claim: A2A (Agent2Agent) was created by Google, moved to the Linux Foundation on 2025-06-23, and reached v1.0.0 on 2026-03-12 (v1.0.1 on 2026-05-28). The repo is Apache-2.0 with SDKs in Python, Go, JavaScript, Java, .NET and Rust, and describes itself as complementary to MCP.
findings.relevance: A2A is the stable choice if sub-agents built on different frameworks (for example, an ADK black-box agent and a MAF reviewer) must talk to the commander across processes.
findings.correction: No correction. Google launched A2A in April 2025. v1.0.0 has breaking changes from v0.3.0, including OAuth flow updates, tasks/list and gRPC multi-tenancy.

findings.claim: Pydantic (pydantic/pydantic) is MIT-licensed according to the GitHub license API.
findings.relevance: Core validation library license.
findings.correction: No correction.

findings.claim: LiteLLM's LICENSE states that content under the 'enterprise/' directory is licensed under enterprise/LICENSE and that everything else is MIT ('Copyright (c) 2023 Berri AI').
findings.relevance: Enterprise-directory features must not be used without accepting their separate license.
findings.correction: No correction. (Note: the GitHub license API reports NOASSERTION for BerriAI/litellm because of the dual-part LICENSE.)

findings.claim: PyPI metadata (checked 2026-09-24): jsonschema 4.26.0 license_expression MIT; PyYAML 6.0.3 license MIT (OSI MIT classifier); tzdata 2026.4 (uploaded 2026-09-12) license Apache-2.0.
findings.relevance: Licenses of the validator's direct dependencies (tools/validate_schemas.py).
findings.correction: No correction. (Note: jsonschema 4.26.0 was uploaded 2026-01-07. PyYAML has no license_expression, only license 'MIT' plus the OSI MIT classifier. tzdata has license 'Apache-2.0' with no license_expression.)

findings.claim: PostgreSQL is released under the PostgreSQL License, described by the project as a liberal open-source license similar to BSD or MIT. It permits use, copying, modification and distribution for any purpose without fee, provided the copyright notice and license paragraphs appear in all copies.
findings.relevance: License for the Z1 database.
findings.correction: No correction.

findings.claim: langgraph-checkpoint-postgres 3.1.2 (MIT, uploaded 2026-08-07) depends on psycopg>=3.2.0 and psycopg-pool>=3.2.0, and psycopg 3.3.6 declares license_expression LGPL-3.0-only.
findings.relevance: The PostgresSaver checkpointer pulls in an LGPL-3.0 transitive dependency that the license registry must list.
findings.correction: No correction.

findings.claim: RFC 8032 (EdDSA, January 2017) is an Informational document from the IRTF CFRG. Ed25519 public keys and private keys are 32 octets, signatures are 64 octets, and the RFC states that EdDSA signatures are deterministic.
findings.relevance: Supports D11's choice of Ed25519. Deterministic signing means signing needs no per-signature randomness.
findings.correction: No correction.

findings.claim: RFC 8785, JSON Canonicalization Scheme (JCS, June 2020), is an Informational RFC on the Independent Submission stream, not an IETF standard. It restricts input to the I-JSON subset (no duplicate property names), requires numbers to be IEEE 754 double precision serialized per ECMAScript, sorts property names by UTF-16 code units, and recommends encoding higher-precision numbers or long integers as JSON strings.
findings.relevance: Defines D11's canonicalization contract and its numeric and duplicate-key limits.
findings.correction: No correction.

findings.claim: The Python package 'rfc8785' (Trail of Bits, pure Python, Apache-2.0) is at version 0.1.4 (2024-09-27). The alternative package 'jcs' is at 0.2.1 (2022-04-10, Apache-2.0, classifiers only up to Python 3.10).
findings.relevance: Implementation options for JCS. Both are small, low-release-cadence packages, so pinning and test vectors are needed.
findings.correction: No correction. (rfc8785 declares Apache-2.0 only through the OSI classifier, not through a license_expression field.)

findings.claim: The Python 'cryptography' package latest version is 50.0.1 with license expression 'Apache-2.0 OR BSD-3-Clause'. Its Ed25519 API provides Ed25519PrivateKey.generate()/sign(data) (64-byte signature) and Ed25519PublicKey.verify(signature, data), which raises InvalidSignature on failure. Raw keys are 32 bytes.
findings.relevance: The concrete library API for D11 signing and verification.
findings.correction: No correction.

findings.claim: OpenSSH 8.1 (2019-10-09) added experimental signing and verification to ssh-keygen. ssh-keygen -Y sign/verify require a namespace (-n) to prevent signature confusion across domains. -Y verify takes an allowed-signers file (-f) and an optional revocation file (-r), and allowed_signers entries support namespaces, valid-after and valid-before options.
findings.relevance: An offline Ed25519-capable alternative with built-in key validity windows and revocation.
findings.correction: No correction.

findings.claim: minisign uses Ed25519 (by default over a BLAKE2b-512 prehash). Its signatures carry an untrusted comment and a signed 'trusted comment'. No key revocation or expiry mechanism is described on the project page.
findings.relevance: A simple offline alternative without built-in revocation, so a separate registry would still be needed.
findings.correction: No correction.

findings.claim: Sigstore cosign sign-blob in keyless mode obtains a certificate from Fulcio and records the signature in the Rekor transparency log. Key-based signing uses --key (key file, KMS URI or Kubernetes secret). cosign verify-blob offers --insecure-ignore-tlog for signatures not uploaded to the transparency log.
findings.relevance: Keyless mode depends on online public infrastructure. Air-gapped use means key mode, which gives up the transparency-log benefit.
findings.correction: No correction.

findings.claim: RFC 9162 (Certificate Transparency Version 2.0, December 2021) is Experimental and obsoletes RFC 6962. It uses a Merkle tree with inclusion and consistency proofs against signed tree heads, and warns that a misbehaving log can present different, inconsistent views of itself to different clients.
findings.relevance: Even Merkle-tree logs need external monitors or witnesses to detect rewrites, which supports D12's external anchoring.
findings.correction: No correction.

findings.claim: Crosby and Wallach, 'Efficient Data Structures for Tamper-Evident Logging' (USENIX Security 2009), model an untrusted logger kept honest by auditors who hold earlier commitments and check that the log remains consistent with them. They note that a classic hash chain may need a proof linear in log size (e.g. an 800 MB trace for an 80-million-event log) versus about 3 KB with their tree-based structure.
findings.relevance: Hash-chain tamper evidence depends on commitments held outside the logger. Proof size is linear, which is acceptable at per-run scale.
findings.correction: No correction. (The body text gives the tree proof size as 3100 bytes. The abstract says 3 KB.)

findings.claim: The YAML 1.2.2 specification says YAML 1.2's primary focus was making YAML a strict superset of JSON, defines a JSON schema with only null, bool, int and float scalar tags, and requires mapping keys to be unique.
findings.relevance: A JSON-schema-only YAML subset maps cleanly onto the JCS input model.
findings.correction: Confirmed: the 1.2.2 spec says YAML 1.2's 'primary focus was making YAML a strict superset of JSON', and it requires mapping keys to be unique. Wrong: the JSON schema does not have 'only' null, bool, int and float scalar tags. Section 10.2.1 says the JSON schema uses those tags 'in addition to those defined by the failsafe schema' (map, seq, str). So !!str is also a scalar tag in the JSON schema.

findings.claim: PyYAML's PyPI description says it includes 'a complete YAML 1.1 parser'.
findings.relevance: YAML 1.1 implicit typing (e.g. timestamps and yes/no booleans) differs from the YAML 1.2 JSON schema, so the signed-document loader must restrict types.
findings.correction: No correction.

findings.claim: PyYAML GitHub issue #41 (open as of 2026-09-24) reports that PyYAML silently accepts duplicate mapping keys, with the last value overwriting earlier ones, and that libyaml behaves the same way.
findings.relevance: A signed ROE could be parsed differently by different parsers. The canonicalizer must reject duplicate keys explicitly.
findings.correction: Issue #41 ('pyyaml should detect duplicate keys and report an error') is open and was created 2016-11-22, migrated from pyyaml.org ticket #128. Its body says 'currently libyaml silently accepts duplicate keys', and a 2019 comment refers to 'PyYAML silently accepting duplicate mapping keys'. The 'last value overwrites earlier ones' detail was not found in the issue body. The body also frames the problem around libyaml rather than stating 'libyaml behaves the same way'.

findings.claim: PyPI metadata (checked 2026-09-24): datamodel-code-generator 0.82.0, license MIT, requires_python >=3.10. Its project description states it generates Python data models (Pydantic v1/v2 BaseModel, dataclasses, TypedDict, msgspec) from inputs including OpenAPI 3 and JSON Schema.
findings.relevance: docs/08 proposes generating the Pydantic models under src/vibecheck/models/_generated/ from docs/schemas (single source of truth). Coverage of every JSON Schema 2020-12 keyword used in docs/schemas is NOT claimed; contract round-trip tests must catch gaps.

However, the current PyPI description lists outputs as 'Pydantic v2, Pydantic v2 dataclass, dataclasses, TypedDict, or msgspec' and does not mention Pydantic v1; drop 'v1' from the claim (or source it separately). findings.relevance: docs/08 uses Hypothesis for property tests of the adjudicator, clusterer, JCS signing payload and strict YAML loader. License already recorded as pending_d-41; this entry adds the version and Python requirement for pinning.

findings.claim: Nemotron 3 family, part 1: Nemotron 3 Nano 30B-A3B was released on Hugging Face on 2025-12-15. It has 30B total parameters (about 3.5B active) and a hybrid Mamba-Transformer MoE architecture.
findings.relevance: The smallest current open Nemotron. It is realistic to self-host as a white-box reviewer agent.
findings.correction: The HF card says 'December 15, 2025', '3.5B active parameters and 30B parameters in total', and describes 23 Mamba-2/MoE layers plus 6 attention layers. NVIDIA's research page gives more precise figures of 31.6B total and 3.2B active, so give the count as 'about 30B total / ~3.2-3.5B active'. The arXiv paper (submitted 2025-12-24) confirms the hybrid Mamba-Transformer MoE design.

findings.claim: Nemotron 3 family, part 2: Nemotron 3 Super 120B-A12B (12B active) was released on Hugging Face on 2026-03-11. Nemotron 3 Ultra 550B-A55B (55B active) was released on 2026-06-04. Both use a LatentMoE hybrid Mamba-2/MoE/attention design with Multi-Token Prediction.
findings.relevance: These are the larger Nemotron options for the commander or reviewer agents. NVIDIA's Dec 2025 press release gave earlier size estimates (about 100B and 500B); the model cards give the final sizes.
findings.correction: Both HF cards say 'LatentMoE - Mamba-2 + MoE + Attention hybrid with Multi-Token Prediction (MTP)'. The NVIDIA blog is dated June 4, 2026 and confirms 550B/55B active. The arXiv paper confirms LatentMoE and MTP for Super and Ultra only. The Super date rests only on the HF card; no second source found for it.

findings.claim: Nemotron 3.5 Lightning 30B-A3B was released on 2026-08-11. It is under OpenMDW-1.1, supports up to 1M context (256K validated on a single H100), and uses the qwen3_coder tool-call parser.
findings.relevance: The newest small Nemotron. It is a fast worker-agent candidate.
findings.correction: Precision on the context figures: the card lists 256K on a single H100 80GB as 'memory-bound', and 1M on 8x H100 (TP8), GB200 or B200. The NIM guide says the NIM defaults to 262,144 tokens; going beyond that needs VLLM_ALLOW_LONG_MAX_MODEL_LEN=1.

findings.claim: The older generations are still published. Nemotron Nano 2 (NVIDIA-Nemotron-Nano-9B-v2, released 2025-08-18, and 12B-v2, released 2025-08-29) is a Mamba2-Transformer hybrid with 128K context. Llama-Nemotron models (Nano 4B v1.1, Nano 8B v1, Super 49B v1/v1.5, Ultra 253B v1) are Llama derivatives with 131,072-token context.
findings.relevance: Prefer Nemotron 3 or 3.5 for new builds. Llama-Nemotron adds the Llama community license on top of NVIDIA's license.
findings.correction: All the model cards exist and match the claim. Nano 4B v1.1 comes from Llama-3.1-Minitron-4B-Width-Base, which was pruned from Llama 3.1 8B, so it is an indirect Llama derivative. Release dates: Nano 8B v1 on 2025-03-18, Super 49B v1 on 2025-03-18, Nano 4B v1.1 on 2025-05-20, Super 49B v1.5 on 2025-07-25 and Ultra 253B v1 on 2025-04-07. All sources are NVIDIA's own HF cards.

findings.claim: Nemotron 3 Nano, Super and Ultra all list up to 1M-token context. Nano's Hugging Face config defaults to 256K because of VRAM limits.
findings.relevance: Long context means whole-repo review is possible, but the memory needed at 1M context limits self-hosting.
findings.correction: The Nano card says 'the default context size in the Hugging Face configuration is 256k due to higher VRAM requirements'.

findings.claim: Licensing: Nemotron 3 Nano and Super are under the NVIDIA Nemotron Open Model License (last modified 2025-12-15). It allows commercial use and derivatives, requires attribution, and terminates rights if you bring patent or copyright litigation. NVIDIA claims no ownership of outputs.
findings.relevance: Commercial use inside a toolkit is permitted under this license.
findings.correction: The license page shows Last Modified December 15, 2025. The required notice is 'Licensed by NVIDIA Corporation under the NVIDIA Nemotron Model License', and the page says 'NVIDIA does not claim ownership to any outputs'. Unlike the older NVIDIA Open Model License, this license has no clause that ends your rights for circumventing guardrails. This is a legal summary; have counsel review it.

findings.claim: Licensing: Nemotron 3 Ultra and 3.5 Lightning are under OpenMDW-1.1, a permissive model license released by the Linux Foundation on 2026-05-28. NVIDIA said it plans to use OpenMDW for future Nemotron releases.
findings.relevance: The license differs by model, so the toolkit should record the license per model.
findings.correction: The press release is dated May 28, 2026, but the license text itself says 'last updated 2026-05-27'. The release says NVIDIA will adopt OpenMDW-1.1 'across future releases' of Nemotron. OpenMDW also ends patent rights for anyone who starts patent litigation, and it puts no restrictions on outputs.

findings.claim: Licensing: Nemotron Nano 2 and Llama-Nemotron use the older NVIDIA Open Model License (last modified 2025-10-24). It says rights terminate automatically if you bypass or circumvent safety guardrails. Llama-Nemotron also carries the Llama 3.1 or 3.3 Community License.
findings.relevance: This is a compliance constraint if agents are prompted or fine-tuned in ways that weaken the model's guardrails.
findings.correction: Section 2.1 of the page (Last Modified October 24, 2025) ends rights automatically if you 'bypass, disable, reduce the efficacy of, or circumvent any ... safety guardrail ... without a substantially similar Guardrail appropriate for your use case'. The Super 49B cards carry Llama 3.3; Ultra 253B, Nano 8B and Nano 4B carry Llama 3.1. A defensive testing toolkit should not strip model guardrails, or it risks this clause.

findings.claim: Hosted access through build.nvidia.com uses the OpenAI-compatible base URL https://integrate.api.nvidia.com/v1. NVIDIA describes this API catalog as a trial for evaluation and prototyping, with per-model rate limits.
findings.relevance: Fine for trying Nemotron. Not a production endpoint.
findings.correction: The API reference shows https://integrate.api.nvidia.com/v1/chat/completions, marked 'Compatible with OpenAI'. The FAQ says 'The NVIDIA API catalog is a trial experience ... designed to serve evaluation and prototyping needs only' and 'The rate of requests will vary per model'. NVIDIA publishes no fixed rate-limit numbers.

findings.claim: The NVIDIA API Trial Terms (v. 2025-09-19) forbid submitting confidential information and forbid production use. They also say NVIDIA collects User Content and Generated Content 'to improve NVIDIA products and services, including AI models', and logs usage for security and abuse monitoring.
findings.relevance: Critical: do not send proprietary source code to build.nvidia.com. I found no zero-data-retention option for NVIDIA-hosted trial endpoints.
findings.correction: Checked by reading the PDF text directly (it ends 'v. September 19, 2025'). Sec 1.2 grants access 'for limited trial purposes only and without use of the API Service or Generated Content in production'. Sec 2.6(a) says you will not 'include any confidential information'. Sec 3.3(iv) covers 'User Content and Generated Content to improve NVIDIA products and services, including AI models', and usage is 'logged for security, fraud or abuse monitoring'. Sec 4.10 also bans security testing of the API Service itself without written authorization. No independent secondary source; the primary document is authoritative.

findings.claim: Self-hosting: open weights can be served with vLLM, SGLang or TRT-LLM behind an OpenAI-compatible API. The Nemotron 3 model cards give recipes, and the download is governed only by the model license. A NIM container is instead governed by the NVIDIA Software License Agreement.
findings.relevance: Self-hosting is the only Nemotron path confirmed here that keeps source code fully on your own infrastructure.
findings.correction: Confirmed: the cards give vLLM, SGLang and TRT-LLM recipes plus OpenAI-compatible client examples, and say 'Use of this model is governed by the [model license]'. The NGC page for the Lightning NIM says the container is governed by 'the NVIDIA Software License Agreement and the Product-Specific Terms for AI Products', so the SLA is not the only term. The word 'only' for the weight download is my inference; no source states it. The NIM terms were checked for the Lightning NIM, not the Super NIM.

findings.claim: Downloadable NIM containers may be self-hosted free for research, development and test on up to 16 GPUs through the NVIDIA Developer Program. NVIDIA defines anything beyond that as production, which requires an NVIDIA AI Enterprise license.
findings.relevance: Affects whether the toolkit should ship NIM containers or plain vLLM/SGLang deployments.
findings.correction: The free license covers 'research, application development, and experimentation on up to 16 GPUs', and production requires NVIDIA AI Enterprise (from about $4,500 per GPU per year). The claim is wrong on one point: NVIDIA defines production by purpose, not GPU count. Production is 'any use of NIM for purposes other than development, testing, research or evaluation ... including activity serving real end-users'. Using more than 16 GPUs is outside the free license, but NVIDIA does not call that production.

findings.claim: Hardware for self-hosting: Nano 30B-A3B runs on a single A100/H100-class GPU (the card also lists RTX PRO 6000 96GB and DGX Spark). Super BF16 needs at least 8x H100-80GB. Ultra needs 8x B200/H200 or 16x H100.
findings.relevance: For a typical developer, self-hosting Super or Ultra is not practical. Nano or Lightning is the realistic local option.
findings.correction: The Nano recipe uses --tensor-parallel-size 1, and the card lists testing on A100 80GB, H100 80GB, B200, RTX PRO 6000 96GB, Jetson Thor and DGX Spark. The Ultra card's minimum is '8x GB200/B200/GB300/B300, 16x H100, 8x H200'. All sources are NVIDIA's own cards; no independent benchmark found.

findings.claim: Tool calling: Nemotron 3 and 3.5 models support it through vLLM/SGLang with --enable-auto-tool-choice --tool-call-parser qwen3_coder. Nano 2 uses a 'nemotron_json' parser and Llama-Nemotron uses 'llama_nemotron_json'; both parsers ship in the Hugging Face repos.
findings.relevance: The harness must configure the right parser per model, or tool calls come back as plain text.
findings.correction: Minor: --enable-auto-tool-choice is a vLLM flag. The SGLang recipe on the Super card uses only --tool-call-parser qwen3_coder, with reasoning parser nemotron_3 (vLLM uses nemotron_v3). Nano 2 loads nemotron_toolcall_parser_no_streaming.py through --tool-parser-plugin. Llama-Nemotron uses llama_nemotron_toolcall_parser_no_streaming.py.

findings.claim: In NIM 2.x containers, Nemotron 3 tool calling is turned on with NIM_PASSTHROUGH_ARGS="--reasoning-parser nemotron_v3 --enable-auto-tool-choice --tool-call-parser qwen3_coder". NIM does not connect to MCP servers itself; the client converts MCP tools into the OpenAI tools array.
findings.relevance: MCP tool bridging must live in the commander harness, not in the model server.
findings.correction: The exact NIM_PASSTHROUGH_ARGS string is documented only in the NIM 2.0.10 get-started guide for Nemotron 3.5 Lightning. I found no NIM 2.x page that documents it for Nemotron 3 Nano, Super or Ultra (the guessed get-started URLs return 404), so treat it as confirmed for 3.5 Lightning only. The MCP statement is confirmed verbatim: 'NIM LLM and VLM does not connect to MCP servers directly ... converts tool definitions to the OpenAI tools format'.

findings.claim: Reasoning control: Nemotron 3 switches reasoning on or off with a chat-template flag (enable_thinking=True/False) and has a low- or medium-effort mode. Nano 2 uses /think and /no_think system prompts plus budget control.
findings.relevance: Useful for cost and latency tuning per agent. Reasoning tokens share the max_tokens budget with the answer.
findings.correction: enable_thinking is confirmed. The Super card documents only a 'low_effort': True chat-template flag; no 'medium' effort mode was found. The Nano 3 card documents enable_thinking plus a reasoning_budget token threshold and does not mention low_effort. The Nano 2 part (/think, /no_think, thinking-token budget) is confirmed.

findings.claim: Structured output on NIM: 1.x supports guided_json, guided_regex, guided_choice and guided_grammar (via nvext) on an xgrammar backend. NVIDIA recommends guided_json over response_format json_object because json_object accepts any valid JSON, including an empty object.
findings.relevance: Use schema-constrained decoding, not plain JSON mode, for machine-readable findings.
findings.correction: The four guided_* parameters, the xgrammar default (falling back to outlines) and the json_object warning are confirmed. The 'via nvext' part is not: the 1.14.0 page never mentions nvext and passes the parameters directly, as in extra_body={"guided_json": json_schema}.

findings.claim: Structured output on NIM 2.x and vLLM: requests can use OpenAI-style response_format {type: json_schema} or guided_json. vLLM has deprecated guided_* in favour of a structured_outputs parameter (since v0.12.0), and NIM 2.0.12 has a known HTTP 500 for guided decoding with codestral.
findings.relevance: Parameter names differ between NIM/vLLM versions, so the harness should abstract them and validate outputs on the client side.
findings.correction: Correction: vLLM docs say the guided_* fields 'were removed in v0.12.0', not deprecated from v0.12.0. Use {"structured_outputs": {"json": ...}} or response_format json_schema. The NIM issue is confirmed but narrower: with codestral on the model-free NIM, structured requests to the text /v1/completions endpoint return HTTP 500, whether they use response_format or guided_json. It has been present since 2.0.10. The NIM 2.x structured-generation page returns 404, so NIM 2.x support rests only on the release note.

findings.claim: The Nemotron 3 and 3.5 model cards say the models were trained on tool-calling and structured-output data, including RL environments for structured output.
findings.relevance: Suggests good JSON reliability. Still enforce the schema through decoding or validation.
findings.correction: The Lightning card lists 'Tool Calling Data' (26.2B tokens) and 'Synthetic Structured Outputs', with RL covering 'multi-step tool use ... and structured output environments'. The Nano card also mentions 'structured output environments'. Being trained for it does not guarantee schema compliance, so use constrained decoding and validate outputs.

findings.claim: LiteLLM confirms an nvidia_nim provider: the model prefix is nvidia_nim/<model>, with NVIDIA_NIM_API_KEY and optional NVIDIA_NIM_API_BASE (default https://integrate.api.nvidia.com/v1/). It covers chat/completions, completions, responses, embeddings and rerank.
findings.relevance: One gateway can route Claude, OpenAI and Nemotron agents.
findings.correction: Rerank uses a different default base, https://ai.api.nvidia.com/v1/.

findings.claim: LiteLLM's NvidiaNimConfig passes tools, tool_choice, parallel_tool_calls and response_format through for most models. Its model list was last updated in July 2024, and LiteLLM's JSON-schema docs do not list nvidia_nim as having native schema support.
findings.relevance: Treat structured output via nvidia_nim as best-effort passthrough. Turn on litellm.enable_json_schema_validation or validate yourself.
findings.correction: The code comment reads 'Updated on July 5th, 2024 - based on https://docs.api.nvidia.com/nim/reference'. Special-cased with reduced parameter lists: Gemma, CodeGemma, and nemotron-4-340b-instruct/reward. The json_mode page lists OpenAI, Azure, xAI, Gemini, Vertex, Bedrock, Anthropic, Groq, Ollama and Databricks, but not NVIDIA NIM.

findings.claim: For self-hosted vLLM servers (for example local Nemotron), LiteLLM uses the hosted_vllm/<model> prefix with a required api_base. Tools and response_format are passed through unchanged.
findings.relevance: This is how to route source code to a Nemotron that never leaves your infrastructure. The passthrough statement comes from a model summary of the page, not a direct quote.
findings.correction: The prefix and the api_base requirement are correct; api_base can also come from the HOSTED_VLLM_API_BASE env var. Tools are not passed through unchanged. HostedVLLMChatConfig.map_openai_params runs _remove_additional_properties and _remove_strict_from_schema on tools and converts custom tools into function tools. response_format has no special handling and appears to pass through. Strict tool schemas (additionalProperties:false, strict:true) are therefore stripped before reaching vLLM.

findings.claim: Current Claude models (2026-09-23): Claude Fable 5.1 (claude-fable-5-1), Claude Opus 5.5 (claude-opus-5-5) and Claude Sonnet 5 (claude-sonnet-5) have 1M context and 128K max output. Claude Haiku 4.5 (claude-haiku-4-5-20251001) has 200K context and 64K output.
findings.relevance: Model IDs and limits for the Claude-backed agents.
findings.correction: Confirmed on Anthropic's models overview; no independent third-party source checked. Max output is the synchronous Messages API limit. On the Batch API, Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5 support up to 300K output with the output-300k-2026-03-24 beta header.

findings.claim: Claude structured outputs are generally available: output_config.format with type json_schema, plus strict tool use (strict: true). The old output_format field and structured-outputs-2025-11-13 beta header are still accepted during a transition period.
findings.relevance: Gives schema-guaranteed findings and test-case objects from Claude agents.
findings.correction: GA on the Claude API, Claude Platform on AWS, Bedrock, Google Cloud and Foundry. Python SDK v1.0+ no longer accepts output_format= on beta.messages.create; use output_config. Checked only on Anthropic docs.

findings.claim: Claude's schema subset does not support recursive schemas, numeric constraints (minimum/maximum) or string length constraints, and array minItems is limited to 0 or 1. Compiled grammars are cached for 24 hours after last use.
findings.relevance: A shared findings schema must use the common subset that every provider accepts.
findings.correction: multipleOf, complex enum types and external $ref are also unsupported. The data-retention page independently confirms the 24-hour schema cache.

findings.claim: Claude Opus 5.5 rejects forced tool_choice ({type: any} or {type: tool}) with a 400 error. Anthropic's guidance is to use tool_choice auto with strict tool use or structured outputs.
findings.relevance: A LiteLLM harness that forces tool calls must handle this per model.
findings.correction: The guide quotes the error 'tool_choice: type "tool" and "any" are not supported for this model.' It applies to the token-counting endpoint as well. {type: none} is allowed. With strict: true, every object must set additionalProperties: false.

findings.claim: Anthropic default retention: inputs and outputs are deleted from the backend within 30 days (policy updated 2026-07-01). Content flagged for Usage Policy violations may be kept up to 2 years, and API data is not used for training without express permission.
findings.relevance: This is the baseline exposure for source code sent to Claude.
findings.correction: Trust-and-safety classification scores are kept up to 7 years and feedback submissions 5 years. Exceptions include the Files API, Covered Models and legal holds. Both sources are Anthropic's own.

findings.claim: Anthropic zero data retention (ZDR) is set up per organization through sales. It covers the Messages and Token Counting APIs for eligible features. Not covered: Batch API (29-day retention), Files API, code execution, Managed Agents and Console usage. Structured outputs is only 'Yes (qualified)' because the JSON schema is cached up to 24 hours.
findings.relevance: To keep the ZDR guarantee, send code only through /v1/messages, keep secrets out of schemas, and avoid Batch and Files.
findings.correction: Under ZDR the API does not block ineligible features; using one moves that data outside ZDR. Programmatic tool calling, MCP tunnels, consumer apps and CORS are also excluded. Anthropic's own documentation only.

findings.claim: Anthropic 'Covered Models' (Claude Fable 5.1, Mythos 5.1, Fable 5, Mythos 5) require 30-day retention and are not available under ZDR unless Anthropic expressly authorizes it. Organizations set to ZDR get a 400 error from them.
findings.relevance: A ZDR harness should default to Opus 5.5 or Sonnet 5 rather than Fable 5.1.
findings.correction: The doc's example error is 400 invalid_request_error: 'your organization or workspace must have data retention enabled'. A workspace-level Privacy controls override in Console can turn on retention for one workspace so Covered Model requests from it succeed.

findings.claim: On Amazon Bedrock and Google Cloud, the cloud provider (not Anthropic) is the data processor for Claude, and its own retention controls apply.
findings.relevance: An alternative for organizations that already have cloud data agreements.
findings.correction: On Claude Platform on AWS and Microsoft Foundry, Anthropic is the data processor. Bedrock and Google Cloud documentation were not checked separately.

findings.claim: Current OpenAI flagship models: GPT-6 Astra (released 2026-09-03) and GPT-6 Sol and Luna (released 2026-09-22). Astra and Sol have a 1,050,000-token context and 128K max output, work with Chat Completions, Responses and Batch, and support function calling and structured outputs.
findings.relevance: Model IDs for the GPT-backed agents.
findings.correction: Dates, 1,050,000 context, 128,000 output and support for all three endpoints are confirmed. Function calling is restricted by endpoint. The changelog says Astra 'Tool calling requires the Responses API', so no tools on Chat Completions. Sol's page says 'Chat Completions supports function calling only with reasoning_effort set to none'. Astra also lacks the 'none' reasoning effort, custom temperature/top_p and logprobs. Luna's specs were not checked; OpenAI sources only.

findings.claim: OpenAI Structured Outputs: Chat Completions uses response_format {type: json_schema, strict: true}; the Responses API uses text.format. Schemas need additionalProperties: false and every field listed as required. Safety refusals come back in a separate refusal field.
findings.relevance: OpenAI's schema rules are stricter than the others, so design the shared findings schema to satisfy them.
findings.correction: Microsoft Learn independently confirms it (Azure OpenAI; message.refusal and a refusal content item in Responses). Optional fields are emulated with a null union type.

findings.claim: OpenAI data handling, part 1: API data is not used for training unless you opt in. Abuse-monitoring logs, which can contain prompts and responses, are kept up to 30 days by default. Zero Data Retention and Modified Abuse Monitoring both require prior approval.
findings.relevance: This is the baseline exposure for source code sent to OpenAI.
findings.correction: Logs can be kept longer if the law requires it or it is 'reasonably necessary to protect our services'. Checked by reading the page HTML directly; OpenAI source only.

findings.claim: OpenAI data handling, part 2: the Responses API keeps application state for 30 days by default or when store=true; ZDR forces store=false. Background mode writes to disk for about 10 minutes, and prompt caching can hold KV tensors on GPU-local storage for up to 24 hours.
findings.relevance: Without ZDR, the harness should still set store=false and avoid background mode for code-review calls.
findings.correction: The page says response data is stored for 'at least 30 days'. ZDR also forces store=false for /v1/chat/completions. Cache TTL controls differ by model family (for example, prompt_cache_options.ttl for GPT-5.6 and later).

findings.claim: OpenAI endpoints that are not ZDR-eligible include files, batches, vector_stores, assistants/threads, conversations, agents, evals and fine-tuning. OpenAI also says it may make specific models ineligible for ZDR for specific customers, with advance written notice.
findings.relevance: Keep a ZDR-compatible pipeline on /v1/chat/completions or /v1/responses only.
findings.correction: /v1/chatkit/threads and /v1/videos are also not eligible. Quote: 'we reserve the right to make models ineligible for Zero Data Retention or Modified Abuse Monitoring for specific customers, as notified in advance to the impacted customers in writing'. Content is then kept in encrypted abuse logs.

findings.claim: OpenAI classifies structured-output schemas as 'system data' rather than Customer Content, and says system data may be stored outside the selected data-residency region.
findings.relevance: As with Claude, never put code, secrets or customer identifiers in JSON schemas.
findings.correction: Quote: 'Data residency does not apply to system data, which may be processed and stored outside the selected region. System data means ... data that do not contain Customer Content ... and structured output schema.' Keep secrets and sensitive details out of schemas.

findings.claim: OpenAI's open-weight gpt-oss-120b is Apache-2.0 licensed and supports function calling and Structured Outputs. It gives a self-hosted OpenAI-family option.
findings.relevance: Adds model diversity without sending code to an outside provider.
findings.correction: Both sources say 'Permissive Apache 2.0 license' and list native function calling and Structured Outputs. A usage policy file also applies. It fits on a single 80GB GPU with MXFP4. Structured Outputs on a self-hosted server depends on the serving engine's constrained decoding.

findings.claim: NVIDIA announced NeMo Switchyard, an open-source library that routes each step of an agent workflow to a suitable model.
findings.relevance: A possible reference for the commander's model routing. I have not checked its repository or maturity.
findings.correction: The GitHub repo exists under Apache-2.0 (about 3.2k stars) and routes each LLM call or request. It ships as a NeMo Relay plugin, an embedded library, or a standalone proxy compatible with the OpenAI and Anthropic APIs. It is pre-1.0 (core Beta, other parts Alpha/Demo), so APIs may change. Announced August 11, 2026.

findings.claim: vLLM (vllm-project/vllm) and SGLang (sgl-project/sglang) are both Apache-2.0-licensed according to the GitHub license API.
findings.relevance: Inference-engine licenses are separate from model-weight licenses.
findings.correction: No correction.

findings.claim: NVIDIA's NIM FAQ says NVIDIA Developer Program members may use self-hosted NIM for research, application development and experimentation on up to 16 GPUs. It defines production use as any use of NIM for purposes other than development, testing, research or evaluation, and says production use requires an NVIDIA AI Enterprise license.
findings.relevance: Whether operating the toolkit on customer engagements counts as 'testing' or 'production' is a legal question. Quotes are from a summarizer.
findings.correction: No correction. (The full definition adds 'such as conducting business transactions and any non-testing activity including activity serving real end-users'.)

findings.claim: The NVIDIA API Trial Terms of Service (v. September 19, 2025) limit access to trial purposes without production use (s.1.2), limit use without a paid subscription to internal testing and evaluation (s.1.4), forbid submitting confidential information or controlled or sensitive data (s.2.6(a)), and forbid security testing of the API Service (probe, scan or vulnerability test) unless NVIDIA authorizes it in writing (s.4.10).
findings.relevance: Confirms that hosted Nemotron is limited to evaluation and non-confidential code.
findings.correction: No correction. (s.2.6(a) also lists PHI, personal data, PCI information and sensitive human-subject research data.)

findings.claim: The NVIDIA API Trial Terms (v. September 19, 2025) say in s.2.3 that NVIDIA will not store or use User Content or Generated Content at the end of each session except as described in s.2.4, while s.3.3 says NVIDIA collects User Content and Generated Content to improve NVIDIA products and services, including AI models, and logs usage for security, fraud or abuse monitoring shared with third-party service providers. The terms offer no zero-data-retention option.
findings.relevance: The hosted trial API has no ZDR path and the terms are internally inconsistent on retention, so it cannot receive class-C data.
findings.correction: No correction. (s.3.3 says the collection is done 'without identifying specific users'. s.2.4 lets NVIDIA keep User Content for 30 days and Fine Tuning Generated Content for 90 days on some services. The terms never mention zero data retention.)

findings.claim: Anthropic's Commercial Terms of Service state that the customer retains all rights to its Inputs and owns its Outputs, incorporate the Usage Policy by reference, and bar using the Services to build a competing product or train competing AI models. No explicit clause on security testing or red teaming was found.
findings.relevance: Ownership of generated tests and reports, plus the Usage Policy's governing role.
findings.correction: No correction.

findings.claim: Anthropic's Usage Policy, under 'Do Not Compromise Computer or Network Systems', prohibits using Claude to discover or exploit vulnerabilities in systems, networks or applications without authorization of the system owner, to create malware, or to bypass security controls.
findings.relevance: System-owner authorization (ROE/ownership proof) is the policy's own condition for vulnerability work.
findings.correction: No correction.

findings.claim: The OpenAI Services Agreement (effective 2026-01-01; read via the r.jina.ai proxy because openai.com returned 403) states that the customer owns all Output and incorporates the OpenAI Policies. The OpenAI Usage Policies prohibit compromising or breaching another's system, including malicious or abusive cyber activity. No explicit security-testing permission clause was found.
findings.relevance: Same pattern as Anthropic. Must be checked directly on openai.com.
findings.correction: No correction. (Confirmed: openai.com returns 403 to direct fetch. The Services Agreement reads 'Effective: January 1, 2026'. Section 4.1 says the customer 'owns all Output', and Section 16.1 incorporates the OpenAI Policies. The Usage Policies prohibit 'compromise, or breach of another's system or property, including malicious or abusive cyber activity'.)

findings.claim: OpenAI's model catalog lists API model IDs gpt-6-astra, gpt-6-sol and gpt-6-luna, each with a 1.05M-token context window and 128K max output. The changelog records GPT-6 Astra on 2026-09-03 and GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna on 2026-09-22.
findings.relevance: Exact model IDs for models.yaml. Confirms the release dates in providers-31.
findings.correction: No correction.

findings.claim: The gpt-6-sol and gpt-6-luna model pages both list function calling and structured outputs on Chat Completions and Responses, and both state: 'Chat Completions supports function calling only with reasoning_effort set to none.' The gpt-6-sol page lists 1,050,000 context, 922,000 max input and 128,000 max output tokens.
findings.relevance: Luna has the same Chat Completions tool-calling restriction as Sol, which the docs did not state.
findings.correction: Confirmed: both pages list Function calling and Structured outputs as Supported, list the Chat Completions and Responses endpoints, and contain the exact sentence 'Chat Completions supports function calling only with reasoning_effort set to none.' The gpt-6-sol page shows '1,050,000 context window' and '128,000 max output tokens'. The '922,000 max input tokens' figure was NOT found on the gpt-6-sol page, either in the rendered text or in the raw HTML. Treat it as unconfirmed.

findings.claim: OpenAI's 'your data' guide lists gpt-6-astra, gpt-6-sol and gpt-6-luna in its data-residency tables. Its only GPT-6-specific caveat found was that for GPT-6 Sol and Luna, EU data residency is available only with Standard processing. No statement excluding GPT-6 models from ZDR was found. Endpoints listed as not ZDR-eligible include /v1/conversations, /v1/assistants, /v1/threads, /v1/vector_stores, /v1/files, /v1/batches and /v1/evals.
findings.relevance: GPT-6 ZDR eligibility is still not affirmatively documented per model, so a contract confirmation is still needed.
findings.correction: No correction. (Note: the guide has a general clause letting OpenAI make models ineligible for ZDR/MAM for specific customers with advance written notice. This clause is not GPT-6-specific.)

findings.claim: As of 2026-09-24, Anthropic's models overview lists the current models Claude Fable 5.1 (claude-fable-5-1), Opus 5.5 (claude-opus-5-5), Sonnet 5 (claude-sonnet-5) and Haiku 4.5 (claude-haiku-4-5-20251001, alias claude-haiku-4-5), with retirement not sooner than 2027-09-01, 2027-09-22, 2027-06-30 and 2026-10-15 respectively.
findings.relevance: Haiku 4.5's earliest retirement date is weeks away, so example configs using it need a replacement plan.
findings.correction: No correction.

findings.claim: The model list at integrate.api.nvidia.com/v1/models (2026-09-24) includes nvidia/nemotron-nano-3-30b-a3b, nvidia/nemotron-3-super-120b-a12b, nvidia/nemotron-3-ultra-550b-a55b, nvidia/nemotron-3.5-lightning-30b-a3b, nvidia/nemotron-3-nano-omni-30b-a3b-reasoning, nvidia/nemotron-3.5-content-safety and nvidia/nemotron-3-embed-1b.
findings.relevance: Exact hosted model IDs. Note that the Nano ID ordering (nemotron-nano-3) differs from the others.
findings.correction: No correction.

findings.claim: build.nvidia.com model pages list Nemotron-3-Super-120B-A12B (2026-03-11, NVIDIA Nemotron Open Model License), Nemotron-3-Ultra-550B-A55B (2026-06-04, OpenMDW-1.1) and Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B (2026-08-11, OpenMDW-1.1), with hosted use governed by the NVIDIA API Trial Terms of Service.
findings.relevance: Confirms the current Nemotron line-up and that hosted access remains under trial terms.
findings.correction: No correction.

findings.claim: As of 2026-09-25, Anthropic documents Claude Opus 4.8 with Claude API model ID claude-opus-4-8, released 2026-05-28, status Active (legacy; Claude Opus 5.5 is the current Opus model), tentative retirement not sooner than 2027-05-28, 1M-token context window, 128K max output, adaptive thinking, and base pricing of $5 input / $25 output per million tokens (Claude Haiku 4.5: $1 / $5, 200K context).
findings.relevance: U-11 replacement for claude_haiku (Claude Haiku 4.5, earliest retirement 2026-10-15) in models.yaml
findings.correction: Vendor documentation only (three separate Anthropic pages agree on ID, status, retirement date and pricing); retirement is a 'not sooner than' commitment for Anthropic-operated platforms, Bedrock and Google Cloud set their own dates.

limitations: I found no zero-data-retention or data-processing agreement for NVIDIA-hosted endpoints (build.nvidia.com or partner serverless NIM). Third-party hosts of Nemotron (OpenRouter, Together, Fireworks, etc.) have their own policies, which I did not review.

The Trial Terms say NVIDIA does not store content after a session (2.3) but also collects User Content to improve products (3.3). I report both clauses as written; how they interact in practice is unconfirmed.

Anthropic's two pages phrase default retention differently. The privacy article says inputs and outputs are deleted within 30 days. The API retention doc says conversation content is not retained by default, except for Covered Models. I could not reconcile this exactly.

I could not confirm whether GPT-6 Astra, Sol or Luna carry model-specific ZDR restrictions like Anthropic's Covered Models. OpenAI only reserves the right to make models ineligible for specific customers.
I did not check that build.nvidia.com's hosted Nemotron endpoints accept response_format json_schema or guided_json. Structured-output support is confirmed only for self-hosted NIM and vLLM.

LiteLLM's nvidia_nim parameter list was last updated in July 2024 and I did not test it live. That the tools and response_format passthrough works with Nemotron 3 models on NIM is inferred from source code, not tested end to end.
Nemotron 3 Super and Ultra are not in the LiteLLM json_mode support list. Schema reliability for Nemotron has no independent benchmark here.
The OpenMDW summary was produced by a fetch tool, not a full legal reading. Have legal review all licenses before commercial distribution.
Model availability and names change fast (for example, Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Sol/Luna launched on 2026-09-22). Check model IDs again before implementation.
Hardware sizing comes from vendor model cards. I did not benchmark it.

findings.claim: Kim et al. (ICML 2025) tested more than 350 LLMs and found substantial error correlation. On one leaderboard dataset, two models agree 60% of the time when both are wrong, and larger, more accurate models have highly correlated errors even when their architectures and providers differ.
findings.relevance: This directly undercuts the assumption that routing agents to different vendors (Claude, ChatGPT, Nemotron) gives independent errors. Strong frontier models are the ones most likely to share blind spots.
findings.correction: No correction. The arXiv and PMLR abstracts match word for word, and OpenReview lists the paper as an ICML 2025 poster.

findings.claim: In the same paper's LLM-as-judge experiment, a judge inflates the accuracy of models less accurate than itself and of models from its own provider. The data were MMLU multiple-choice questions (HELM with 71 models, Hugging Face Open LLM Leaderboard with 349). The authors did not test training-data overlap as a cause, and they list open-ended and complex reasoning tasks as future work.
findings.relevance: The strongest correlated-error evidence comes from multiple-choice QA, not code review or security. Claims that it transfers to code review should be marked as extrapolation. So should the claim that 'shared training data causes shared blind spots', which this paper does not test.
findings.correction: Small nuance: the paper says judges inflate less-accurate models 'especially models from the same provider or family', so same-provider inflation is a stronger case of the same effect, not a separate one. Judges also deflate models more accurate than themselves. The regression uses provider, architecture and size as covariates, and I found no test of training-data overlap. The future-work sentence is quoted exactly ('Richer evaluation of open-ended generation and complex reasoning tasks remains an important direction for future work'). The counts are 349 models on 12,032 questions and 71 models on 14,042 questions.

findings.claim: Goel et al. propose CAPA, a chance-adjusted similarity metric built on overlap in model mistakes. They show that LLM-as-a-judge scores favor models similar to the judge, and that model mistakes become more similar as capability increases.
findings.relevance: This supports a design step: measure pairwise error similarity (for example CAPA or kappa) between candidate reviewer models on a labeled calibration set before assuming diversity. Venue: arXiv, listed by ML Anthology as an ICLR 2025 workshop paper; main-conference acceptance not confirmed.
findings.correction: No correction on content. On venue: OpenReview lists the main version as an ICML 2025 spotlight poster, plus an ICLR 2025 SSI-FM workshop poster, which is the version the mlanthology link points to.

findings.claim: Zheng et al. (NeurIPS 2023, MT-Bench/Chatbot Arena) documented position, verbosity and self-enhancement biases in LLM judges. They reported that GPT-4 favors its own answers by about a 10% higher win rate.
findings.relevance: This is the baseline evidence that one model reviewing its own (or its family's) generated code is biased. The 10% figure came from a search summary and was not re-read in the full text.
findings.correction: The venue (NeurIPS 2023 Datasets and Benchmarks Track), the three bias types and the figure 'GPT-4 favors itself with a 10% higher win rate' are all confirmed (Claude-v1 was 25%). However, the authors hedge on self-enhancement: 'Due to limited data and small differences, our study cannot determine whether the models exhibit a self-enhancement bias.' Present the 10% as a tentative observation, not an established finding.

findings.claim: Panickssery, Bowman and Feng (NeurIPS 2024 oral) found that GPT-4 and Llama 2 can recognize their own outputs well above chance. Through fine-tuning, they found a linear correlation between self-recognition and the strength of self-preference bias.
findings.relevance: This supports a rule that the model that generated the vibe-coded app, or its family, should not be the sole reviewer or judge of that code.
findings.correction: No correction. The NeurIPS virtual site lists it as a 2024 Oral, and the proceedings abstract matches arXiv.

findings.claim: Wataoka et al. (NeurIPS 2024 SafeGenAI workshop) found that LLM judges give higher scores to lower-perplexity (more 'familiar') text than humans do, whether or not the judge wrote it. They conclude that self-preference is rooted in familiarity.
findings.relevance: Switching the judge to another vendor may not remove bias if that vendor's model also finds typical AI-generated code 'familiar'. Cross-vendor judging is a mitigation, not a cure.
findings.correction: No correction. The abstract says: 'LLMs assign significantly higher evaluations to outputs with lower perplexity than human evaluators, regardless of whether the outputs were self-generated.' OpenReview lists it as a NeurIPS 2024 SafeGenAi workshop poster. OpenReview also shows it was rejected at ICLR 2025, so the only peer-reviewed venue is the workshop.

findings.claim: Chen et al. tested verifiable tasks (math, factual knowledge, code generation) across 7 model families. Much of stronger models' self-preference is legitimate, because their outputs really are better. Harmful self-preference persists when the judge was wrong as a generator, and long chain-of-thought before judging reduces it.
findings.relevance: The bias is concentrated on the cases that matter, where the generator made a mistake. Requiring reasoning before a verdict is an evidence-backed mitigation. This is an arXiv preprint (v3, Dec 2025).
findings.correction: No correction on content, which the abstract states verbatim. Note it has no peer-reviewed venue: OpenReview shows it as a rejected ICLR 2026 submission. The latest version also adds that stronger models show more pronounced harmful self-preference when they do err.

findings.claim: Pombal, Rei and Martins (2026) found self-preference even with objectively verifiable rubrics (IFEval, LiveCodeBench): on rubrics a generator failed, judges were more than 50% more likely to wrongly mark them satisfied when the output was their own. Ensembling multiple judges mitigates this but does not eliminate it.
findings.relevance: This is the most direct evidence that a multi-vendor judge ensemble reduces but does not remove self-preference on code-like objective checks. It is an arXiv preprint and not yet peer-reviewed.
findings.correction: No correction. OpenReview lists the paper as accepted at COLM 2026. It also reports that on HealthBench (subjective rubrics) self-preference skews scores by up to 10 points.

findings.claim: Verga et al. (PoLL) found that a panel of smaller models from disjoint families beat a single GPT-4 judge on agreement with humans across 3 judge settings and 6 datasets. The panel showed less intra-model bias and cost more than 7x less.
findings.relevance: This is the main positive evidence for a cross-family judge panel. It evaluated QA and chat tasks, not code or security review, so transfer to code is unverified.
findings.correction: No correction on content. The panel was three models (Command R, Claude Haiku, GPT-3.5), measured by Cohen's kappa against human judgments. The cost figure is 'seven to eight times less expensive' than a GPT-4 Turbo judge. I could not open the given OpenReview forum (6AjeDjlg3d) because of a bot challenge, so I could not confirm a peer-reviewed venue.

findings.claim: Moon et al. (EACL 2026 Findings) defined six superficial-variation biases in LLM code judges, such as variable names, comments and formatting. Across five programming languages, every judge they tested showed both inflated and unfairly low scores, even when prompted to write test cases before scoring.
findings.relevance: Vibe-coded code often carries confident comments. LLM reviewers can be swayed by surface cues, so verdicts should be backed by execution, tests or static analysis, not by LLM opinion alone.
findings.correction: No correction. The ACL Anthology lists the paper as 2026.findings-eacl.70, and the abstract matches the claim.

findings.claim: CodeJudgeBench benchmarked 26 LLM judges on code generation, code repair and unit-test generation. Thinking models did better, but all models showed significant randomness, and changing the order of responses substantially changed accuracy. Pairwise comparison beat pointwise scoring.
