findings.relevance: This supports order randomization (swap-and-repeat) and pairwise prompting in the review harness. The 'up to 11%' order effect came from a secondary summary and was not re-read in the full text.
findings.correction: No correction on content, which the abstract states verbatim. Only arXiv/dblp records were found; I found no peer-reviewed venue.

findings.claim: Wang et al. (ACL 2024) showed that with ChatGPT as judge, just reordering candidates let Vicuna-13B beat ChatGPT on 66 of 80 queries. They proposed balanced position calibration and human-in-the-loop escalation driven by a 'position diversity entropy' disagreement signal.
findings.relevance: This is peer-reviewed precedent for triage by disagreement: cases where verdicts flip under permutation go to humans.
findings.correction: No correction. The paper also proposes a third method, Multiple Evidence Calibration. The human-in-the-loop method uses a 'balanced position diversity entropy' to measure how hard each example is.

findings.claim: CALM (ICLR 2025) defines 12 types of LLM-as-a-judge bias and reports that significant biases persist in advanced models on certain tasks.
findings.relevance: This gives a checklist of judge biases to test the harness against: position, verbosity, authority, sentiment and others.
findings.correction: No correction. The abstract says '12 key potential biases' and 'significant biases persist in certain specific tasks'.

findings.claim: Du et al. (ICML 2024) reported that multi-round debate among LLM instances improved math and strategic reasoning and reduced hallucinations compared with single-agent baselines.
findings.relevance: This is the original positive evidence for debate. Later work shows that much of the gain comes from voting over several initial answers.
findings.correction: No correction. The ICML 2024 poster page and the official code repository both exist and match.

findings.claim: Smit et al. (ICML 2024) found that multi-agent debate in its current form does not reliably beat simpler strategies like self-consistency and ensembling over multiple reasoning paths. Some debate systems only did better after hyperparameter tuning.
findings.relevance: Debate costs many more tokens. A commander design should use independent sampling plus voting as the default and treat debate as optional.
findings.correction: No correction. PMLR 235:45883-45905. With tuning, Multi-Persona did better, and changing agreement thresholds improved results.

findings.claim: Choi, Zhu and Li (NeurIPS 2025 spotlight) split debate into majority voting and inter-agent discussion across seven NLP benchmarks. Majority voting alone accounts for most of the gains attributed to debate, and they prove that debate on its own is a martingale that does not raise expected correctness. Interventions that bias belief updates toward correction do help.
findings.relevance: This is the strongest evidence that 'let the agents argue until consensus' adds little beyond independent voting. If discussion is used, it needs correction-oriented rules, such as requiring concrete evidence to change a verdict.
findings.correction: No correction. OpenReview lists it as a NeurIPS 2025 spotlight.

findings.claim: Zhang et al. evaluated 5 debate methods on 9 benchmarks with 4 base models and found debate often fails to beat chain-of-thought or self-consistency despite far more compute. Making the debating models heterogeneous consistently improved the debate frameworks.
findings.relevance: This supports mixing model vendors if debate is used at all. It is a position paper on arXiv, and the benchmarks are reasoning and QA, not code security.
findings.correction: No correction on content. Note this is a position paper, and OpenReview shows it was rejected from the NeurIPS 2025 Position Paper Track. The word 'consistently' is the authors' own ('a universal antidote to consistently improve').

findings.claim: ReConcile (ACL 2024) runs round-table discussion among different LLMs with confidence-weighted voting, and its authors state that diversity from different models is critical to its performance. A single-author preprint (Hegazy 2024) reported that a mix of Gemini-Pro, Mixtral and PaLM 2-M reached 91% on GSM-8K, versus 82% for three Gemini-Pro instances.
findings.relevance: There is positive evidence that heterogeneous models help collaborative reasoning, but only on math and commonsense reasoning. The Hegazy result deserves low weight: one author, a minor venue, and older models.
findings.correction: ReConcile is confirmed: ACL 2024 (2024.acl-long.381), confidence-weighted voting, and 'the diversity originating from different models is critical'. The Hegazy numbers are correct (91% after 4 debate rounds vs 82%). But calling it a 'preprint' is not quite accurate: arXiv lists a journal reference, Journal of Robotics and Automation Research (JRAR) Vol. 5 Issue 3, Oct 2024. It is a single-author paper in a small journal, not a major peer-reviewed ML venue.

findings.claim: Li et al. ('Rethinking Mixture-of-Agents') found that mixing different LLMs often lowers average quality. Aggregating several outputs from only the single best model (Self-MoA) beat mixed MoA by 6.6% on AlpacaEval 2.0 and by 3.8% on average across MMLU, CRUX and MATH.
findings.relevance: This is direct counter-evidence to 'more vendors is always better'. Adding a noticeably weaker model to a panel can hurt, so there is a quality-diversity trade-off to measure per task.
findings.correction: No correction. OpenReview shows 'Accepted by TMLR', and there was an earlier NeurIPS 2024 LanGame workshop poster.

findings.claim: Trad and Chehab (ISPR 2024) compared prompt-based, model-based and hybrid majority voting for phishing URL classification. Ensembles helped only when the members performed at similar levels, and with large performance gaps they did not beat the best single LLM.
findings.relevance: This supports per-agent calibration and weighted (not equal) voting. It is a security classification task, but not code.
findings.correction: The three strategies and the ISPR24 acceptance are confirmed. The claim overstates the authors' hedged wording. They say ensembles are 'most suited' when components perform at equivalent levels (not 'only'), and that with large gaps the ensemble 'may not exceed' the best single LLM or prompt (not 'did not'). I found no independent confirmation.

findings.claim: Wynn, Satija and Hadfield (ICML 2025 MAS workshop) found that debate accuracy can decline over rounds, even when stronger models outnumber weaker ones. Models frequently switch from correct to incorrect answers after reading peers' reasoning, which they attribute to sycophancy and conformity.
findings.relevance: Letting agents see each other's findings before committing can suppress correct minority findings. Agents should commit independent verdicts before any discussion.
findings.correction: The accuracy decline and the correct-to-incorrect switches are confirmed, and the arXiv comment says 'ICML MAS Workshop 2025'. But the authors do not firmly attribute the switches to sycophancy and conformity. They 'investigate various potential contributing factors... including sycophancy, social conformity, and model and task type', find that agents 'may be influenced by social effects', and find large variation by dataset and model. I found no independent venue record.

findings.claim: Wu, Li and Li (2025) ran a controlled study on Knight-Knave-Spy logic puzzles. The underlying reasoning strength and the diversity of the group were the main drivers of debate success; structural knobs like speaking order or confidence visibility added little, and majority pressure suppressed independent correction.
findings.relevance: This backs spending effort on picking strong, diverse agents over elaborate debate protocols. It is an arXiv preprint on logic puzzles.
findings.correction: No correction on content, which the abstract states verbatim. No peer-reviewed venue: OpenReview shows only an ACL ARR May 2026 submission.

findings.claim: Liang et al. (EMNLP 2024) identified 'Degeneration-of-Thought': once confident, a self-reflecting LLM cannot produce new ideas even when its first stance is wrong. They also found that an LLM judge might not be fair when the debating agents are different LLMs.
findings.relevance: Self-review loops by a single agent are weak, and the commander/judge itself is a bias point when it evaluates agents from other vendors.
findings.correction: No correction. The ACL Anthology lists it as EMNLP 2024 main (2024.emnlp-main.992). The abstract says 'LLMs might not be a fair judge if different LLMs are used for agents'.

findings.claim: Huang et al. (ICLR 2024) found that without external feedback, LLMs struggle to correct their own reasoning, and performance sometimes gets worse after self-correction.
findings.relevance: Agents should get external feedback — test runs, SAST results, execution traces — rather than being asked to 're-check' their own review.
findings.correction: No correction.

findings.claim: PrimeVul (ICSE 2025) showed that common vulnerability benchmarks overestimate performance through label errors, duplication and leakage. A 7B model scored 68.26% F1 on BigVul but 3.09% on PrimeVul, and GPT-3.5/GPT-4 were close to random guessing in the strictest settings.
findings.relevance: Ensemble gains reported on Devign, ReVeal or BigVul may not carry over to real code. If every member is near-random, voting cannot recover the signal, so realistic, deduplicated evaluation data is required.
findings.correction: No correction. The ICSE 2025 Research Track page confirms the venue and the figures. The dataset repo is MIT-licensed.

findings.claim: SecLLMHolmes (IEEE S&P 2024) evaluated 8 LLMs on 228 code scenarios and found non-deterministic answers and unfaithful reasoning. Just renaming functions or variables, or adding library functions, gave incorrect answers in 26% of cases for PaLM2 and 17% for GPT-4.
findings.relevance: Single LLM security verdicts are unstable. Repeated sampling and metamorphic re-checks (renaming, reformatting) are justified before a finding is accepted.
findings.correction: Confirmed: 8 LLMs, 228 scenarios, S&P 2024 (the repo README also says so), non-determinism and unfaithful reasoning. The mapping of 26%/17% to specific models is ambiguous. The abstract reads 'by merely changing function or variable names, or by the addition of library functions... these models can yield incorrect answers in 26% and 17% of cases, respectively'. Grammatically, 'respectively' may refer to the two perturbation types rather than to PaLM2 and GPT-4. The body confirms only '17% of cases for GPT-4' across the robustness tests. Safer wording: 'up to 26% and 17% incorrect answers under these perturbations for PaLM2/GPT-4.'

findings.claim: Sun et al. (2025) found that bagging, boosting and stacking over five fine-tuned 6.7B–15B code models significantly improved vulnerability detection on Devign, ReVeal and BigVul, with boosting best on imbalanced data. Their proposed Dynamic Gated Stacking beat plain stacking.
findings.relevance: This is evidence for ensembles, but of trained small models on benchmarks that PrimeVul showed to be leaky. It is not evidence about prompting Claude, ChatGPT or Nemotron as reviewers. arXiv preprint.
findings.correction: No correction. The five models are DeepSeek-Coder-6.7B, CodeLlama-7B, CodeLlama-13B, CodeQwen1.5-7B and StarCoder2-15B, and the repo documents QLoRA fine-tuning. The repo is by the same authors, so it confirms the models and setup but is not an independent check of the results.

findings.claim: Widyasari, Lo and Liao (2024) evaluated GPT-3.5, GPT-4o, LLaMA-3-70B/8B, Gemma-7B and Mixtral-8x7B on fault localization and vulnerability detection. Voting improved results by more than 10% over GPT-3.5, and a cross-validation scheme gave about 4% over the best single LLM.
findings.relevance: This is some direct evidence that heterogeneous LLM voting helps software-QA and vulnerability tasks, though the gain over the best single model is modest. arXiv preprint.
findings.correction: No correction on content, which the abstract states verbatim. The cross-validation gains were 16% (fault localization) and 12% (vulnerability detection) over GPT-3.5, and 4% over the best LLM. The abstract also notes that 'even the lower-performing LLMs provided unique correct predictions'. I found no independent source or venue.

findings.claim: Mao et al.'s multi-role consensus (tester and developer roles discussing to consensus) used gpt-3.5-turbo for every role, and the authors label it a preliminary evaluation. The latest abstract reports +13.48% precision, +18.25% recall and +16.13% F1, with different figures in v1, and about 478% more tokens.
findings.relevance: This is evidence for role diversity within one model, not model diversity, and the result is small and preliminary. The token cost is a real constraint for the commander's budget.
findings.correction: The token figure mixes versions. v1 and v2 say 478% more tokens, but the latest versions (v3/v4, May 2024) say 'a 484% increase in the number of tokens consumed'. v1 reported +4.73% precision, +58.9% recall and +28.1% F1. v4 says all roles are 'instances of the gpt-3.5-turbo-0125 model', and the section is titled 'Preliminary Evaluation'.

findings.claim: VulTrial (2025) is a courtroom-style multi-agent framework (security researcher, code author, moderator, review board) with GPT-4o as the base LLM. The authors report it nearly doubles the best prior baselines and that it also runs on LLaMA-3.1-8B.
findings.relevance: The gains come from role-structured single-model agents. The abstract does not show whether mixing vendors adds anything. arXiv preprint.
findings.correction: No correction on content, which the abstract states verbatim ('almost doubles the efficacy of prior best-performing baselines'). The authors are Widyasari et al. I found only arXiv/dblp CoRR records and no peer-reviewed venue.

findings.claim: IRIS (ICLR 2025) pairs LLM-inferred taint specifications with CodeQL. On CWE-Bench-Java's 120 validated vulnerabilities, IRIS with GPT-4 detected 55 versus 27 for CodeQL alone, and it lowered the average false discovery rate by 5 percentage points.
findings.relevance: Peer-reviewed evidence favors hybrid designs (LLM plus a deterministic analyzer) over LLM-only ensembles for the white-box stage.
findings.correction: No correction. The abstract says 'improves upon CodeQL's average false discovery rate by 5% points'.

findings.claim: Multi-LLMSecCodeEval (2026) compared ten pipelines for secure code generation. Ensembles combined with static analysis improved security by up to 47.3% (SecLLMEval) and 19.3% (SecLLMHolmes) over single LLMs, while LLM-only collaboration gained 8.9–22.3%.
findings.relevance: This reinforces that deterministic tools, not just more LLMs, drive most of the improvement. It studies code generation rather than review, and it is an arXiv preprint.
findings.correction: No correction on content, which the abstract states verbatim (Sabir et al., CSIRO et al., March 2026). Hybrid ensemble+detection+patching pipelines did best. I found no independent source or venue; treat as a single unreviewed preprint.

findings.claim: Xiong and Zhang (ISSTA 2026) found that LLM agent frameworks (Aider, OpenHands, SWE-agent) cut the SAST false-positive rate on the OWASP Benchmark from over 92% to 6.3% in the best configuration. The benefit depends strongly on the backbone model and the CWE, with limited or inconsistent gains for weaker models.
findings.relevance: This supports using LLM agents to triage SAST alerts in the white-box phase, and it warns that weaker or cheaper backbones may not deliver the same benefit.
findings.correction: No correction. The ISSTA 2026 research-papers program lists it (Monash University authors). The abstract also warns that aggressive FP reduction can suppress true vulnerabilities.

findings.claim: 'Trust or Escalate' (ICLR 2025 oral) gives a selective-evaluation framework that trusts a judge only above a calibrated confidence threshold and escalates the rest to stronger models or humans, with a provable human-agreement guarantee. On a Chatbot Arena subset it guaranteed over 80% human agreement at almost 80% coverage.
findings.relevance: This is the best peer-reviewed template for disagreement/confidence-based triage. Its 'Simulated Annotators' confidence comes from a single model prompted N times with different few-shot sets, not from cross-vendor disagreement, so cross-vendor triage is an extrapolation.
findings.correction: The ICLR 2025 Oral status and the figure (>80% human agreement at almost 80% coverage, using cheap judges such as Mistral-7B) are confirmed. Correction: Cascaded Selective Evaluation escalates only to stronger LLM judges and abstains when none is confident. The paper does not describe routing abstained items to humans; that is an implication, not part of the method.

findings.claim: Valentin et al. (AAAI 2026) define 'incoherence': the probability that two independently sampled programs give different outputs on generated inputs. It provably lower-bounds error and flagged about 69% and 66% of incorrect programs on MBPP and HumanEval without an oracle.
findings.relevance: Disagreement checked by execution is a sound triage signal, but about one third of incorrect programs showed zero incoherence. Agreement is not proof of correctness. These samples come from one model at a time.
findings.correction: No correction. The definition is quoted from the paper, and 69%/66% are mean detection rates across 16 LLMs, reported with no false positives. The AAAI 2026 venue comes from the arXiv journal-ref; the AAAI site returned 403, so I could not check it independently.

findings.claim: Research on homogenization supports shared-blind-spot concerns only indirectly. Bommasani et al. (NeurIPS 2022) found that sharing training data reliably homogenizes outcomes, but that foundation models do not always make it worse. 'Artificial Hivemind' (NeurIPS 2025) documented strong homogeneity between different LMs in open-ended generation.
findings.relevance: This backs caution that vendor diversity does not equal error independence. Neither study measures code-security review, so 'similar training data leads to shared security blind spots' remains a plausible hypothesis, not a measured fact.
findings.correction: No correction, with one wording note. Bommasani et al. report 'mixed results' for foundation models, where the adaptation method strongly affects homogenization; 'do not always make it worse' is a fair paraphrase. Artificial Hivemind is in the NeurIPS 2025 Datasets and Benchmarks Track (Infinity-Chat, 26K queries).

findings.claim: Across these sources, the following is supported: single-LLM judges show self-preference, position, verbosity and surface-cue biases. Cross-family panels and ensembles reduce but do not eliminate these biases. Majority voting captures most of debate's benefit, and hybrid LLM plus static-analysis or execution pipelines beat LLM-only ones.
findings.relevance: This is the evidence-backed core for a commander harness: independent verdicts first, then weighted voting, deterministic tool verification, and escalation of disagreements to a human.
findings.correction: The first three points are well supported (Zheng; Wang; Panickssery; Pombal; Moon; PoLL; Choi et al.). Two caveats. First, the majority-voting result comes from one paper on seven NLP benchmarks, not security review. Second, 'hybrid beats LLM-only' is shown directly only by Multi-LLMSecCodeEval (secure code generation). IRIS compares against CodeQL alone, not against LLM-only. Execution-based checking (incoherence) is shown as an error detector, not in a head-to-head with LLM-only review. Present hybrid superiority as supported on specific benchmarks, not as general.

findings.claim: The following is assumed and not demonstrated in any source found: that assigning Claude, ChatGPT and Nemotron to different agents yields meaningfully independent errors on security code review of AI-generated apps. No study was found that measures cross-vendor error correlation on that task, and the strongest correlation evidence (MMLU) shows frontier models increasingly err together.
findings.relevance: The plan should present multi-vendor diversity as an unverified mitigation. It should include a step that measures inter-model error correlation and each model's accuracy on a labeled calibration set of the user's own code before relying on it.
findings.correction: The supporting evidence is confirmed: Kim et al. (MMLU) and Goel et al. (CAPA) show correlation rising with capability. I found no study measuring Claude/GPT/Nemotron error correlation on security review of AI-generated apps, but an absence cannot be proven. Two sources give partial counter-evidence of complementarity in vulnerability detection. Widyasari et al. 2024 found 'even the lower-performing LLMs provided unique correct predictions'. Sun et al. 2025 note 'notable discrepancies in detection results... among architecturally distinct LLMs'. Neither measures error correlation directly or covers frontier vendors on AI-generated apps, so the claim holds as an unproven assumption, but with this nuance.

findings.claim: The BIG-bench repository states that all task files (including README.md and task.json) contain a 'canary' string that should not be edited, intended to help detect and prevent benchmark tasks leaking into web-scraped training data.
findings.relevance: Precedent for the canary-string contamination control of the 05 §5.1 calibration corpus. Canary strings only help detect verbatim inclusion; they do not prove absence of contamination.
findings.correction: README confirms: 'All task files (including README.md and task.json) contain a "canary" string, which should not be edited. This is to prevent benchmark tasks from leaking into web-scraped training data.' The README states only the prevention purpose; it does not say the canary is meant to 'detect' leakage (docs/doc.md says it helps 'avoid training on benchmark data'). Drop or qualify 'detect'.

findings.claim: ReasonVul, 'Three Heads Are Better Than One: A Multi-perspective Reasoning Framework for Enhanced Vulnerability Detection' (arXiv 2605.18153, 2026-05-18, preprint): three reasoning-mode agents analyze independently, then a structured debate resolves conflicts. On PrimeVul it reports 40.00% pair-wise accuracy and 72.52% F1, and says 389 of 542 conflicts were resolved correctly.
findings.relevance: A new multi-agent vulnerability-detection result on a de-duplicated benchmark. Not peer-reviewed, and uses a single model family.
findings.correction: No correction.

findings.claim: 'The Capability Paradox: How Smarter Auditors Make Multi-Agent Systems Less Secure' (arXiv 2605.17480, v3 2026-07-29, preprint) reports that mean attack success rate rose from 18.4% to 63.9% as worker capability increased, with certainty mediating 74% of the effect across 47,807 interactions. It also reports that heterogeneous ensemble verification reduced attack success from 52.8% to 2.0%.
findings.relevance: Suggests heterogeneous verifiers resist manipulation (e.g. injected text in audited repos) better than homogeneous ones. Preprint.
findings.correction: 18.4% -> 63.9% mean ASR (peak 94.4%), 52.8% -> 2.0% with heterogeneous ensemble verification, v3 2026-07-29 are confirmed. Qualification: 47,807 interactions is the total across two datasets used for mediation analysis; the 74% certainty mediation figure is specific to the larger Worker-Only setting (n_W=14), while the Full-MAS setting (n_W=6) only shows a directionally consistent effect.

findings.claim: 'The Cost of Consensus: Isolated Self-Correction Prevails Over Unguided Homogeneous Multi-Agent Debate' (arXiv 2605.00914, 2026-04-29) found that debate among 10 identical 7-8B models underperformed isolated self-correction. It reports sycophantic conformity (modal adoption up to 85.5%) and debate using 2.1-3.4x more tokens for equal or lower accuracy.
findings.relevance: Supports independent judgments over homogeneous debate. Small models only.
findings.correction: No correction. (Teams of N=10 homogeneous agents of Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B or Ministral-3-8B; arXiv comment lists 'ACM Conference on AI and Agentic Systems'.)

findings.claim: 'Beyond Consensus: Mitigating the Agreeableness Bias in LLM Judge Evaluations' (arXiv 2510.11822, preprint) reports that LLM judges had a true-positive rate around 96% but a true-negative rate below 25% on a code-feedback task (366 Python programs, 14 LLMs). A minority-veto ensemble plus regression-based bias correction cut maximum absolute error to 1.2%, about half that of standard ensembles.
findings.relevance: Code-domain evidence that simple majority voting of judges inherits an agreeableness bias. Relevant to verifier aggregation rules.
findings.correction: TPR ~96%, TNR <25%, 366 high-school Python programs, 14 LLMs, 1.2% max absolute error and 2x improvement confirmed. Correction: the 1.2% figure is attributed to the regression-based framework (not a combination with minority-veto), and the 2x comparison is against 'the best-performing ensemble of 14 state-of-the-art LLMs', not standard ensembles in general. Minority-veto is presented as a separate, earlier mitigation.

findings.claim: 'Bias in the Loop: Auditing LLM-as-a-Judge for Software Engineering' (arXiv 2604.16790, 2026-04-18, preprint) reports that judge decisions on software-engineering tasks are highly sensitive to prompt biases even when the code is unchanged, enough to change model rankings. It recommends reporting bias sensitivity alongside accuracy.
findings.relevance: Supports measuring prompt-sensitivity in the calibration lab. The abstract gives no numbers.
findings.correction: No correction.

findings.claim: 'Preference Leakage: A Contamination Problem in LLM-as-a-judge' (arXiv 2502.01534, Li et al.; listed as accepted at ICLR 2026) shows that judges favor student models related to them (same model, inheritance relationship, or same family), and that this bias is harder to detect than previously identified judge biases.
findings.relevance: Peer-reviewed support for choosing verifiers from a family different from the reporter's.
findings.correction: No correction. (arXiv comment: 'Accepted by ICLR 2026'; first author Dawei Li.)

findings.claim: 'Extreme Self-Preference in Language Models' (arXiv 2509.26464, Lehr, Cipperman and Banaji, preprint) ran 72 experiments with about 41,000 queries across eight LLMs. Models consistently favored their own identity, and preferences followed the assigned identity rather than the true one.
findings.relevance: Supports stripping model and vendor identity from content shown to verifiers (anonymization).
findings.correction: No correction.

findings.claim: 'Self-Preference Is Weak or Absent in Verifiable Instruction-Following Revision' (arXiv 2606.20093, 2026-06-18, 7-page preprint) found no detectable self-preference across 85 author-vs-fresh comparisons on IFEval with four mid-tier model families (gap -5.1 pp, 95% CI [-12.9, +2.7]).
findings.relevance: Counter-evidence: self-preference may shrink when outcomes are objectively verifiable. Small sample, but it motivates measuring rather than assuming.
findings.correction: No correction. (Full title continues ': A Four-Model Test Under Genuine Authorship'; authors Guey and Bougault; '7 pages, 3 tables'.)

limitations: I found no primary study that measures error correlation between Claude, ChatGPT/GPT and Nemotron on code review or vulnerability detection. Nemotron does not appear in any of the confirmed studies.

The strongest correlated-error evidence (Kim et al., ICML 2025) uses MMLU multiple-choice data from HELM and the Hugging Face leaderboard, not code. Transfer to code or security review is an extrapolation.

Many cited works are arXiv preprints or workshop papers, not peer-reviewed main-conference papers: Goel et al. (listed as an ICLR 2025 workshop), PoLL, Chen et al. 2025, Pombal et al. 2026, Zhang et al. (MAD position paper), Widyasari et al. 2024, Sun et al. 2025, Multi-LLMSecCodeEval 2026, Wu et al. 2025, VulTrial, and Hegazy 2024 (single author, minor journal).

Some figures come from search-result summaries rather than full text I read myself: Zheng et al.'s roughly 10% self-enhancement win rate, CodeJudgeBench's 'up to 11%' order effect, Mao et al. appearing at QRS 2024, and the Self-MoA paper's TMLR 2026 venue (from ML Anthology only).
Mao et al.'s headline numbers differ between arXiv v1 and v4, so the reported gains are unstable.

Two PDF fetches (the NeurIPS proceedings copy of Panickssery et al. and the Trust or Escalate PDF) returned binary. I used the arXiv abstract and HTML pages instead, so some method details were not checked against the full text.
Most ensemble results for vulnerability detection use Devign, ReVeal or BigVul, which PrimeVul (ICSE 2025) shows to be leaky and mislabeled, so ensemble gains there may be inflated.
Most studies test older models (GPT-3.5/4, Llama 2/3, PaLM 2, Gemini-Pro). Whether their error-correlation and bias results hold for 2026 frontier models is not established.

I found no peer-reviewed study that directly evaluates cross-vendor disagreement as a triage signal for security code review. The confirmed triage evidence uses confidence from a single model (Trust or Escalate), permutation disagreement (Wang et al.) or execution disagreement among one model's samples (Incoherence).

'Bias' in this literature means evaluator biases (self-preference, position, verbosity, familiarity), not fairness bias. The user's goal of 'reducing bias from model differences' is best matched to these evaluator biases and correlated errors.

findings.claim: Veracode's Spring 2026 update tested more than 150 LLMs on 80 tasks (4 CWEs, 4 languages) with no security prompting. The overall security pass rate stayed at about 55% while syntax correctness passed 95%, and the XSS (CWE-80) and log injection (CWE-117) pass rates were only 15% and 13%. The 2025 report had framed this as risky flaws in 45% of tests.
findings.relevance: Supports the premise that vibe-coded apps need mandatory security gates. This is vendor data limited to 4 CWEs, so use it for motivation, not as a baseline.
findings.correction: All figures match Veracode's pages, and tech-insider.org (an independent outlet) independently reports the Spring 2026 figure of 55%. Newer data: Veracode's later 2026 GenAI report (Business Wire release, 2026-07-28) gives a 56% pass rate and 12% for log injection. The plan should cite the Spring figures as a snapshot.

findings.claim: Pearce et al. (IEEE S&P 2022) generated 1,689 Copilot programs across 89 CWE-Top-25 scenarios and found about 40% of them vulnerable.
findings.relevance: A peer-reviewed baseline showing that AI-generated code often contains CWE-class flaws, which justifies running SAST on every change.
findings.correction: Small wording fix: the 89 scenarios cover three axes, not only CWE Top-25 weaknesses. The axes are weakness diversity (MITRE Top 25), prompt diversity and domain diversity (including Verilog).

findings.claim: USENIX Security 2025 (Spracklen et al.) analyzed 576,000 code samples from 16 LLMs. The average share of hallucinated package names was at least 5.2% for commercial models and 21.7% for open-source models, with 205,474 unique hallucinated names.
findings.relevance: The SCA agent must check that each dependency actually exists and has a sane provenance and age in its registry (slopsquatting risk), not only look up CVEs.
findings.correction: No correction. The repo README also gives an overall rate of 19.7%.

findings.claim: Semgrep CE's engine is still LGPL-2.1, but Semgrep-maintained rules moved to the non-open-source Semgrep Rules License v1.0 in December 2024. CE is limited to single-file, single-function analysis; cross-file taint needs the paid platform.
findings.relevance: With CE alone, cross-file source-to-sink flows (typical in multi-file vibe-coded web apps) will be missed. The rules license can also restrict redistribution if the toolkit is shipped as a product or SaaS.
findings.correction: No correction. Socket (independent) confirms the December 2024 rules license and that the engine stayed LGPL 2.1. The single-function and single-file limit is stated in Semgrep's own docs.

findings.claim: Semgrep's GitHub releases list v1.177.0 on 2026-09-10, so the project is actively released.
findings.relevance: Confirms current maintenance. Pin exact versions in the toolkit.
findings.correction: No correction. The Atom feed timestamps v1.177.0 at 2026-09-10T19:37:56Z. Earlier releases: v1.176.0 on 2026-09-01 and v1.174.0 on 2026-08-20.

findings.claim: Opengrep is an LGPL-2.1 fork of Semgrep CE 1.100.0 backed by a vendor consortium (Aikido, Endor Labs, Kodem, Orca, others). It adds intrafile cross-function taint and extra languages, and outputs JSON and SARIF.
findings.relevance: A fully open alternative engine for the deterministic SAST layer, avoiding the Semgrep rules-license constraint for the engine.
findings.correction: No correction. The README lists Aikido, Amplify, Endor Labs, Kodem and Orca; Socket also names Jit. Cross-function taint needs the --taint-intrafile flag. Added languages include Visual Basic, Apex and Elixir (Semgrep's docs also mention Crystal).

findings.claim: CodeQL supports C/C++, C#, Go, Java/Kotlin, JavaScript/TypeScript, Python, Ruby, Rust, Swift and GitHub Actions. Its CLI license allows free use only for open-source codebases and academic research; private or commercial code needs a paid license, which since April 2025 is sold as GitHub Code Security at $30 per active committer per month.
findings.relevance: CodeQL is the strongest free data-flow engine for public repos, but a toolkit for users' private repos cannot bundle it without a license. It must be an optional or licensed plugin.
findings.correction: Nuance: the license text still says a 'paid GitHub Advanced Security' license is required. Since 2025-04-01 GHAS has been sold as Code Security ($30) and Secret Protection ($19). GitHub docs list the CodeQL CLI and code scanning under Code Security, which requires a Team or Enterprise plan.

findings.claim: Bandit (PyCQA, Apache-2.0) is an AST-plugin security linter for Python and includes a SARIF output formatter.
findings.relevance: A cheap, deterministic, Python-only first-pass scanner whose output can be merged into the same SARIF pipeline.
findings.correction: No correction. Both sources are PyCQA's own; no third-party source was checked.

findings.claim: The gitleaks README now says it is feature complete and will get security patches only, as the author moves to Betterleaks. Betterleaks is MIT-licensed, launched in March 2026, drop-in CLI compatible, adds CEL-based validation, and reports 98.6% recall versus 70.4% for entropy filtering on CredData.
findings.relevance: Plan for gitleaks as frozen and consider Betterleaks. The recall figure comes from the author and vendor and has not been independently verified (medium confidence on that number).
findings.correction: The launch facts are confirmed: MIT license, a March 2026 launch (Aikido blog 2026-03-12, BleepingComputer 2026-03-15), a drop-in claim that 'old Gitleaks CLI options will continue working', and the 98.6% vs 70.4% CredData recall. However, the current Betterleaks README says validation 'Previously...was implemented in CEL'. New configs should use Expr, and CEL-style configs are still accepted only for compatibility. Describe validation as Expr-based with CEL kept for compatibility.

findings.claim: TruffleHog (AGPL-3.0) classifies 800+ secret types, and 700+ of its detectors actively verify candidates against the provider's API (for example, AWS GetCallerIdentity). Results are labelled verified, unverified or unknown, and it supports --results=verified and --no-verification.
findings.relevance: Verification gives near-zero-false-positive secret findings but sends found credentials to third-party APIs. The toolkit should make verification an explicit opt-in. The AGPL license also affects redistribution.
findings.correction: No correction. AGPL-3.0 applies from v3.0; earlier versions are GPL-2.0. The detector counts come only from the vendor README; the vendor site confirms programmatic verification but gives no counts.

findings.claim: OSV-Scanner V2.0.0 (Apache-2.0) shipped on 2025-03-17. It added layer-aware container scanning, guided remediation (including Maven) and HTML output, and it uses call analysis to report whether a vulnerable function is actually reachable.
findings.relevance: Call-graph reachability lowers SCA false positives. The OSV.dev data also supports the package-existence and advisory checks.
findings.correction: Nuance: call analysis is an optional feature ('has the option of using call analysis') that existed before V2. The V2 announcement lists broader reachability integration as future work, so do not present reachability as new in V2 or as available for all ecosystems.

findings.claim: The OSV-Scanner releases page lists v2.6.0 as the latest release (September 14). The year could not be read reliably.
findings.relevance: Only the exact version pin is uncertain; the project itself is active.
findings.correction: The year is 2026: the Atom feed gives v2.6.0 at 2026-09-14T02:55:16Z. The previous releases were v2.5.1 on 2026-08-17 and v2.5.0 on 2026-08-07.

findings.claim: Trivy (Apache-2.0) scans for vulnerabilities, misconfigurations/IaC, secrets and licenses, and produces SBOMs. On 2026-03-19 its distribution was compromised (CVE-2026-33634): Trivy v0.69.4 to v0.69.6, trivy-action below 0.35.0 and setup-trivy below 0.2.6 shipped a credential stealer. The advisory says to pin Actions to full commit SHAs, verify binaries with cosign and rotate secrets.
findings.relevance: The scanners themselves are part of the attack surface. The harness should pin tool versions and digests, verify signatures, and run scanners in sandboxes with no CI secrets.
findings.correction: Precision fix: the advisory names the v0.69.4 binary, with v0.69.5 and v0.69.6 affected as Docker images. The advisory window is 2026-03-19 to 03-23. The safe versions are Trivy v0.69.2/v0.69.3, trivy-action v0.35.0 and setup-trivy v0.2.6. Microsoft independently confirms the 2026-03-19 date, the credential harvesting and the advice to pin to a SHA.

findings.claim: Syft (Apache-2.0) generates SBOMs in CycloneDX, SPDX and Syft JSON, including signed in-toto attestations. Grype (Apache-2.0) scans images, filesystems or Syft SBOMs, prioritizes with EPSS and KEV, and filters with OpenVEX.
findings.relevance: Provides the SBOM artifact and a second, independent vulnerability database to cross-check OSV-Scanner and Trivy results.
findings.correction: No correction. Both sources are Anchore's own repos; no third-party source was checked.

findings.claim: SonarQube Community Build has quality gates and basic secrets detection. Taint analysis, branch and PR analysis/decoration, and AI Code Assurance are only in the Developer, Enterprise and Data Center editions.
findings.relevance: The free Community Build is a code-quality gate, not a data-flow security engine. AI Code Assurance needs a paid edition.
findings.correction: No correction, but the only source is the vendor. Community Build secrets detection covers 'public services'; Developer and above add commercial and enterprise services.

findings.claim: In a 2026.1 community thread, a user says SonarQube's automatic AI-code detection has been deprecated, leaving manual 'contains AI code' project labeling plus the 'Sonar way for AI Code' quality gate. A Sonar staff member says more AI Code Assurance features are coming.
findings.relevance: Do not rely on vendor auto-detection of AI code. The deprecation claim comes from a forum user and was not confirmed in official docs; the toolkit should track provenance itself.
findings.correction: Attribution nuance: the 'deprecated' remark came from another community member, not the person who started the thread. On 2026-05-26 Sonar staff (Vivek Reghunath) confirmed 'AI code detection will be removed' and said new AI Code Assurance features are coming. The 2025.1 docs confirm the 'Sonar way for AI Code' gate and the 'Qualify for AI Code Assurance' manual option. This is forum evidence, not official deprecation documentation.

findings.claim: SARIF 2.1.0 (plus Errata 01, 2023-08-28) is the OASIS standard JSON format for static-analysis results.
findings.relevance: Makes a good shared schema for the harness to normalize, de-duplicate and cross-compare findings from deterministic tools and from agents on different LLMs.
findings.correction: No correction. The status is 'OASIS Standard incorporating Approved Errata', dated 2023-08-28, serialized as JSON.

findings.claim: IRIS (Li, Dutta, Naik; ICLR 2025) uses LLMs to infer CWE-specific taint sources and sinks for CodeQL and then to triage paths in context. On CWE-Bench-Java (120 real vulnerabilities), IRIS with GPT-4 found 55 versus CodeQL's 27, improved the false discovery rate by about 5 percentage points, and found 4 previously unknown vulnerabilities.
findings.relevance: The best-documented pattern for pairing an LLM with a deterministic engine. It is Java-only (MIT license, actively updated), and its false discovery rate stays high even after the improvement.
findings.correction: The numbers match the paper. Note that the repo's CWE-Bench-Java has since grown to 213 CVEs across 49 CWEs, so '120' applies only to the paper's evaluation. ICLR 2025 is confirmed by the repo BibTeX, which is from the same authors.

findings.claim: Vulnhuntr (Protect AI, AGPL-3.0) has LLMs trace call chains from remote input to output in Python code only, covering 7 classes (LFI, AFO, RCE, XSS, SQLi, SSRF, IDOR), with 1-10 confidence scores. Its README recommends Claude over GPT, and the latest main-branch commits are from 2025-02-06.
findings.relevance: A usable reference design for call-chain-driven LLM review, but it is Python-only and appears to have little recent maintenance.
findings.correction: Minor points: the README gives thresholds (below 7 unlikely, 7 investigate, 8+ likely) rather than stating a 1-10 scale explicitly. It also requires exactly Python 3.10. The last commits were on 2025-02-06, with the previous ones on 2024-10-31.

findings.claim: Anthropic's claude-code-security-review GitHub Action (MIT) and the /security-review command do diff-aware, language-agnostic LLM review with configurable false-positive filtering; by default they exclude DoS, rate limiting and open redirect. The README warns it 'is not hardened against prompt injection attacks and should only be used to review trusted PRs.'
findings.relevance: A ready-made reviewer that one white-box agent could wrap. The harness must treat the code under review as untrusted input to the LLM.
findings.correction: No correction. The LICENSE file is MIT (Copyright 2025 Anthropic), and the prompt-injection warning is quoted verbatim in the README.

findings.claim: Claude Code Security launched on 2026-02-20 as a limited research preview for Enterprise and Team customers. Anthropic says it uses multi-stage self-verification, gives each finding a confidence rating, requires human approval of patches, and that Opus 4.6 found 500+ vulnerabilities in open-source code. It moved to public beta as Claude Security around 2026-04-30, alongside a beta Claude Code plugin.
findings.relevance: A commercial option for the Claude-backed reviewer. No public precision or false-positive rate was found, and the model named on the product page has changed over time.
findings.correction: Confirmed: the 2026-02-20 research preview and its features, the 500+ vulnerabilities found with Opus 4.6, and the public beta for Claude Enterprise on 2026-04-30 (ITPro covered it on 2026-05-04), running on Opus 4.7. Not confirmed: that the Claude Code plugin launched alongside it. The April 30 announcement does not mention a plugin; the current product page says the plugin is 'now available in beta for all Claude Code users' (and now names Claude Mythos 5.1), without giving a launch date.

findings.claim: GitHub Copilot Autofix is GA for CodeQL alerts in C#, C/C++, Go, Java/Kotlin, Swift, JS/TS, Python, Ruby and Rust. At launch GitHub said its suggestions fix more than two-thirds of vulnerabilities with little or no editing, and the beta median time to fix was 28 minutes versus 1.5 hours manually.
findings.relevance: GitHub's own docs warn that fixes can fail to remediate, change semantics or suggest fabricated dependencies, and that validation only re-runs the default CodeQL suite. Any auto-fix must be re-verified by tests and rescans.
findings.correction: Timing: the two-thirds claim is from the public beta announcement (2024-03-20); the 28 minutes vs 1.5 hours figure is from the GA post (2024-08-14). Language support covers only a subset of the default and security-extended queries. All sources are GitHub's own.

findings.claim: OpenAI announced Aardvark (GPT-5 based) on 2025-10-30 as a private beta. It reported 92% recall on known and synthetic vulnerabilities in 'golden' repos and 10 CVEs. On 2026-03-06 it became Codex Security, a research preview that builds a threat model, validates findings in a sandbox and proposes patches.
findings.relevance: A reference for the pipeline of building a threat model, then finding, then validating in a sandbox. The 92% benchmark is unspecified and self-reported, and OpenAI's own pages returned HTTP 403 to my fetch.
findings.correction: No correction. openai.com returned 403 directly, so its pages were read through the r.jina.ai proxy. The Aardvark page carries a 2026-03-06 update note, and THN covered Codex Security on 2026-03-07. The research preview is for ChatGPT Pro, Enterprise, Business and Edu.

findings.claim: Press coverage of Codex Security reports that in its first 30 days it scanned 1.2M commits and surfaced 792 critical and 10,561 high-severity findings. OpenAI reportedly claims false-positive rates fell by more than 50% during beta.
findings.relevance: Scale figures only; there is no independent precision measurement. The 50% false-positive claim was seen only in secondary sources.
findings.correction: No 'reportedly' needed: OpenAI's own post states false-positive rates fell by more than 50%, noise was cut by 84% in one case, and over-reported severity fell by more than 90%. These are vendor figures that have not been independently audited.

findings.claim: Google's Big Sleep (Project Zero plus DeepMind, evolved from Naptime) found an exploitable stack buffer underflow in SQLite in October 2024 that AFL did not find in 150 CPU-hours. Google later credited it with CVE-2025-6965. Project Zero itself cautioned that 'a target-specific fuzzer would be at least as effective,' and the tool is not publicly available.
findings.relevance: Relevant only at a high level, as evidence for LLM variant analysis. It cannot be integrated into the toolkit.
findings.correction: CVE-2025-6965 is a separate bug, not the October 2024 underflow. It is an integer overflow causing an out-of-bounds read, fixed in SQLite 3.50.2 (2025-06-28), which Google credited to Big Sleep in mid-2025. The October 2024 seriesBestIndex underflow has no CVE on SQLite's CVE page. The 'not publicly available' part could not be confirmed from a primary source; Project Zero only calls the results 'highly experimental'.

findings.claim: Google DeepMind's CodeMender (announced 2025-10-06) had upstreamed 72 security fixes. It validates patches with a critique agent, an LLM judge, tests and program analysis (static and dynamic analysis, differential testing, fuzzing, SMT). It entered preview on Google Cloud (Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform / AI Threat Defense) on 2026-07-21.
findings.relevance: A second commercial example of checking LLM patches with multiple independent validators, which supports a verifier-agent role in the design.
findings.correction: No correction. The 72 fixes were made over six months, with human review before upstreaming. The Gemini 3.5 Flash Cyber variant is limited to governments and trusted partners. Both sources are Google's own.

findings.claim: Semgrep reports that its AI triage initially agreed with its security researchers only about 55% of the time (about 91% on true positives, 25% on false positives), later reaching 96%. Its docs say the 96% figure means users can trust a false-positive verdict when one is given, not that the tool catches all false positives.
findings.relevance: Shows why the toolkit should report agreement separately for true and false positives, and separate precision from recall. These are vendor-internal figures.
findings.correction: The blog's final 96% is agreement on true positives only; agreement on false positives reached just 41%, and no overall figure is given. The docs' 96% is a different metric: the 'false positive confidence rate' and 'human-agree rate' from user feedback (3,500+ customers, 6.5M+ findings as of 2025-08-21). The docs' caveat about trust is quoted correctly. Do not report '96% overall agreement'.

findings.claim: SecLLMHolmes (IEEE S&P 2024) tested 8 LLMs on 228 code scenarios. The models answered non-deterministically and with unfaithful reasoning, and merely renaming functions or variables, or adding library functions, flipped answers in 26% and 17% of cases.
findings.relevance: Direct evidence that one LLM pass is unreliable. Use multiple samples, multiple models and deterministic anchors, and require evidence such as a reproducing test before accepting a finding.
findings.correction: Wording: the abstract says these changes produced incorrect answers in 26% and 17% of cases (reported for PaLM2 and GPT-4). 'Flipped' is a paraphrase. The IEEE Xplore page was not read.

findings.claim: A 2026 preprint on contextual-bias injection found that crafted PR metadata biased LLM security review in Claude Code and CodeRabbit pipelines. An LLM-refined framing attack succeeded on 32 of 33 CVEs (97%).
findings.relevance: Reviewer agents should see code and diffs without the author's narrative (PR descriptions, 'this is safe' comments), or should run a second blind pass. This is a preprint.
findings.correction: No correction. This is a preprint by Mitropoulos, Alexopoulos, Alexopoulos and Spinellis (first submitted 2026-03-19, latest revision 2026-09-12), not yet peer-reviewed. Template-based attacks were ineffective.

findings.claim: LLM judges show self-preference bias. Panickssery et al. (NeurIPS 2024) found GPT-4 and Llama 2 can recognize and favor their own outputs, and Wataoka et al. measured high self-preference in GPT-4.
findings.relevance: Supports the user's multi-vendor design: the model family that wrote the vibe code should not be the only reviewer or judge of it.
findings.correction: No correction. Wataoka et al. is a NeurIPS 2024 Safe Generative AI Workshop paper, not the main conference. The NeurIPS PDF could not be parsed, so arXiv 2404.13076 was used instead.

findings.claim: DVDR-LLM (arXiv 2512.12536) reported 10-12% higher detection accuracy than the average individual model by ensembling diverse LLMs, and +18% recall and +11.8% F1 on multi-file vulnerabilities. The agreement threshold trades fewer false positives against more false negatives.
findings.relevance: Evidence that cross-model voting helps, and that the harness needs a configurable consensus threshold for each severity or phase. This is a preprint.
findings.correction: No correction. The paper is by Zibaeirad and Vieira and is a preprint.

findings.claim: The Refute-or-Promote methodology (arXiv 2604.19049) used adversarial 'kill' agents and a cross-model critic. It discarded about 79% of 171 LLM-generated vulnerability candidates, and the authors state that 'no vulnerability was discovered autonomously.'
findings.relevance: A concrete design for a commander-run adversarial verification stage. It also shows that raw LLM candidate lists are dominated by false positives.
findings.correction: No correction. The pipeline also produced 4 CVEs, with human-in-the-loop structure.

findings.claim: In 'Sifting the Noise' (arXiv 2601.22952), agent frameworks (Aider, OpenHands, SWE-agent) cut the residual false-positive rate on OWASP Benchmark from over 92% to as low as 6.3%, with gains inconsistent on weaker models. The authors warn that aggressive false-positive reduction can suppress true vulnerabilities. ZeroFalse reports F1 0.912 on the OWASP Java Benchmark and 0.955 on OpenVuln.
findings.relevance: LLM triage of SAST output is promising but benchmark-specific. Log all suppressions for audit and never auto-drop high-severity findings.
findings.correction: No correction. Both are preprints.

findings.claim: Meta's TestGen-LLM (FSE 2024 companion) extends existing tests and keeps a generated test only if it builds, passes repeatedly and adds coverage. On Instagram, 75% of generated tests built, 57% passed reliably and 25% increased coverage; overall it improved 11.5% of classes, and engineers accepted 73% of its recommendations.
findings.relevance: The filter chain (builds, passes, not flaky, adds coverage) is the core pattern for a test-generation agent. The tool itself is internal to Meta.
findings.correction: Scope nuance: the 75/57/25% figures come from Instagram Reels and Stories. The 11.5% of classes and 73% acceptance come from Instagram and Facebook test-a-thons.

findings.claim: Meta's ACH (FSE 2025 industry) generated 9,095 mutants from plain-text concern descriptions and 571 privacy-hardening tests across 10,795 Android Kotlin classes. Engineers accepted 73% of the tests and judged 36% privacy-relevant. Its LLM equivalent-mutant detector scored precision 0.79 / recall 0.47, rising to 0.95 / 0.96 with preprocessing.
findings.relevance: Shows how to turn threat or compliance concerns into targeted mutants and tests that kill them, bridging white-box findings to verification tests. It is an internal tool, but the method can be reproduced.
findings.correction: No correction. The classes span 7 Meta platforms. The Meta engineering blog was not read.

findings.claim: CoverUp (Pizzorno and Berger, FSE 2025) iterates coverage analysis with LLM dialogue. It reached 80% median per-module line+branch coverage versus 47% for CodaMosa, and 89% overall versus 77% for MuTAP, on Python.
findings.relevance: A peer-reviewed coverage-guided loop that fits a Python test-generation agent.
findings.correction: No correction. The ACM DL page returned 403; acceptance at FSE'25 is taken from the arXiv record.

findings.claim: Qodo Cover (formerly cover-agent, AGPL-3.0) was an open-source take on TestGen-LLM that could use 100+ models via LiteLLM. Its README now states 'This repository is no longer maintained.'
findings.relevance: Useful as a design reference only. Do not depend on it without forking.
findings.correction: No correction. Qodo's 2024-05-20 blog confirms it implemented TestGen-LLM in cover-agent.

findings.claim: Pynguin (MIT since v0.30.0, Python 3.10 or newer) does search-based unit test generation for Python. It warns that it executes the module under test and 'can cause serious harm to your computer,' and recommends running it in containers.
findings.relevance: A deterministic, non-LLM test-generation baseline. All test execution of vibe code must be sandboxed.
findings.correction: No correction. It was LGPL through v0.29.0. The README calls it 'only a research prototype' not meant for production use.

findings.claim: EvoSuite (LGPL) generates JUnit tests. Its latest release is v1.2.0 (2024-09-16, adding JUnit 5 output), and it lists Java 9+ support with caveats (DSE only up to Java 8/9).
findings.relevance: A search-based Java baseline, but support for modern JDKs (17 and later) is unconfirmed and releases are infrequent.
findings.correction: V1.2.0 was released on 2021-09-16, not 2024. It did add JUnit 5 output and Java 9 support for DSE. The license is LGPL-3.0. Issue #433 (2022-09-19) says EvoSuite supports Java only up to 11 and fails on Java 17 class files. Treat EvoSuite as unmaintained since 2021 and limited to Java 11 or older.

findings.claim: Hypothesis (Python) and fast-check (JS/TS; works with Jest, Mocha, Vitest) are mature property-based testing libraries that generate inputs and shrink failures to a minimal counterexample.
findings.relevance: Properties can come from specs or requirements rather than from the implementation, which counters the oracle problem in vibe code.
findings.correction: No correction. The Hypothesis README says it 'reports the simplest possible' failing case. The fast-check README describes shrinking and replay 'on the minimal counterexample', and fast-check.dev lists Jest, Mocha and Vitest.

findings.claim: Agentic Property-Based Testing (Maaz, DeVoe, Hatfield-Dodds, Carlini; arXiv 2510.09907) ran an LLM agent that infers properties and writes Hypothesis tests across 100 Python packages. 56% of its bug reports were valid (32% worth reporting), rising to 86% valid for the top-scored 21, and 3 patches were merged.
findings.relevance: A concrete, measured design for a property-based-testing agent. About half of raw reports are invalid, so a verification stage is required.
findings.correction: No correction. It is a NeurIPS 2025 DL4Code workshop paper. 5 bugs were reported and 3 patches merged; 81% of the top 21 were worth reporting.

findings.claim: Vikram et al. (arXiv 2307.04346) propose judging LLM-written property-based tests on validity, soundness and property coverage, the last measured with property mutants.
findings.relevance: Gives the harness quality metrics for property tests produced by the test-writing agents.
findings.correction: No correction.

findings.claim: arXiv 2410.21136 found that LLM-based test generation tends to produce oracles that capture the program's actual behaviour rather than its expected behaviour.
findings.relevance: Critical for vibe coding: tests generated from buggy AI code can lock the bugs in. Oracles should come from the requirements or spec agent, not from the implementation.
findings.correction: No correction. The paper is by Konstantinou, Degiovanni and Papadakis and covers 24 Java repositories.

findings.claim: An ISSTA 2026 replicability study (arXiv 2607.22880) found that coverage and mutation scores of LLM-generated suites are useful comparative signals for regression testing. When the code may already contain bugs, they 'no longer serve as reliable indicators.'
findings.relevance: Coverage and mutation thresholds should not be the only pass/fail gate for vibe code; combine them with spec-based and property tests. This is a recent paper and I did not read the full text.
findings.correction: No correction. Acceptance at ISSTA 2026 (PACMSE) is taken from the arXiv record only.

findings.claim: The mutation-testing options are mutmut (Python, BSD-3, needs fork() so Windows requires WSL), Stryker (JS/TS, C#, Scala; Apache-2.0) and PIT (JVM; Kotlin via the commercial Arcmutate add-on).
findings.relevance: Deterministic mutation engines to measure the strength of LLM-generated tests. Choose the engine per language.
findings.correction: No correction. The mutmut LICENSE text is the BSD 3-clause text, and the README says Windows needs WSL because mutmut needs fork. pitest.org says Arcmutate adds Kotlin support.

findings.claim: OWASP ASVS 5.0.0 requirement 1.2.4 is Level 1 and reads: "Verify that data selection or database queries (e.g., SQL, HQL, NoSQL, Cypher) use parameterized queries, ORMs, entity frameworks, or are otherwise protected from SQL Injection and other database injection attacks. This is also relevant when writing stored procedures."
findings.relevance: docs/examples/invariants.yaml baseline entry and the requirement.asvs example cite ASVS 5.0.0 1.2.4 at Level 1
findings.correction: No correction.

findings.claim: Hypothesis's LICENSE.txt says all code in the repository, except where explicitly noted otherwise, is released under the Mozilla Public License v2.0 (the GitHub license API reports NOASSERTION because of this wording).
findings.relevance: Fills a 'to be checked' license entry. MPL-2.0 is file-level copyleft.
findings.correction: No correction. (The file says 'Mozilla Public License v 2.0'. The API reports spdx_id NOASSERTION, name 'Other'; blaming this on the wording is a reasonable inference.)

findings.claim: fast-check (dubzzz/fast-check) is MIT-licensed according to the GitHub license API.
findings.relevance: Fills a 'to be checked' license entry.
findings.correction: No correction.

findings.claim: gitleaks (gitleaks/gitleaks) and Betterleaks (betterleaks/betterleaks) are both MIT-licensed according to the GitHub license API.
findings.relevance: Permissive secret scanners, as alternatives to AGPL TruffleHog in W0.
findings.correction: No correction.

findings.claim: OWASP Benchmark for Java (OWASP-Benchmark/BenchmarkJava) is GPL-2.0 according to the GitHub license API.
findings.relevance: Relevant if Benchmark code is redistributed as part of the calibration corpus. Running it as a separate target is a different situation.
findings.correction: No correction.

findings.claim: The TruffleHog README states that since v3.0 TruffleHog is released under the AGPL 3 license. The README mentions an enterprise product, but no statement offering an alternative commercial license for the open-source code was found.
findings.relevance: AGPL obligations remain the only licensing path found for the OSS code.
findings.correction: No correction. (The README reads 'Since v3.0, TruffleHog is released under a AGPL 3 license'; pre-v3 work stays under GPL 2.0 and contributions need a CLA. The README has a 'TruffleHog Enterprise' section but no commercial-license offer.)

findings.claim: The GitHub license API reports LGPL-2.1 for both the Semgrep engine (semgrep/semgrep) and the Opengrep engine (opengrep/opengrep).
findings.relevance: Engine license re-check. Rule-pack licenses are separate.
findings.correction: No correction.

findings.claim: github/codeql (queries and libraries) is MIT, but the CodeQL CLI binaries license (github/codeql-cli-binaries LICENSE.md) permits use for academic research, testing OSI-licensed queries, and analysis of open-source codebases. It prohibits generating databases for or during automated analysis, CI or CD, and use on non-open-source codebases, unless covered by a paid GitHub Advanced Security license.
findings.relevance: Automated CodeQL on private customer code needs a commercial license.
findings.correction: github/codeql is MIT, and the CodeQL Terms permit academic research, demonstrating the Software, testing OSI-licensed queries, and analysis of Open Source Codebases. However, the CI/CD prohibition is not absolute. The Terms expressly allow generating CodeQL databases for or during automated analysis, CI or CD for an Open Source Codebase hosted and maintained on GitHub.com. The restriction covers such use only 'otherwise or in any other context'. The paid GitHub Advanced Security exemption is stated correctly.

findings.claim: The GitHub license API reports Apache-2.0 for CoverUp (plasma-umass/coverup) and MIT for pytest (pytest-dev/pytest).
findings.relevance: Fills license rows for W4 test generation and the test runner.
findings.correction: No correction.

findings.claim: The CycloneDX specification repository is Apache-2.0 (GitHub license API). The SPDX specification LICENSE states it is provided under the Community Specification License 1.0, with pre-existing portions from non-contributing copyright holders under CC-BY-3.0.
findings.relevance: SBOM format specifications. Producing SBOMs in these formats carries no copyleft obligation.
findings.correction: No correction. (Note: the GitHub license API reports NOASSERTION for spdx/spdx-spec. The claim relies on the LICENSE text, which matches.)

findings.claim: The official SARIF 2.1.0 JSON schema (errata01) defines result.baselineState with the values new, unchanged, updated and absent ('The state of a result relative to a baseline of a previous run'); result.kind with notApplicable, pass, fail, review, open, informational (default fail); result.level with none, note, warning, error (default warning); and result properties webRequest, webResponse, partialFingerprints, fingerprints, suppressions (suppression.kind inSource/external, status accepted/underReview/rejected), rank and properties; location has logicalLocations.
findings.relevance: Basis of the SARIF mapping spec in docs/08 (baselineState for cross-run cluster fingerprints, webRequest/webResponse for black-box evidence, logicalLocations for endpoints).
findings.correction: No correction. Enum values read directly from the schema file (sha256 c3b4bb2d…682e).

findings.claim: PyPI metadata (checked 2026-09-26): presidio-analyzer 2.2.364 has license expression MIT; its homepage link points to github.com/data-privacy-stack/presidio.
findings.relevance: Candidate named PII detector for B5 response redaction (docs/08); candidate only, not selected.
findings.correction: No correction. The repository location differs from the older microsoft/presidio path; verify the maintainer before adoption.

findings.claim: PyPI metadata (checked 2026-09-26): the Python binding tree-sitter 0.26.0 (py-tree-sitter) carries the classifier 'License :: OSI Approved :: MIT License'.
findings.relevance: Candidate parser for W0 extractors and the Slicer (docs/08); grammar packages have their own licenses and are not covered by this entry.
findings.correction: No correction. Covers the Python binding only, not the core library or individual grammars.

limitations: openai.com and help.openai.com returned HTTP 403, so the Aardvark and Codex Security figures (92% recall, 1.2M commits, the >50% false-positive drop) come only from press coverage (CyberScoop, SecurityWeek, The Hacker News), not OpenAI's primary pages.

I found no independent, peer-reviewed precision or false-positive rates for Claude Code /security-review, Claude Security, Codex Security, CodeMender or Copilot Autofix detection; all published numbers are vendor-reported.

Vendor metrics that were not independently verified: the Semgrep Assistant 96% agreement and the Multimodal '8x true positives / 50% less noise' claims, Veracode's pass rates, and Betterleaks' 98.6% recall.

Many LLM-triage and ensemble results (DVDR-LLM, Refute-or-Promote, Sifting the Noise, ZeroFalse, contextual-bias injection) are arXiv preprints from 2025-2026, some not peer reviewed. They are also benchmark-specific (for example, OWASP Benchmark results may not carry over to real vibe-coded apps).

The official SonarQube AI Code Assurance docs pages returned 404 or timed out. Edition gating comes from a Sonar blog (Oct 2025); the auto-detection deprecation comes only from a community forum post.
I could not confirm the exact release dates or latest versions of OSV-Scanner (the fetched page gave an inconsistent year), Bandit, Trivy, Grype or Syft; pin versions after checking at build time.
I could not confirm that EvoSuite supports Java 17 or newer.
The '20 vulnerabilities' Big Sleep figure (August 2025) comes from press reports (TechCrunch and others), not a Google primary page, so I left it out of the claims.
The model name shown on the claude.com Claude Security product page could not be cross-verified; earlier sources name Opus 4.6 (Feb 2026) and Opus 4.7 (beta).
I did not research Nemotron or other specific model providers' coding-security performance, cost or latency per tool; that is out of scope for this white-box topic.

No source I found shows that multi-vendor LLM assignment by itself removes model bias. The evidence (self-preference bias, ensemble gains, cross-model critics) supports reducing correlated errors, not eliminating bias.

findings.claim: The Threat Modeling Manifesto (November 2020) is built on four questions: What are we working on? What can go wrong? What are we going to do about it? Did we do a good enough job? It also sets out values such as continuous refinement over a single delivery.
findings.relevance: These questions work as the harness's phase gates. Question 4, 'Did we do a good enough job?', is the step that justifies generating tests from the threat model.
findings.correction: Correct. The four questions and five values (including 'Continuous refinement over a single delivery') match the site word for word. Shostack's post gives the date as 17 Nov 2020; the manifesto site itself shows no date, and I found no source outside shostack.org for the date. The OWASP cheat sheet independently confirms the four questions.

findings.claim: The OWASP Threat Modeling Cheat Sheet turns the four questions into four phases: system modeling, threat identification, mitigations, and review/validation. Validation asks whether each mitigation can be tested and whether success can be measured. It recommends using OWASP ASVS and MITRE CWE when writing mitigations as requirements.
findings.relevance: OWASP's own guidance for going from threat to requirement to test is to run it through ASVS/CWE.
findings.correction: Correct. The phase names are System Modeling, Threat Identification, Response and Mitigations, and Review and Validation. It quotes: 'Can the agreed upon mitigations be tested? Can success or failure ... be measured?' It names ASVS and CWE as useful 'when formulating these responses'. Only the primary source was checked.

findings.claim: STRIDE (Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege) first appeared in Kohnfelder and Garg's internal Microsoft paper 'The Threats to Our Products' (April 1999).
findings.relevance: STRIDE is the base taxonomy used by nearly every LLM threat-modeling tool and study below.
findings.correction: Correct. Both sources give 1 April 1999 and the Microsoft internal 'Interface' journal. Wikipedia independently credits Garg and Kohnfelder.

findings.claim: The Microsoft Threat Modeling Tool uses 'STRIDE per Element': only some STRIDE categories apply to each DFD element type. Processes get all six, external entities get S and R, data flows get T, I and D, and data stores get T, R, I and D.
findings.relevance: This gives a fixed element-to-category checklist that can bound and check LLM output. The rule table itself comes from Microsoft blog material, not the current tool documentation.
findings.correction: Microsoft's overview page does list 'STRIDE per Element' as a tool feature. The mappings for processes, external entities and data flows are confirmed. However, Microsoft's 2006 MSDN chart (Figure 5) gives data stores only T, I and D. Repudiation for data stores is conditional (it applies when the store holds audit logs, in Shostack's later treatment). The T/R/I/D mapping for stores is how OWASP Threat Dragon does it; I could not confirm it as the MS TMT rule.

findings.claim: The Microsoft Threat Modeling Tool is a free, Windows-only click-to-download app (Windows 10 Anniversary Update or later, .NET 4.7.1 or later). The latest GA release is 7.3.51110.1, dated 10 November 2025.
findings.relevance: No Linux or headless use and no CLI or API is documented on the pages read, so it does not fit well inside a CI-driven multi-agent harness.
findings.correction: Correct as of 2026-09-23. The release notes list 7.3.51110.1 (November 10, 2025) as the newest GA release, and the requirements match. An Internet connection is also required for updates. I found no non-Microsoft source.

findings.claim: PASTA (UcedaVélez and Morana, 'Risk Centric Threat Modeling', Wiley 2015) has seven stages: Define Objectives, Define Technical Scope, Application Decomposition, Threat Analysis, Vulnerability & Weakness Analysis, Attack Modeling, and Risk & Impact Analysis. Stage 6 uses attack patterns and attack trees, and the output guides the testing that follows.
findings.relevance: PASTA ties each threat to business impact, which suits ranking black-box test cases by risk.
findings.correction: The stage names and the use of attack patterns and attack trees in stage 6 are confirmed. Crossref independently confirms the book (Wiley, 15 May 2015). VerSprite, which UcedaVélez founded, says PASTA guides the penetration testing that follows. It does not say stage 6 output directly drives testing, so treat that link as a reasonable reading, not a quote.

findings.claim: LINDDUN, from the DistriNet unit at KU Leuven, is a privacy threat framework with seven categories: Linking, Identifying, Non-repudiation, Detecting, Data Disclosure, Unawareness, and Non-compliance. It comes in three variants: LINDDUN GO (lean), PRO (systematic), and MAESTRO (model-driven; not the CSA framework of the same name).
findings.relevance: This is the privacy track for apps handling personal data. Threat Dragon still uses the older category names (Linkability, Identifiability, ...), so names need normalizing.
findings.correction: Correct. linddun.org describes MAESTRO as a 'systematic and exhaustive approach using enriched system descriptions', with details still 'forthcoming'. 'Model-driven' is a paraphrase. Threat Dragon still uses the older LINDDUN names (Linkability, Identifiability, Detectability, Disclosure).

findings.claim: Schneier's attack trees (Dr. Dobb's Journal, December 1999) place the attacker goal at the root and use OR and AND nodes. Attributes roll up the tree: an OR node takes its cheapest child's cost, an AND node takes the sum of its children, and possible/impossible values follow the same pattern.
findings.relevance: Attack-tree paths can be listed mechanically, one candidate test scenario per path, and the rolled-up attributes give a ranking.
findings.correction: Correct, including the quoted roll-up rules. Only the primary source was checked.

findings.claim: OWASP Threat Dragon is an OWASP Production project under Apache-2.0. It supports STRIDE, LINDDUN, PLOT4ai, CIA, CIA-DIE and Generic threat types, and its rule engine suggests threats limited by element type (actor, process, store, flow).
findings.relevance: An open-source DFD editor and rule engine with a JSON format that humans can review and agents can write to.
findings.correction: Correct. Element-based restriction applies to STRIDE, LINDDUN and PLOT4ai diagrams, not to CIA or CIA-DIE. 'Generic' removes the restrictions.

findings.claim: Threat Dragon's latest release is 2.6.2 (10 May 2026); 2.6.0 (March 2026) added OWASP Cornucopia EoP game diagrams and templates. Models are saved in a v2 JSON Schema, and the CycloneDX TM-BOM format is planned as the long-term primary format (the docs describe it as still in development).
findings.relevance: TM-BOM export is not reliably available yet, so the harness should treat Threat Dragon v2 JSON or OTM as its interchange format.
findings.correction: The release facts are confirmed: 2.6.2 on 10 May 2026 and 2.6.0 on 30 Mar 2026. The schema docs do not mention CycloneDX. They say the TM-BOM schema is 'being developed as part of the OWASP Threat Model Library project' and that the long-term plan is to adopt it as the primary format. Issue #850 (now closed) is where TM-BOM is described as 'described by CycloneDX' and targeted for Threat Dragon 3.x.

findings.claim: OWASP pytm is a Python threat-modeling-as-code framework. It generates DFDs and sequence diagrams and matches threats from threats.json, where each threat is a condition on element attributes (for example target.crosses(Boundary)) and cites CAPEC and CWE. Version 1.4.0 (July 2025) added an LLM element class with LLM threats.
findings.relevance: Its rule-based matching gives a non-LLM baseline to cross-check LLM-generated threats. An agent can emit the pytm model from the code.
findings.correction: The date is wrong: v1.4.0 was released on 6 July 2026 (PyPI upload 2026-07-06), not July 2025. The previous release was v1.3.1 in April 2024. Everything else holds: the tool is MIT-licensed, generates DFDs (Graphviz) and sequence diagrams (PlantUML), and has an LLM element with threats LLM01–LLM09. Not every threat cites both: 98 of 114 threats reference CAPEC and 75 reference CWE.

findings.claim: Threagile takes YAML architecture models, checks them against built-in and custom YAML risk rules, and outputs PDF, Excel, JSON and DFD/data-asset diagrams. It runs from Docker, the CLI, or a REST server mode, under the MIT license.
findings.relevance: Another deterministic threat-modeling-as-code engine for CI. How actively it is maintained is unclear (see limitations).
findings.correction: Correct. The README lists custom rules as YAML scripts (older .so plugins are also still supported), flags for PDF, Excel and JSON output and DFD/data-asset diagrams, a '-server <port>' mode, and 'Open-Source (MIT License)'.

findings.claim: IriusRisk's Open Threat Model (OTM) is a tool-agnostic, semver-versioned JSON/YAML format for components, trust zones, threats and mitigations. It can be generated from IaC such as Terraform or CloudFormation.
findings.relevance: A candidate shared schema for handing threat models between the commander agent and sub-agents.
findings.correction: Correct. The spec uses Semantic Versioning 2.0.0 and can be written in JSON or YAML. Generating it from IaC is done by IriusRisk's StartLeft tool, which supports CloudFormation, Terraform (and plan files), Visio/Lucidchart, draw.io and MTMT. OTM itself does not do the generation.

findings.claim: STRIDE-GPT (MIT, v0.19) routes calls through LiteLLM to OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Mistral, Groq, DeepSeek and local LM Studio models. It produces STRIDE threat models, attack trees, DREAD scores, mitigations and Gherkin test cases, and exports Markdown, JSON, SARIF or HTML.
findings.relevance: The closest existing open-source match for multi-provider threat modeling plus threat-to-Gherkin test generation. Its SARIF output fits code-scanning UIs.
findings.correction: Correct. PyPI independently shows version 0.19.0 (19 Jul 2026) under the MIT license.

findings.claim: STRIDE-GPT's agentic 'analyze' mode ties each threat to evidence. The model quotes a code snippet, the tool matches it against the file on disk, and records file:line. A snippet it cannot find is marked 'unverified' rather than dropped.
findings.relevance: A concrete anti-hallucination pattern for the white-box stage: require quoted code checked by a deterministic tool before a finding is accepted.
findings.correction: Correct. This came in PR #205 (merged 15 Sep 2026), which added deterministic snippet matching in agent/evidence.py with no LLM in the check.

findings.claim: STRIDE-GPT fills in MITRE ATT&CK/ATLAS IDs from reference cards regenerated from upstream STIX/YAML rather than model recall, to eliminate ID hallucination. It also maps threats to OWASP LLM Top 10 and ASI categories and detects agentic architecture patterns based on MAESTRO.
findings.relevance: Taxonomy IDs such as CWE, CAPEC, ATLAS and ASVS should come from official data files, never from LLM memory.
findings.correction: It is the cards that are regenerated from upstream data (ATT&CK Enterprise v17.1, ATLAS 2026.05). The LLM still chooses the IDs; the cards only instruct it to use catalogued IDs. 'Eliminating ID hallucination' is the author's own claim and has not been independently tested. The pattern detection is described as 'inspired by' MAESTRO. The LLM Top 10 and ASI mappings are confirmed.

findings.claim: STRIDE-GPT PR #170 tried an opt-in adversarial verifier: an LLM agent that tries to refute each threat by opening the source files. It was closed unmerged on 20 September 2026, superseded by the deterministic evidence check (PR #205).
