findings.relevance: One project's experience that deterministic evidence checks worked better than a second LLM judge. Useful when designing the commander's verification step.
findings.correction: PR #170 was closed unmerged on 20 Sep 2026. The maintainer says it was superseded by a redesigned verifier tracked in issue #210, which is still open (advisory-only verdicts that reuse evidence), not by #205. PR #205 (merged 15 Sep 2026) added the deterministic evidence system, and that made parts of #170 redundant. So adversarial verification is still planned, not replaced.

findings.claim: mcp-stride-gpt is an MCP server exposing threat-modeling tools, including generate_security_tests and validate_threat_coverage. The MCP client's own LLM does the actual semantic analysis.
findings.relevance: Shows threat-modeling steps packaged as MCP tools that any provider's agent can call.
findings.correction: Correct. The README says the tools 'provide structure and rubrics; your client does the analysis'. It is a serverless Vercel HTTP server under the MIT license.

findings.claim: TM-Bench, from the STRIDE-GPT author, scores LLM threat models for STRIDE coverage, completeness, technical validity and JSON compliance. Its ground truth is synthetic and Claude Sonnet 4.6 acts as the judge.
findings.relevance: There are no human-expert labels, so its scores should not be read as real-world accuracy.
findings.correction: The metrics are confirmed with weights 30/30/30/10. The ground truth is synthetic, and Claude Sonnet 4.6 is the judge (v1 used Claude 3.7 Sonnet). The author is not named on the site; the only clue is a 'Buy me a coffee' link to mrwadams. That is not confirmed authorship.

findings.claim: AbdulGhaffar and Matrawy (arXiv 2505.04101, 2025) tested five LLMs with four prompting techniques on STRIDE classification of 5G threats. Average accuracy rose from 63% (zero-shot) to 71% (few-shot with internet), and the best was 72%. Some threats were misclassified by all models because the models took a different perspective than the 3GPP baseline.
findings.relevance: Evidence that about 30% STRIDE misclassification is realistic, so human review or a cross-model check is needed.
findings.correction: Correct. Note the small sample: only six 5G threats were classified. The paper attributes the errors to an 'incorrect threat perspective' (for example, the AMF's view instead of the user's) and to missed second-order threats.

findings.claim: Pourhanifeh et al. (arXiv 2605.10808, May 2026) tested 52 configurations across 8 models. Domain-adapted models did not consistently beat general models, and gains from larger models were 'neither consistent nor sufficient for reliable threat modelling'.
findings.relevance: Switching to a bigger or security-tuned model alone will not fix accuracy. The design needs grounding and verification steps.
findings.correction: Correct. Submitted 11 May 2026 by Pourhanifeh, AbdulGhaffar and Matrawy, the same group as claim 20, so the two papers are not independent of each other.

findings.claim: Zelenskiy and Sadovykh (ICTSS 2025, Springer LNCS 16107) compared single-agent and two-agent STRIDE extraction with o1, o3 and Sonnet on 24 system descriptions with 745 known threats. The LLMs sped up the work and found plausible threats outside the reference set, but lacked the depth and reliability of expert models. The dataset is on Zenodo under CC-BY-4.0.
findings.relevance: Direct evidence on multi-agent versus single-agent threat extraction, plus a public dataset the harness could use for evaluation.
findings.correction: Confirmed: title, authors, ICTSS 2025 (Limassol) in LNCS, pages 231–247. The Zenodo dataset is CC-BY-4.0, and I counted exactly 24 systems and 745 threat rows. Not confirmed: the LNCS volume number 16107, the models used (o1, o3, Sonnet) and the conclusions. Springer blocked access and Crossref/OpenAlex have no abstract. The linked GitHub code references gpt-4o and claude-3-7-sonnet, not o1 or o3.

findings.claim: ACSE-Eval (arXiv 2505.11565) tested GPT-4.1, Gemini 2.5 Pro and Claude 3.7 Sonnet on 100 AWS scenarios with IaC. Gemini did best zero-shot and GPT-4.1 best few-shot. Claude gave the most semantically sophisticated models but struggled with categorization.
findings.relevance: Different models have different strengths, which supports the user's plan to use several providers.
findings.correction: Correct according to the abstract. The abstract also says Claude struggled with 'generalization'.

findings.claim: ThreatModeling-LLM (arXiv 2411.17058, banking) built its dataset with the Microsoft Threat Modeling Tool, then used CoT/OPRO prompting and LoRA fine-tuning. Llama-3.1-8B rose from 0.36 to 0.69 accuracy and from 0.36 to 0.73 recall.
findings.relevance: Shows that prompting and fine-tuning for a specific domain raise small-model scores substantially, but only to about 0.7.
findings.correction: Correct. The accuracy figure is specifically for 'identifying mitigation codes' (NIST 800-53), and precision also rose from 0.49 to 0.73. These numbers are in the paper body, not the abstract.

findings.claim: Auspex (arXiv 2503.09586) encodes expert 'tradecraft' in chained prompts: first decompose the architecture, then identify, classify and mitigate threats. Evaluation was qualitative feedback from SMEs on banking systems.
findings.relevance: A prompt-chaining pattern the threat-modeling sub-agent can reuse. No quantitative accuracy data.
findings.correction: Correct. It is a two-stage prompt chain, evaluated through SME feedback on threat models of real banking systems.

findings.claim: ThreatCompute (CCSW '25) combines modular LLM prompting with attack graphs for Kubernetes apps, grounded in MITRE ATT&CK and the Microsoft Threat Matrix for Kubernetes. It reportedly found 29 of 30 known techniques on a single application.
findings.relevance: Grounding in a fixed technique catalog plus graph structure works better than free text, though this was evaluated on only one app.
findings.correction: Confirmed: it combines LLMs with attack graphs for Kubernetes, uses ATT&CK and the Microsoft Threat Matrix for Kubernetes, and appeared at CCSW 2025 (Taipei, pp. 14–27). Not confirmed: the '29 of 30 techniques' result and the word 'modular'. Neither appears in the abstract, and the ACM full text was blocked (403). Drop or flag the 29/30 figure.

findings.claim: AegisShield (arXiv 2509.10482) grounds STRIDE plus ATT&CK generation in NVD and AlienVault OTX data. Across 243 threats in 15 case studies it reports statistically significant semantic alignment with expert threats and an 85.4% success rate in mapping threats to ATT&CK.
findings.relevance: Further evidence that retrieval grounding helps. It is a single-author study.
findings.correction: Correct: semantic alignment p<0.05 and mapping p<0.001, from over 8,000 AI-generated threats. Context worth noting: it is a single-author (Grofsky) George Washington University dissertation (ProQuest 32167210), not peer-reviewed conference work.

findings.claim: ThreatLens (IEEE VTS 2025, arXiv 2505.06821) is a multi-agent framework that uses RAG, LLM reasoning and interactive user feedback to generate both threat models and security test plans. It was validated on the NEORV32 SoC.
findings.relevance: A peer-reviewed precedent for multi-agent threat modeling that produces a test plan, though for hardware rather than web or AI apps.
findings.correction: Correct. It targets hardware security verification, not software applications.

findings.claim: ASTRIDE (arXiv 2512.04785, December 2025) adds an 'A' category for AI-agent-specific attacks to STRIDE and uses fine-tuned VLMs plus a reasoning LLM to threat-model from architecture diagrams. The abstract gives no quantitative results.
findings.relevance: One of several proposals to extend STRIDE for agentic apps. Not validated enough to adopt as a standard.
findings.correction: Correct. The reasoning model is OpenAI gpt-oss. The abstract claims 'accurate, scalable, and explainable' results but gives no numbers.

findings.claim: Díaz Ferreyra et al. (ESEM 2026, arXiv 2607.28431) applied three threat-modeling methods to an industrial GenAI system and found traditional methods such as STRIDE insufficient for GenAI-specific risks. Support was weakest for supply-chain and human-centered risks.
findings.relevance: Supports running STRIDE together with OWASP LLM/ASI, MAESTRO and ATLAS for AI-built or AI-containing apps.
findings.correction: The claim misreads the paper. That STRIDE is insufficient for GenAI risks is the paper's premise, not a finding. The three methods applied were GenAI-aware threat-modeling methods chosen by a rapid literature review, tested in an SME. The finding is that these GenAI-aware methods gave limited support for supply-chain and human-centered risks. It was accepted at ESEM 2026.

findings.claim: The OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 (released November 2024) covers: LLM01 Prompt Injection, LLM02 Sensitive Information Disclosure, LLM03 Supply Chain, LLM04 Data and Model Poisoning, LLM05 Improper Output Handling, LLM06 Excessive Agency, LLM07 System Prompt Leakage, LLM08 Vector and Embedding Weaknesses, LLM09 Misinformation, and LLM10 Unbounded Consumption.
findings.relevance: Threat categories for the app under test when it embeds an LLM.
findings.correction: Correct. The resource page dates it 17 Nov 2024.

findings.claim: The OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications 2026 (published 9 December 2025) covers: ASI01 Agent Goal Hijack, ASI02 Tool Misuse (& Exploitation), ASI03 Identity & Privilege Abuse, ASI04 Agentic Supply Chain Vulnerabilities, ASI05 Unexpected Code Execution, ASI06 Memory & Context Poisoning, ASI07 Insecure Inter-Agent Communication, ASI08 Cascading Failures, ASI09 Human-Agent Trust Exploitation, and ASI10 Rogue Agents.
findings.relevance: Applies both to agentic apps under test and to the harness itself: a multi-agent toolkit is exposed to ASI01, ASI02, ASI07 and ASI08.
findings.correction: Correct. The OWASP blog names ASI02 'Tool Misuse'; Teleport calls it 'Tool Misuse & Exploitation' and ASI05 'Unexpected Code Execution (RCE)'.

findings.claim: OWASP 'Agentic AI – Threats and Mitigations' v1.0 (17 February 2025) set out a threat-model-based taxonomy of 15 threats (T1 Memory Poisoning to T15). Secondary sources say v1.1 (December 2025) added T16 Insecure Inter-Agent Protocol Abuse and T17 Supply Chain Compromise to match the Top 10.
findings.relevance: The detailed taxonomy behind the ASI Top 10. The v1.1 T16/T17 additions were confirmed only from secondary sources.
findings.correction: Confirmed from primary files. The official download now serves 'Version 1.1, December 2025', which lists T1 Memory Poisoning through T17 Supply Chain Compromise, including T16 Insecure Inter-Agent Protocol Abuse. The April 2025 multi-agent guide uses T1–T15, which supports a 15-threat v1.0. The resource page still reads 'v1.0, Feb 17 2025'. The reason for the additions ('to match the Top 10') is not stated in the document.

findings.claim: The OWASP Multi-Agentic System Threat Modeling Guide v1.0 (23 April 2025) applies the Agentic Threats taxonomy to systems where multiple autonomous agents coordinate.
findings.relevance: Directly applicable to threat-modeling the commander and sub-agent harness itself.
findings.correction: Correct. The PDF itself is dated 22 April 2025; the web page says 23 April. It uses CSA MAESTRO as its working framework and adds example-specific 'extended' threats, whose numbers T16/T17 there mean something different from the v1.1 taxonomy.

findings.claim: CSA MAESTRO (Ken Huang, 6 February 2025) has seven layers: 1 Foundation Models, 2 Data Operations, 3 Agent Frameworks, 4 Deployment and Infrastructure, 5 Evaluation and Observability, 6 Security and Compliance (a vertical layer), and 7 Agent Ecosystem. It adds cross-layer threats and a six-step process from decomposition through monitoring.
findings.relevance: A layered checklist for decomposing agentic apps; it is a method, not a control catalog.
findings.correction: Correct. The six steps are System Decomposition, Layer-Specific Threat Modeling, Cross-Layer Threat Identification, Risk Assessment, Mitigation Planning, and Implementation and Monitoring. The CSA GitHub repo is an MIT-licensed LLM-based analyzer tool.

findings.claim: A CSA blog (February 2026) shows MAESTRO run in CI with a third-party static-analysis tool (TITO). It notes that static analysis covers only MAESTRO layers 1–3, and layers 4–7 need IaC scanning and runtime signals.
findings.relevance: Evidence that white-box analysis alone cannot cover deployment and ecosystem threats, which justifies the black-box stage.
findings.correction: TITO (Threat In and Threat Out) is not an independent third-party tool. It is an open-source tool written by the blog's co-author, Steven Leath (with Ken Huang, 11 Feb 2026). The quote says TITO focuses on Layers 1–3. For Layers 4–7 it says static analysis must be paired with runtime signals: IaC scanning, observability-pipeline analysis and policy-as-code evaluation.

findings.claim: MITRE ATLAS data release 2026.09 (14 September 2026) contains 1 matrix, 16 tactics, 120 techniques, 88 sub-techniques, 40 mitigations and 73 case studies. It ships as YAML, with tooling to produce STIX and Excel, and 2026 releases have added many AI-agent techniques.
findings.relevance: A machine-readable AI technique and mitigation catalog to ground agents' IDs. Releases come roughly monthly, so versions must be pinned.
findings.correction: Correct. The README says tools/ generates STIX, Navigator layers and Excel from the YAML. Monthly 2026 releases added many 'AI Agent' techniques, such as tool poisoning, agent communication and runtime capability discovery.

findings.claim: OWASP AI Testing Guide v1 (26 November 2025, leads Matteo Meucci and Marco Morana) organizes tests into application, model, infrastructure and data layers, with IDs such as AITG-APP-01.
findings.relevance: Test procedures for LLM/agent threats, the AI counterpart to WSTG for the black-box stage.
findings.correction: Correct. The table of contents lists AITG-APP-01..14, AITG-DAT-01..05, AITG-INF-xx and similar IDs.

findings.claim: OWASP AISVS 1.0 has 12 chapters and L1–L3 levels, including Chapter 9 'Orchestration & Agentic Security' and Chapter 10 'Model Context Protocol (MCP) Security'. Secondary sources date its release to June 2026.
findings.relevance: Checkable AI/agent requirements to pair with ASVS when turning AI threats into acceptance criteria.
findings.correction: Correct. The date comes from OWASP itself, not only secondary sources: the project page says it was 'released in June 2026 at the OWASP Global AppSec conference in Vienna' with 191 requirements. There is no GitHub Release object, and 1.01 is in development.

findings.claim: OWASP ASVS 5.0.0 was released in May 2025 at Global AppSec EU Barcelona. It has 17 chapters (V1 Encoding and Sanitization through V17 WebRTC, including new V9 Self-contained Tokens and V10 OAuth and OIDC) and about 345 requirements, with IDs like v5.0.0-1.2.5.
findings.relevance: ASVS 5.0 is the latest version and supplies stable requirement IDs to use as test acceptance criteria. The ~345 count comes from a secondary source.
findings.correction: Correct. Counting the official CSV gives exactly 345 requirements across 17 chapters, V1 Encoding and Sanitization through V17 WebRTC. The preface says 'approximately 350'.

findings.claim: ASVS 5.0.0 is published as CSV, JSON (standard, flat and legacy), XML, DOCX and CycloneDX. Official 4.0.3↔5.0.0 mapping YAMLs are in 5.0/mappings.
findings.relevance: Agents can load the requirements from data files instead of recalling them.
findings.correction: Correct: there is a .cdx.json CycloneDX file, legacy CSV/XML variants, and mapping_v4.0.3_to_v5.0.0.yml plus its reverse.

findings.claim: ASVS 5.0 no longer maintains direct CWE or NIST mappings, citing category-only CWEs and imprecise mappings. Only an archived beta CWE mapping (v5.0.be_cwe_mapping.json) remains.
findings.relevance: An automated CWE→ASVS 5.0 link is not officially available. Any such mapping is an approximation and must be labeled as one.
findings.correction: Correct, with one small fix: an archived v5.0.be NIST 800-63B mapping (nist.md) also remains, so it is not 'only' the CWE file.

findings.claim: ASVS 5.0 makes documented security decisions explicit, verifiable requirements. Level 1 shrank to 70 requirements (about 20% of the total) and was prioritized for risk reduction against implementation effort.
findings.relevance: L1 is a realistic minimum baseline for vibe-coded apps. The documentation requirements can be checked in the white-box stage.
findings.correction: Correct. The official CSV count gives L1=70, L2=183, L3=92. In v4.0.3 it was 128 of 278 (46%).

findings.claim: The OpenCRE REST API (opencre.org/rest/v1) links ASVS, WSTG, CWE, CAPEC, NIST SSDF, MITRE ATLAS, OWASP Top 10 for LLM and others. A direct query on 2026-09-23 found that all 277 of its ASVS entries still point to ASVS v4.0.3.
findings.relevance: Usable today for CWE/CAPEC/WSTG cross-links. Reaching ASVS 5.0 needs a second step through OWASP's 4.0.3→5.0.0 mapping file.
findings.correction: Re-checked on 2026-09-23 across 14 pages: 277 ASVS entries, and all 277 hyperlinks point to ASVS v4.0.3. The standards list includes every framework named in the claim.

findings.claim: The latest stable OWASP WSTG is v4.2, and v5.0 is in development. Tests use IDs WSTG-<CAT>-<NN>, versioned as WSTG-v42-INFO-02.
findings.relevance: Test procedures and stable IDs for black-box web tests. Pin to v4.2 until v5 is released.
findings.correction: Correct.

findings.claim: The latest CAPEC is 3.9 (24 January 2023) with 559 attack patterns. Each entry includes Execution Flow, Prerequisites, Mitigations, Related Weaknesses (CWE links) and Taxonomy Mappings.
findings.relevance: CAPEC links threats to weaknesses, but it has not been updated since 2023 and does not cover LLM/agent attacks, so ATLAS fills that gap.
findings.correction: Correct. Taxonomy Mappings cover WASC and OWASP Attacks only, not STRIDE, ASVS or WSTG.

findings.claim: CWE is at version 4.20 (pages dated 30 April 2026) with 944 weaknesses/chains/composites. Entries include Detection Methods, Potential Mitigations and Related Attack Patterns (links back to CAPEC).
findings.relevance: The common weakness vocabulary shared by white-box findings (SAST/SARIF) and black-box test results.
findings.correction: Correct. There are 1,450 entries in total, including categories and views.

findings.claim: The final NIST SSDF is SP 800-218 v1.1 (February 2022). The initial public draft of SP 800-218r1 (SSDF v1.2) came out on 17 December 2025 with comments due 30 January 2026, and no final version appears on the NIST SSDF news page. SP 800-218A (GenAI and dual-use foundation model profile) was finalized on 26 July 2024.
findings.relevance: Cite 800-218 v1.1 as the final standard and v1.2 as a draft only. Add 800-218A where the app contains AI.
findings.correction: Correct. The r1 document history shows only the 12/17/25 draft. SP 800-218 final is dated 3 Feb 2022 on CSRC and 4 Feb 2022 in the news item.

findings.claim: SSDF practice PW.1.1 calls for risk modeling (threat modeling, attack modeling or attack surface mapping). PW.7 covers reviewing and analyzing human-readable code, and PW.8 covers testing executable code to find vulnerabilities and verify security requirements.
findings.relevance: These practices line up with the planned white-box (PW.7) then threat model (PW.1.1) then black-box (PW.8) flow. Task wording was confirmed through secondary summaries, not a full read of the PDF.
findings.correction: Correct. The PW.1.1 wording was extracted from the NIST PDF. The PW.7 and PW.8 titles ('...to Identify Vulnerabilities and Verify Compliance with Security Requirements') are confirmed through IriusRisk and cross-references in the PDF.

findings.claim: Marback et al. (Software: Practice and Experience, 2013) automatically generated security test sequences from threat trees and turned them into executable tests. Xu et al. (IEEE TDSC 9(4), 2012) generated security tests from formal Petri-net threat models.
findings.relevance: Earlier, pre-LLM academic work showing that tests can be derived mechanically from structured threat models.
findings.correction: Correct. Marback et al. is SPE 43(2):241–258, online Jan 2012 and in print Feb 2013. Xu et al. is TDSC 9(4):526–540, July 2012, and uses Predicate/Transition nets (a Petri-net class) built from STRIDE threats. It was applied to Magento and FileZilla Server.

findings.claim: The OWASP Abuse Case Cheat Sheet turns abuse cases into security requirements or agile acceptance criteria and keeps them traceable with IDs such as ABUSE_CASE_001. It checks them with automated CI tests: custom SAST/DAST rules and unit, integration or functional security tests.
findings.relevance: A documented pattern for traceability from threat to acceptance criterion to CI test that the harness can adopt.
findings.correction: Correct; all three points are quoted in the cheat sheet.

findings.claim: My synthesis: a chain that can be checked end to end is threat (STRIDE/LINDDUN/LLM/ASI category) → CAPEC or ATLAS technique → CWE → ASVS 5.0 / AISVS requirement → WSTG / AITG procedure → executable or Gherkin test. Each link in the chain can be taken from official data files rather than from LLM recall.
findings.relevance: A proposed backbone for turning the threat model into test cases. The CWE→ASVS 5.0 link is weak because ASVS 5.0 dropped CWE mappings and OpenCRE is still on 4.0.3.
findings.correction: The chain makes sense as a concept, but not every link exists in official data files. Official links that do exist: CAPEC<->CWE (both directions in MITRE data), the ATLAS YAML, ASVS 4.0.3<->5.0.0 mapping YAMLs, and OpenCRE links for ASVS 4.0.3 only. Their figures (29/30 techniques; 24 descriptions and 745 threats; o1/o3/Sonnet) come from search-result abstracts and the Zenodo record, not the full papers. The one-agent versus two-agent comparison results are not known in detail.
OWASP Agentic AI Threats & Mitigations v1.1 (December 2025) adding T16/T17 was confirmed only from secondary vendor blogs; the genai.owasp.org resource page showed only v1.0 (17 February 2025).
The ASVS 5.0 requirement count (~345) comes from a secondary checklist repo. OWASP primary pages confirm 17 chapters and L1 = 70 requirements (~20%), which implies about 350.
The AISVS 1.0 release date (June 2026) and 191-requirement count come from secondary search results; the OWASP project page confirms only that 1.0 is the latest stable release with 12 chapters.

The SSDF PW.1.1/PW.7/PW.8 task wording was confirmed via secondary summaries and search snippets pointing at the NIST PDF, not a full read of the PDF. Whether SP 800-218r1 (v1.2) has been finalized after the NIST news page was checked is unknown.

No independent, human-expert-labeled benchmark was found that compares STRIDE-GPT, Threat Dragon rules, pytm or Threagile on real web apps. Published LLM accuracy numbers come mostly from narrow domains (5G, banking, AWS, Kubernetes) and cannot be assumed to hold for vibe-coded apps.
TM-Bench results were not read (only its methodology page), and it uses synthetic ground truth with an LLM judge, so it cannot establish real-world accuracy.
The Microsoft Threat Modeling Tool's file format (.tm7) and any CLI or API were not confirmed from Microsoft docs; the pages read document only a Windows GUI app.
ASTRIDE, AegisShield and Auspex have limited or single-author evaluations; their claims are reported but not independently corroborated.
Scope was kept to defensive threat modeling and test derivation. Attack execution details in CAPEC/ATLAS entries were deliberately not researched or summarized.

findings.claim: The ZAP Automation Framework runs a single YAML plan headlessly (e.g. 'zap -cmd -autorun zap.yaml'). The plan's jobs run in order and include openapi, graphql, soap and postman import, spider, spiderAjax, passiveScan-config, activeScan, activeScan-policy, requestor, alertFilter, report and exitStatus. Job tests validate outcomes, and exit codes are 0 (ok), 1 (error) and 2 (warnings).
findings.relevance: A declarative plan the commander agent can generate from the threat model and version-control, instead of letting an LLM drive ZAP interactively.
findings.correction: No correction needed. The documented command is './zap.sh -cmd -autorun zap.yaml'. The overview page does not mention job order, but the add-on help source says 'The Jobs are executed in the order in which they appear (top to bottom) within the Plan.' Exit codes: 0 = ran without problems, 1 = failed with an error, 2 = warnings (even if failOnWarning is false). The job list is longer than claimed and also includes spiderClient, sequence-import, sequence-activeScan, passiveScan-wait, delay, script, insights and mcp-import.

findings.claim: The Automation Framework 'environment' section defines contexts. Each context has mandatory top-level urls plus optional includePaths and excludePaths regex lists, authentication, sessionManagement, and users (TOTP secrets supported).
findings.relevance: A scope allowlist enforced inside the scanner, e.g. only staging hosts, with logout or destructive paths excluded.
findings.correction: No correction needed. 'name' is also mandatory, and 'technology' and 'structure' are further optional fields. The docs state that the TOTP data is 'supported by Browser Based Authentication'. Only the primary ZAP docs were checked.

findings.claim: The ZAP activeScan job exposes delayInMs ('reduce the strain on the target'), threadPerHost, maxRuleDurationInMins, maxScanDurationInMins and policy strength/threshold. The docs warn that active scanning 'should only be used against applications that you have permission to test'.
findings.relevance: Rate limiting and time boxing for the DAST agent, and the tool vendor's own authorization requirement.
findings.correction: No correction needed. Defaults: delayInMs 0, threadPerHost = 2 × available cores, and both duration limits 0 (unlimited). The default strength and threshold are Medium. Only the primary docs were checked.

findings.claim: zap-api-scan.py imports an OpenAPI, SOAP or GraphQL definition and runs an API-tuned active scan. A -c config file sets each rule to IGNORE, INFO or FAIL, -S (safe mode) runs only a baseline scan, and exit codes are 0/1/2/3 (success/fail/warn/other).
findings.relevance: Simple CI gate for API-first vibe-coded backends. Safe mode suits a first, non-intrusive pass.
findings.correction: No correction needed. The script's help text reads '-c config_file config file to use to INFO, IGNORE or FAIL warnings', and alerts default to WARN. Exit codes: 0 success, 1 at least one FAIL, 2 at least one WARN and no FAILs, 3 any other failure.

findings.correction: No correction needed. Both pages are ZAP-owned; no third-party source was checked. The desktop UI still persists these messages by default.

findings.claim: Nuclei (ProjectDiscovery) is MIT-licensed, uses a YAML-based template DSL, and is actively maintained. The latest version is v3.11.1, published 2026-08-08 according to the Go module proxy.
findings.relevance: License and maintenance status. Templates generated from the threat model can encode project-specific regression checks.
findings.correction: No correction needed. The Go proxy returns v3.11.1 with Time 2026-08-08T12:20:01Z. LICENSE.md is MIT, and the README says Nuclei 'leverages simple YAML-based templates'.

findings.claim: Nuclei's rate controls are -rl (default 150 requests/second, which takes precedence), -bs (hosts in parallel per template, default 25) and -c (templates in parallel, default 25). -eh excludes hosts, IPs or CIDRs. Headless, code and fuzzing/DAST templates only run when -headless, -code or -fuzz/-dast is passed explicitly.
findings.relevance: Opt-in flags and rate limits give the harness least-privilege defaults. The harness should set a low -rl for staging.
findings.correction: Correct, with two nuances. The docs say the rate-limit flag 'takes precedence over the other two flags', but the newer -per-host-rate-limit option makes the global limit unlimited when enabled, so precedence applies to the global limit. The README marks -fuzz as 'Deprecated: use -dast instead'.

findings.claim: Nuclei requires signatures for code-protocol templates, and since v3.11.0 (2026-07-06) also for custom javascript-protocol templates. Templates are signed with 'nuclei -sign' using keys in $CONFIG/nuclei/keys. -dut/--disable-unsigned-templates makes the run fail with a non-zero exit if any template is unsigned or has a mismatched signature, and official templates come pre-signed by ProjectDiscovery.
findings.relevance: Supply-chain control. LLM-generated templates should need human review and signing before the harness can execute them.
findings.correction: The -dut part is contradicted. -dut ('disable running unsigned templates or templates with mismatched signature') skips such templates: the loader increments SkippedUnverifiedTemplateStats, logs 'Skipping %d unsigned template[s]', and carries on. It does not fail the run with a non-zero exit. The rest checks out: v3.11.0 is dated 2026-07-06T06:11:09Z, its release notes require signing for custom javascript: templates, 'nuclei -sign' and $CONFIG/nuclei/keys are documented, and official templates are signed. The signing docs page itself still says only the code protocol requires signatures.

findings.claim: The community nuclei-templates repository is MIT-licensed and includes large sets of CVE and KEV-tagged templates. The Nuclei README says the tool is primarily a standalone CLI and that running it as a service needs extra security measures.
findings.relevance: For defensive use on your own app, run an allowlisted, curated template set (your own templates plus selected tags) rather than the full community corpus. The exact template count was not verified.
findings.correction: No correction needed. The templates README lists 3587 'cve' tags, 454 CISA KEV, 1449 VulnCheck KEV and 1496 unique KEV templates (use '-tags kev,vkev'). The Nuclei README says: 'primarily built to be used as a standalone CLI tool. Running nuclei as a service may pose security risks. It's recommended to use with caution and additional security measures.'

findings.claim: Schemathesis is MIT-licensed and actively maintained, with 4.28.0 published to PyPI on 2026-09-22. It generates property-based tests (built on Hypothesis) from OpenAPI 2.0/3.0/3.1/3.2 and GraphQL schemas, in four phases: examples, coverage, fuzzing and stateful.

findings.correction: No correction needed. PyPI shows 4.28.0 uploaded 2026-09-22T22:29:35 under MIT, with hypothesis as a dependency. The README says it is 'built on top of Hypothesis', and the CLI documents --phases with the values examples, coverage, fuzzing and stateful.

findings.claim: Schemathesis has 14 checks. They include ignored_auth ('Verifies authentication is properly enforced'), use_after_free ('Detects when deleted resources remain accessible'), ensure_resource_availability, negative_data_rejection and not_a_server_error. All are enabled by default except max_response_time.
findings.relevance: Checks map directly to threat-model items (broken authentication, stale-object access, input validation), so threat-derived test cases can cite specific checks.
findings.correction: No correction needed. The page lists 14 checks, with max_response_time as the only one disabled by default. Only the primary docs were checked.

findings.claim: Schemathesis CLI safety and scoping options: --rate-limit '<n>/<s|m|h>' or 'auto' (honours Retry-After on 429); include/exclude filters by path, method, tag, name or operation-id, including regex variants; --max-examples; --workers (1-64 or auto); and junit, har, vcr, ndjson, json and allure reports.
findings.relevance: Scope allowlist and rate limiting at the tool level, with machine-readable reports the triage agent can parse.
findings.correction: No correction needed. The CLI also has --include-by/--exclude-by expression filters and --exclude-deprecated. --max-examples affects only the fuzzing and stateful phases. Only the primary docs were checked.

findings.claim: RESTler (Microsoft Research) is an MIT-licensed stateful REST API fuzzer that compiles an OpenAPI spec into a grammar and runs in compile, test (smoke), fuzz-lean and fuzz modes. Its docs warn that fuzz mode 'is more aggressive and may create outages in the service under test' (resource leaks, perf degradation, backend corruptions).
findings.relevance: Useful for stateful API bugs, but should only run against disposable staging with data reset.
findings.correction: No correction needed. The full warning reads: 'The Fuzz mode is the more aggressive and may create outages in the service under test if the service is poorly implemented.' The Microsoft Research publication page credits Atlidakis, Godefroid and Polishchuk (ICSE 2019).

findings.claim: RESTler activity is low. There are no GitHub Releases (only tags), the last tag is v9.3.1 (2025-01-30), and the latest commit on main is dated 2026-02-13. It is built from source (Python 3.12.8 + .NET 8) or as a Docker image.
findings.relevance: Maintenance risk. Treat RESTler as an optional plugin rather than a core dependency.
findings.correction: No correction needed. The releases page reads 'There aren't any releases here'. The newest version tag is v9.3.1 (Jan 30, 2025), and git ls-remote agrees. The newest commit is Feb 13, 2026, and the README specifies Python 3.12.8 and .NET 8.0 or 'docker build'.

findings.claim: EvoMaster is LGPL-3.0 licensed and actively maintained, with 6.2.0 on PyPI dated 2026-09-15. It generates system-level test suites for REST, GraphQL and RPC (gRPC, Thrift) APIs. White-box mode instruments JVM bytecode and needs a driver; black-box mode works for any language.
findings.relevance: One of the few tools covering both white-box and black-box phases. LGPL obligations apply if EvoMaster itself is modified and distributed.
findings.correction: No factual correction. Citation fix: DOI 10.1007/s10515-024-00478-1 is a Springer paper in the Automated Software Engineering journal, not ACM DL: 'Tool report: EvoMaster—black and white box search-based fuzzing for REST, GraphQL and RPC APIs' (Arcuri et al., 2024). PyPI shows 6.2.0 uploaded 2026-09-15T08:14:15.

findings.claim: EvoMaster black-box mode is the default since 6.0.0 ('--blackBox true --schema <url>'). It supports --ratePerMinute to 'avoid doing a DoS attack by bombarding the remote service', and --header0..2 to pass auth tokens. The docs note black-box coverage is usually lower than white-box.
findings.relevance: Built-in rate limiting. It also produces executable regression tests (e.g. JUnit) the toolkit can keep.
findings.correction: No correction needed. The exact wording is that black-box testing is 'unlikely... [to] get good results in terms of code coverage', with white-box recommended for JVM APIs. Only the primary docs were checked.

findings.claim: Two peer-reviewed comparisons exist. Kim et al. (ISSTA 2022) evaluated 10 REST API testing tools on 20 real-world services. Zhang and Arcuri (TOSEM 2023) compared 7 fuzzers on 18 open-source APIs plus 1 industrial API. Both report substantial coverage limitations across tools.
findings.relevance: Supports using several API testers rather than trusting one. The claim that EvoMaster black-box ranked best comes only from a search-result summary; the fetched abstract did not state it.
findings.correction: Kim et al. is confirmed: ISSTA 2022 (Crossref), 10 tools on 20 services, and the best tool (EvoMasterWB) reached under 53% line coverage. Zhang and Arcuri is TOSEM vol. 32, issue 6 (2023), but the API count differs by version. The arXiv preprint says 18 open-source plus 1 industrial. The published TOSEM abstract says '18 open source—1 industrial and 1 artificial—RESTful APIs'. Cite the TOSEM wording, or say which version you mean.

findings.claim: Playwright is Apache-2.0 licensed and actively maintained; playwright and @playwright/test 1.63.0 were published to npm on 2026-09-04. Its auth guide supports storageState, setup projects, and several signed-in roles (e.g. admin and user) in one test via separate BrowserContexts. It warns that state files 'may contain sensitive cookies' and should be kept out of git (e.g. a gitignored playwright/.auth).
findings.relevance: Direct fit for threat-model-driven authorization tests, e.g. user A must not reach user B's resource and a non-admin must not reach admin routes. Auth-state files must be handled as secrets.
findings.correction: No correction needed. npm shows both packages at 1.63.0, published 2026-09-04 (22:45 and 22:44 UTC), under Apache-2.0. The auth guide warns that the file 'may contain sensitive cookies and headers that could be used to impersonate you or your test account'.

findings.claim: Playwright API testing uses the request fixture (APIRequestContext) with baseURL and extraHTTPHeaders. It can share storageState between API and browser contexts, so a test can set up and check state through the API while driving the UI.
findings.relevance: Lets one harness express both UI flows and API-level authorization checks.
findings.correction: No correction needed. The docs also note that the browser-associated APIRequestContext shares cookies with the browser, while apiRequest.newContext() is isolated. Only the primary docs were checked.

findings.claim: Playwright Test Agents (planner, generator, healer) arrived with 1.56 (npm publish 2025-10-06) and are installed with 'npx playwright init-agents --loop=<client>' for VS Code, Claude Code, Codex or OpenCode. The planner writes Markdown plans to specs/, the generator writes tests/, and the healer 'automatically repairs failing tests'.
findings.relevance: Ready-made LLM sub-agents for end-to-end tests. Auto-healing can hide real regressions, so healer changes should require human or commander review.
findings.correction: No correction needed. npm shows 1.56.0 published 2025-10-06T14:54:33Z, and the release notes put Test Agents in 1.56. The loop values are vscode, claude, codex and opencode, and the healer 'executes the test suite and automatically repairs failing tests'.

findings.claim: Playwright MCP (@playwright/mcp, Apache-2.0, 0.0.82 on 2026-09-18) gives LLMs browser control through accessibility snapshots. Its allowed-origins and blocked-origins options exist, but the project states it 'is not a security boundary' and that allowed-origins 'does not affect redirects'.
findings.relevance: Scope enforcement for browser agents must come from network egress controls, not MCP options.
findings.correction: No correction needed. npm shows 0.0.82 published 2026-09-18T23:38Z under Apache-2.0. The README says both --allowed-origins and --blocked-origins '*does not* serve as a security boundary and *does not* affect redirects', and that the blocklist is evaluated before the allowlist.

findings.claim: k6 is AGPL-3.0 licensed. k6 2.0 was tagged 2026-05-11 (blog dated 2026-05-12), and the latest release is v2.3.0 (2026-09-21). The v1 line still receives patches (v1.8.1 on 2026-08-12). v2 changed the Go module path to go.k6.io/k6/v2 and removed the externally-controlled executor and the pause/resume/scale/status commands.
findings.relevance: Maintenance and license status. AGPL obligations matter if the toolkit modifies k6 and offers it as a network service (legal review advised; not verified here).
findings.correction: No correction needed. Go proxy times: v2.0.0 2026-05-11T09:06:51Z, v2.3.0 2026-09-21T15:05:52Z, v1.8.1 2026-08-12T14:41:18Z. The v2.0.0 release notes also remove 'k6 login' and several deprecated flags.

findings.claim: k6 2.0 added AI-oriented subcommands: 'k6 x agent', 'k6 x mcp' (MCP server), 'k6 x docs' and 'k6 x explore'. It also added an expect() Assertions API.
findings.relevance: An MCP path for a load-testing sub-agent. This rests on a single vendor source.
findings.correction: The blog names these four commands, but says they 'are all built as subcommand extensions' that are provisioned on demand, not core built-ins. The GitHub v2.0.0 and rc1 release notes only mention 'k6 x docs' and 'k6 x explore' help hints. In the blog, expect() is imported from the jslib 'https://jslib.k6.io/k6-testing/0.6.1/index.js', not a built-in k6 module. Describe it as 'k6 2.0 ships an extension model; Grafana provides agent, mcp, docs and explore subcommand extensions and the k6-testing expect() library'.

findings.claim: k6 thresholds are pass/fail criteria (e.g. http_req_failed rate<0.01, http_req_duration p(95)<200), and k6 exits non-zero when any threshold fails. abortOnFail (with delayAbortEval) stops a run as soon as a threshold fails.
findings.relevance: Machine-checkable CI gate plus an automatic safety brake that stops a load test if staging degrades.
findings.correction: No correction needed. The docs say that if any threshold fails, 'k6 would exit with a non-zero exit code', and 'When you set abortOnFail, the test run stops as soon as the threshold fails'. Only the primary docs were checked.

findings.claim: Grafana's k6 guidance says a QA environment is 'unsuitable for assessing the performance and scalability of the application', and that pre-release environments make reliability goals hard to assess. It calls production testing with minimal load (smoke/synthetic) safe and advises low-traffic windows for larger production tests.
findings.relevance: Staging-only load tests catch regressions but cannot certify production capacity; the plan should state this limitation.
findings.correction: No correction needed. Exact wording: 'it can be challenging to effectively assess all reliability goals', 'Testing production with minimal load is safe', and 'consider scheduling nightly tests or when the system handles less traffic'. The guide also warns that heavy-load tests 'might cause outages'.

findings.claim: NIST SP 800-115 (final, September 2008, supersedes SP 800-42; the NIST page shows no revision notice) gives a Rules of Engagement template in Appendix B. It covers scope, risks and mitigations, personnel and contacts, test schedule, authorized tools, incident handling with 'criteria for halting', target systems with an 'exclude list', allowable and unallowable activities, data handling, and a signature page. At minimum the test team leader and senior management sign the signature page.
findings.relevance: Authoritative template for a machine-readable 'engagement manifest' that the commander agent must load and validate before any black-box job runs.
findings.correction: Confirmed from the PDF text. CSRC shows Final, 09/30/08, superseding SP 800-42, with no revision notice. Section numbers: authorized tools sit under 2.4 Test Equipment, risks and mitigations under 1.4 Risks. The signature page wording is 'the test team leader and the organization's senior management (CSO, CISO, CIO, etc.)'. Both links are NIST-published; no third-party source was checked.

findings.claim: SP 800-115 says deviations from the ROE need permission 'normally in writing' from the original signatory. A technique 'likely to cause a denial of service... should probably be used against a non-production system', and tests that could expose PII should use non-production systems with test data.
findings.relevance: Primary-source basis for staging-only execution, synthetic data, and a written change-approval step for scope changes.
findings.correction: No correction needed. Section 7.2 reads: 'specific permission to deviate has been obtained, normally in writing, from the original signatory or individual in command.' The DoS and PII sentences appear verbatim in the planning section. Only the primary PDF was checked.

findings.claim: SP 800-115 Appendix C says white-box techniques 'tend to be more efficient and cost-effective for finding security defects in custom applications'. It says black-box techniques should be used for interactions between components and with users, other systems and the environment, and it calls the combination gray-box testing.
findings.relevance: Standards-body support for the user's white-box-first, then black-box methodology.
findings.correction: No correction needed. The text also says black-box should be used 'primarily to assess the security of individual high-risk compiled components', and 'this combination is known as gray box testing'. Only the primary PDF was checked.

findings.claim: OWASP LLM06:2025 'Excessive Agency' lists mitigations: minimize the extensions agents may call, avoid open-ended tools such as shell commands, grant least-privilege permissions, require human approval for high-impact actions, enforce authorization downstream ('complete mediation'), and apply monitoring and rate limiting.
findings.relevance: Design rules for the harness's tool layer: narrow typed tool wrappers per scanner rather than raw shell, plus human approval gates. OWASP released an LLM Top 10 2026 on 2026-08-03 whose entries I could not read.
findings.correction: No correction needed. OWASP lists logging/monitoring and rate limiting as damage-limitation measures, not prevention. The list also includes 'execute extensions in user's context' and 'sanitise inputs/outputs'. Only OWASP's own page was checked.

findings.claim: OWASP published the 'Top 10 for Agentic Applications for 2026' (ASI01-ASI10) on 2025-12-09. It covers risks such as agent goal hijack, tool misuse, memory poisoning and rogue agents.
findings.relevance: Threat-model reference for the multi-agent toolkit itself. The full ASI list was not retrieved.
findings.correction: No correction needed. The full list is ASI01 Agent Goal Hijack, ASI02 Tool Misuse, ASI03 Identity & Privilege Abuse, ASI04 Agentic Supply Chain Vulnerabilities, ASI05 Unexpected Code Execution, ASI06 Memory & Context Poisoning, ASI07 Insecure Inter-Agent Communication, ASI08 Cascading Failures, ASI09 Human-Agent Trust Exploitation, ASI10 Rogue Agents. Both sources are OWASP-owned; a third-party confirmation was attempted but not found.

findings.claim: gVisor (Apache-2.0) is a user-space 'application kernel' that intercepts syscalls; its OCI runtime runsc plugs into Docker ('sudo runsc install', then 'docker run --runtime=runsc') and Kubernetes. Its docs state the trade-offs: 'reduced application compatibility and higher per-system call overhead', and not every syscall or /proc//sys file is implemented. The main branch had commits on 2026-09-23.
findings.relevance: A drop-in stronger isolation layer for scanner containers and for executing LLM-generated test code.
findings.correction: Minor fix: gVisor's default branch is 'master', not 'main' (git ls-remote --symref shows HEAD -> refs/heads/master). It had several commits on 2026-09-23, and the Go proxy's latest pseudo-version is v0.0.0-20260923022641-f806214b59b1.

findings.claim: Firecracker (Apache-2.0) is a KVM-based VMM for lightweight microVMs. Its jailer 'applies a cgroup/namespace isolation barrier and then drops privileges', and overall security 'depends on a well configured Linux host'. Releases come every two to three months; the latest is v1.17.0 (2026-09-10).
findings.relevance: VM-grade isolation for untrusted agent tool execution. It needs Linux hosts with KVM, so it does not run natively on macOS or Windows dev laptops.
findings.correction: No correction needed. The releases page marks v1.17.0 (10 Sep) as Latest; v1.16.2 shipped the same day. git ls-remote confirms the v1.17.0 tag. All sources are GitHub-hosted.

findings.claim: E2B is open-source sandbox infrastructure for running AI-generated code. Its runtime (e2b-dev/infra) uses 'one Firecracker microVM per sandbox, in its own cgroup and network namespace', with Python and JS/TS SDKs (e2b 2.51.0 on PyPI and npm, 2026-09-18). The repo LICENSE files are Apache-2.0, but the SDK package metadata declares MIT.
findings.relevance: A managed or self-hosted microVM sandbox option for agents. The license metadata mismatch should be resolved before redistribution.
findings.correction: No correction needed. PyPI 2.51.0 was uploaded 2026-09-18T12:06:52 with license_expression MIT. npm 2.51.0 was published 2026-09-18T12:09Z with license MIT. Both repo LICENSE files are Apache 2.0. The infra README adds a per-sandbox nftables egress firewall.

findings.claim: E2B's infra repo describes its self-hostable 'E2B Embed' package (Terraform for GCP plus a Kubernetes manifest) as 'an evaluation package, not a production deployment pattern'. For production it offers dedicated deployments inside the customer's account.
findings.relevance: Self-hosting E2B is not turnkey production infrastructure. For fully local use, gVisor or plain Firecracker may be simpler.
findings.correction: No correction needed. Embed also ships as Docker Compose for a single Linux host with KVM. Only the E2B repo was checked.

findings.claim: Docker's security docs rely on namespaces, cgroups, a capability allowlist, optional seccomp/AppArmor/SELinux and user-namespace remapping. They warn that 'only trusted users should be allowed to control your Docker daemon' because containers can mount host directories.
findings.relevance: Plain containers are the baseline. Agents must never get the Docker socket, and untrusted code needs gVisor or microVMs on top.
findings.correction: No correction needed. The docs' example is a container whose /host directory is the host's '/', which can 'alter your host filesystem without any restriction'. Only Docker's own docs were checked.

findings.claim: Docker Sandboxes runs coding agents (e.g. Claude Code, Codex, Gemini) in microVMs, each with its own Docker daemon, filesystem and network. The sbx CLI is free for commercial use, while centrally managed network, filesystem and MCP policies need a paid governance subscription.
findings.relevance: A turnkey sandbox for agent sub-processes. The product and CLI naming are changing quickly, and platform requirements were not verified.
findings.correction: No correction needed. The agents page lists Claude Code, Codex, Copilot, Cursor, Devin, Docker Agent, Droid, Gemini, Kiro and OpenCode. The microVM architecture is described in the Docker blog (2026-04-16), not on the docs overview page. All sources are Docker-owned; no third-party confirmation was found.

findings.claim: Anthropic's sandbox-runtime (srt, Apache-2.0) restricts processes at the OS level without containers: bubblewrap with network namespaces on Linux, Seatbelt profiles on macOS, and alpha Windows support. Egress goes through host HTTP and SOCKS5 proxies that enforce an allowedDomains list. It is labelled a 'research preview'.
findings.relevance: A concrete way to enforce the scope allowlist at the network layer, e.g. egress only to the staging hostnames in the signed engagement manifest.
findings.correction: No correction needed. The exact label is 'Beta Research Preview'. By default all network access is denied, and an empty allowedDomains list means no network access. The npm package @anthropic-ai/sandbox-runtime is at 0.0.77 (2026-09-18) under Apache-2.0. No third-party source beyond GitHub and npm.

findings.claim: CVE-2018-19333: in gVisor before 2018-11-01, pkg/sentry/kernel/shm/shm.go mishandled reference counts, letting attackers overwrite memory in processes running as root 'but not escape the sandbox' via IPC_RMID shmctl calls.
findings.relevance: A historical gVisor memory-corruption CVE that its record describes as contained within the sandbox.
findings.correction: No correction.

findings.claim: CVE-2025-2713 (published 2025-03-28): a local privilege escalation in gVisor runsc caused by incorrect file-permission handling (processes ran with elevated permissions until their first fork). CWE-266, fixed in release-20250319.0.
findings.relevance: gVisor has recent CVEs, so the runsc release must be pinned and tracked.
findings.correction: Published 2025-03-28, CWE-266 and the description are confirmed. Qualification: the CVE record only lists release-20250319.0 as 'unaffected' (no affected range); the referenced fix commit 586c38d is dated 2024-03-15, so the fix landed much earlier than release-20250319.0. NVD scores it CVSS 3.1 7.8 High; Google CNA CVSS 4.0 6.8 Medium.

findings.claim: The google/gvisor GitHub repository's security advisories page shows no published security advisories, so gVisor vulnerabilities have to be tracked through CVE/NVD records.
findings.relevance: Operational: sets the vulnerability-monitoring source for Z2.
findings.correction: No correction. (The API returns an empty list of published advisories as of 2026-09-24. 'Have to be tracked through CVE/NVD' is an inference, not a documented statement.)

findings.claim: Anjali, Caraza-Harter and Swift, 'Blending Containers and Virtual Machines: A Study of Firecracker and gVisor' (VEE '20, DOI 10.1145/3381052.3381315), an independent academic study, found that both Firecracker and gVisor execute substantially more host kernel code than native Linux, and that gVisor and Linux containers execute substantially the same host kernel code, with different frequency.
findings.relevance: An independent (non-vendor) measurement of host-kernel attack-surface exposure for both sandboxes.
findings.correction: No correction. (The abstract says 'kernel code'; it means host kernel code.)

findings.claim: CVE-2019-18960: a buffer overflow in the Firecracker vsock implementation in versions 0.18.0 and 0.19.0 'can result in potentially exploitable crashes' (published 2019-12-11).
findings.relevance: Firecracker's VMM has had memory-safety CVEs.
findings.correction: No correction.

findings.claim: Firecracker advisory GHSA-776c-mpj7-jm3r / CVE-2026-5747 (High, 2026-04-07): a root guest can change virtio-PCI queue registers after device activation, causing DoS or host out-of-bounds writes. It affects 1.13.0-1.14.3 and 1.15.0 only when --enable-pci is used, and is patched in 1.14.4 and 1.15.1.
findings.relevance: A recent guest-to-host memory-safety bug. The default MMIO transport is not affected, which shows that configuration choices matter.
findings.correction: Confirmed: High, published 2026-04-07 (NVD 2026-04-08), affected >=1.13.0 <=1.14.3 and 1.15.0, patched in 1.14.4 and 1.15.1, PCI transport opt-in via --enable-pci (MMIO default not affected). Qualification: changing queue_size by itself gives out-of-bounds writes (up to 524,284 bytes) beyond the virtio queues but still inside guest memory. Reaching host process memory needs extra preconditions, such as a custom guest kernel or specific snapshot configurations.

findings.claim: Firecracker advisory GHSA-36j2-f825-qvgc / CVE-2026-1386 (Moderate, 2026-01-23): symlink-following in the Jailer lets a local host user with write access to pre-created Jailer directories overwrite arbitrary host files when the Jailer runs as root. Patched in 1.13.2 and 1.14.1.
findings.relevance: Host-side deployment hygiene (Jailer directory permissions) is part of the isolation guarantee.
findings.correction: No correction. (Affected: v1.13.1 and earlier, and 1.14.0. CNA CVSS 6.0 Medium.)

findings.claim: Weissman, Tiemann, Eisenbarth and Sunar, 'Microarchitectural Security of AWS Firecracker VMM for Serverless Cloud Platforms' (arXiv 2311.15999, 2023-11-27), report that Firecracker 'offers little protection against Spectre or MDS attacks'. They found a Medusa variant not mitigated by AWS-recommended defenses and a Spectre-PHT variant exploitable even with countermeasures and SMT disabled.
findings.relevance: Independent evidence that microVM isolation does not stop hardware side channels between co-tenants on one host.
findings.correction: No correction.

findings.claim: CVE-2020-2023: Kata Containers did not stop containers from accessing the guest root filesystem device, letting a malicious container gain code execution in the guest and masquerade as the kata-agent. Affects 1.11 before 1.11.1, 1.10 before 1.10.5, and 1.9 and earlier.
findings.relevance: Part of a documented Kata escape chain.
findings.correction: No correction.

findings.claim: CVE-2020-2026 (CVSS 3.1 7.8): a malicious Kata guest could make the kata runtime mount untrusted container filesystems on arbitrary host paths through improper link resolution, potentially giving code execution on the host. Same affected versions as CVE-2020-2023.
findings.relevance: VM-based sandboxes have had guest-to-host escapes through host-side runtime components.
findings.correction: Description and affected versions are confirmed. The CVSS 3.1 7.8 score is the CNA (Palo Alto Networks) score; NVD's own CVSS 3.1 score is 8.8 High. NVD describes the guest as 'compromised before a container creation' and lists CWE-59 (link following).

findings.claim: The Kata Containers GitHub security advisories page lists 10 advisories from January to August 2026, five rated Critical, including GHSA-rr59-xxvx-96qr 'VM Escape via virtiofsd Argument Injection through Default-Enabled Pod Annotations' (2026-05-20) and GHSA-mp2j-xm59-qfgw 'Config Path Annotation Arbitrary File Loading' (Critical, 2026-07-20).
findings.relevance: Kata's host-side surface (virtiofsd, annotations) has an active 2026 escape history.
findings.correction: No correction. (2026 advisories: 01-29, 02-19, 04-22, 05-20, 05-21, 07-20, 07-21 x3, 08-20 = 10. Critical: GHSA-5fc8, GHSA-wwj6, GHSA-q49m, GHSA-2gv2, GHSA-mp2j = 5. Note that GHSA-rr59-xxvx-96qr is rated Medium, CVE-2026-44210.)

findings.claim: GHSA-2gv2-cffp-j227 / CVE-2026-47243 (Critical): a guest-root to host-root escape in Kata runtime-rs <= 3.30.0 (patched in 3.31.0). With an unsandboxed host virtiofsd (--sandbox none --seccomp none), raw FUSE_SYMLINK requests with absolute paths can create symlinks at host paths.
findings.relevance: The VM boundary alone is insufficient if host helpers run unsandboxed.
findings.correction: No correction. (Critical; GitHub CVSS 4.0 9.2; published 2026-05-21.)

findings.claim: Kata advisory GHSA-fgm4-mv68-h344 (High, 2026-07-21), titled 'Dragonball: missing length validation in virtio-blk allows guest-to-host VM escape', describes process_aio_request() validating only the first byte of guest descriptors, allowing out-of-bounds read/write of host shim memory by a guest kernel. It affects Kata >= 3.0.0 with Dragonball and is patched in 4.0.0. The advisory page shows the CVE ID CVE-2026-93417.
findings.relevance: A VMM memory-safety escape in a Rust hypervisor. The CVE number looks unusual and should be re-checked in the CVE list.
findings.correction: No correction. (CVE-2026-93417 was not yet in NVD on 2026-09-24; it appears only on the GitHub advisory.)

findings.claim: CVE-2019-5736: runc through 1.0-rc6 (Docker before 18.09.2) lets attackers overwrite the host runc binary, and so gain host root, through file-descriptor mishandling of /proc/self/exe when running as root in a container.
findings.relevance: Baseline evidence that a shared-kernel runc container is not a strong boundary for untrusted code.
findings.correction: No correction.

findings.claim: CVE-2024-21626: a file-descriptor leak in runc v1.0.0-rc93 through v1.1.11 enables host filesystem access and container escape. Fixed in runc v1.1.12, CVSS 3.1 8.6.
findings.relevance: A recent runc container-escape baseline.
findings.correction: No correction.

findings.claim: CVE-2025-31133 (published 2025-11-06): runc did not verify that the /dev/null bind-mount source used for maskedPaths was a real /dev/null inode, allowing mount races that can lead to host information disclosure, DoS or container escape. Fixed in 1.2.8, 1.3.3 and 1.4.0-rc.3.
findings.relevance: runc escape bugs continued to appear in 2025.
findings.correction: No correction. (GHSA was published 2025-11-05; NVD published 2025-11-06.)

findings.claim: As of 2026-09-24, the E2B GitHub repository (e2b-dev/E2B) LICENSE is Apache License 2.0 ('Copyright 2023 FoundryLabs, Inc.'), while the published 'e2b' 2.51.0 packages declare MIT (PyPI license_expression 'MIT'; npm license 'MIT'). The mismatch persists.
findings.relevance: Resolves the open item factually: both licenses are permissive, but which one governs the packages is unresolved upstream.
findings.correction: No correction. (On 2026-09-24 the latest PyPI and npm 'e2b' release is 2.51.0: PyPI license_expression 'MIT', npm license 'MIT'. The repo LICENSE is Apache 2.0 with 'Copyright 2023 FoundryLabs, Inc.')

findings.claim: github.com/e2b-dev/infra now redirects (HTTP 301) to github.com/e2b-dev/runtime, whose license the GitHub license API reports as Apache-2.0.
findings.relevance: The self-hosted E2B backend is Apache-2.0, and references to the old repository name need updating.
findings.correction: No correction. (The web URL returns 301 to github.com/e2b-dev/runtime, and the API returns 301 to repositories/677083126.)

findings.claim: grafana/k6 is AGPL-3.0 (LICENSE.md). Grafana's licensing page and FAQ discuss the AGPL relicensing of Grafana, Loki and Tempo and offer commercial licenses to customers who want to avoid AGPL obligations, but do not mention k6 specifically.
findings.relevance: No k6-specific licensing guidance from the vendor was found.
findings.correction: No correction. (k6 appears on the licensing page only in the site navigation, not in the licensing text. The FAQ answer 'Is there a non-AGPL option?' offers a commercial license to customers who modify and distribute the AGPL version or offer it as a network service.)

findings.claim: AGPL-3.0 section 13 (as reproduced in k6's LICENSE.md) requires that 'if you modify the Program', the modified version must prominently offer users interacting with it remotely over a network an opportunity to receive its Corresponding Source. Section 5 says inclusion of a covered work in an 'aggregate' does not cause the license to apply to the other parts of the aggregate.
findings.relevance: By the license text, the network source-offer duty is tied to modification. Whether invoking an unmodified binary is an aggregate is a legal question.
findings.correction: No correction.

findings.claim: The GNU GPL FAQ (MereAggregation) says the line between separate programs and one combined program is a legal question that judges ultimately decide. It says pipes, sockets and command-line arguments are communication mechanisms normally used between separate programs, unless the communication is intimate enough to exchange complex internal data structures. Another FAQ entry says running a modified AGPL program on a public website requires releasing the modified source.
findings.relevance: This is FSF guidance, not a legal ruling. It describes the separately-invoked-CLI situation for TruffleHog and k6.
findings.correction: No correction. (The second entry is #UnreleasedModsAGPL, which says 'the company must release the modified source code'.)

findings.claim: GitHub license API results: promptfoo MIT, ZAP (zaproxy/zaproxy) Apache-2.0, Nuclei (projectdiscovery/nuclei) MIT, Schemathesis MIT, Playwright Apache-2.0, RESTler (microsoft/restler-fuzzer) MIT.
findings.relevance: Independent re-check of the black-box tool licenses already in the registry.
findings.correction: No correction.

findings.claim: The Kata Containers repository (kata-containers/kata-containers) states that its code is licensed under the Apache 2.0 license.
findings.relevance: License for an alternative Z2 runtime.
findings.correction: No correction.

findings.claim: The GitHub license API reports Apache-2.0 for sigstore/cosign, OWASP/threat-dragon and moby/moby (Docker Engine).
findings.relevance: Supply-chain, visualization and container-runtime licenses.
findings.correction: No correction.

findings.claim: The OWASP API Security Top 10 2023 lists: API1:2023 Broken Object Level Authorization, API2:2023 Broken Authentication, API3:2023 Broken Object Property Level Authorization (which combines API3:2019 Excessive Data Exposure and API6:2019 Mass Assignment), API4:2023 Unrestricted Resource Consumption, API5:2023 Broken Function Level Authorization, API6:2023 Unrestricted Access to Sensitive Business Flows, API7:2023 Server Side Request Forgery, API8:2023 Security Misconfiguration, API9:2023 Improper Inventory Management, API10:2023 Unsafe Consumption of APIs.
findings.relevance: Taxonomy for the REST/GraphQL rows of the docs/04 binding table (BFLA, mass assignment, excessive data exposure, inventory drift, unsafe consumption).
findings.correction: No correction. Read from the official OWASP project page on 2026-09-26.

findings.claim: Schemathesis ignored_auth: 'When an operation declares authentication, Schemathesis tests whether the API accepts requests without credentials or with invalid credentials. Either 401 or 403 counts as enforcement.' It sends two extra requests per operation (one without auth, one with invalid auth). use_after_free expects 404 Not Found after a successful DELETE; the stateful checks do not fire in a single case.call_and_validate() call.
findings.relevance: ignored_auth only covers operations whose API schema declares security, so apps without an accurate OpenAPI security section need a drafted spec (docs/08, H-E10); use_after_free deletes generated IDs, which the docs/04 §5 safety algorithm classifies S3 unless seed-bound.
findings.correction: Refines E:blackbox-14: the check depends on the schema's authentication declaration.

findings.claim: PyPI metadata (checked 2026-09-26): mitmproxy 12.2.3 carries the classifier 'License :: OSI Approved :: MIT License'.
findings.relevance: Candidate for the intercepting proxy decision U-13 (docs/08 §10); still a candidate, not selected.
findings.correction: No correction. Only PyPI metadata was checked, not the repository LICENSE file.

limitations: The GitHub REST API was blocked in this session, so release dates and licenses come from GitHub pages and Atom feeds, PyPI, npm and the Go module proxy. The WebFetch summarizer misreported several years as 2024; I used registry timestamps wherever it disagreed.
I could not confirm whether the Linux Foundation Software Security Project still formally hosts ZAP after the 2024 Checkmarx deal, or whether Checkmarx has changed ZAP governance since then.
The ZAP 2.17.0 release date is inferred from the blog URL (2025-12-15); the release-notes page does not state it.
The claim that EvoMaster black-box ranked best in Zhang and Arcuri (TOSEM 2023) comes only from a search-result summary; the fetched arXiv abstract did not state it.

The entries of the OWASP LLM Top 10 2026 (released 2026-08-03) and the ASI01-ASI10 list of the Agentic Top 10 were not retrieved, so I could not confirm whether 'Excessive Agency' was renumbered or changed.
E2B has a license mismatch: the repo LICENSE files say Apache-2.0 while the PyPI and npm SDK metadata says MIT. Not resolved.
The AGPL-3.0 (k6) and LGPL-3.0 (EvoMaster) obligations are only flagged, not analysed legally; a toolkit that modifies or redistributes these tools needs counsel review.
Docker Sandboxes platform requirements, OS support and maturity status were not confirmed; the docs appear to change quickly (the CLI moved to 'sbx').
The Playwright Test Agents details rest on playwright.dev and the npm publish date; I did not read the official 1.56 release notes.
The Nuclei community template counts are unverified approximations from a summarized GitHub page.
The NIST SP 800-115 text was pulled out of the PDF's compressed streams without a proper parser. The quotes match the source text, but page numbers were not verified.
No tool was installed or run hands-on. I found no independent benchmark of ZAP, Nuclei or Schemathesis specifically on AI-generated (vibe-coded) applications.
Sandbox escape resistance of gVisor, Firecracker and E2B was not independently assessed; the isolation claims are the vendors' own.

findings.claim: Andrej Karpathy coined "vibe coding" in an X post on 2 February 2025: "fully give in to the vibes, embrace exponentials, and forget that the code even exists." In the same post he said he uses "Accept All" and does not read diffs, and called it fine for "throwaway weekend projects."
findings.relevance: Defines the target: code the author has not reviewed. The toolkit cannot assume anyone understands the code, so white-box review has to rebuild that understanding. The date comes from Merriam-Webster and from decoding the post ID, which gives 2025-02-02 23:17 UTC; X itself returned HTTP 402 and could not be fetched.
findings.correction: No correction needed. A mirror of the tweet gives the timestamp 2025-02-02 23:17 UTC and the full text. The wording is "I 'Accept All' always, I don't read the diffs anymore" and "It's not too bad for throwaway weekend projects, but still quite amusing."

findings.claim: Collins Dictionary named "vibe coding" its Word of the Year 2025 on 6 November 2025 and credited the term to Karpathy. Merriam-Webster had listed it as "slang & trending" in March 2025.
findings.relevance: Shows how widely the practice has spread. Useful background for motivating the toolkit.
findings.correction: Collins' own blog, dated 6 Nov 2025, says the term was "Coined by AI pioneer Andrej Karpathy." CNN returned HTTP 451 and could not be opened. The Merriam-Webster page confirms the "Slang & Trending" section but shows no entry date; only Wikipedia gives 8 March 2025. So the March date rests on a secondary source.

findings.claim: Simon Willison argues that LLM-written code which a human has reviewed, tested and can explain is "not vibe coding, it's software development."
findings.relevance: Supports the toolkit's goal: add the review and testing that turns vibe-coded output into software-engineered output.
findings.correction: The quote and its framing match the primary source, Willison's own blog. Because it is his own statement, no independent source is needed.

findings.claim: Pearce et al. (IEEE S&P 2022) built 89 scenarios based on MITRE's 2021 CWE Top 25 and got 1,689 programs from GitHub Copilot, of which about 40% were vulnerable. They covered 18 of the 25 CWEs across Python, C and Verilog.
findings.relevance: The baseline peer-reviewed rate of CWEs in assistant-generated code. Supports seeding the white-box SAST/CWE checklist from the CWE Top 25.
findings.correction: The totals (89 scenarios, 1,689 programs, ~40% vulnerable) and the venue (IEEE S&P 2022, DOI 10.1109/SP46214.2022.9833571) are correct. However, not all 89 scenarios are Top-25 based. There were 54 DOW scenarios covering 18 Top-25 CWEs in Python and C only, 17 DOP scenarios that were CWE-89 variants, and 18 DOD Verilog scenarios. The Verilog scenarios used six hardware CWEs (CWE-1234, 1242, 1245, 1254, 1271, 1294), which are NOT from the Top 25. Correct wording: 18 of the Top-25 CWEs in Python and C, plus six hardware CWEs in Verilog.

findings.claim: In Pearce et al.'s "diversity of weakness" axis, 477 of 1,084 valid programs (44.00%) were vulnerable: 50.29% for C and 38.35% for Python. Path traversal (CWE-22), OS command injection (CWE-78) and NULL dereference (CWE-476) were among the worst.
findings.relevance: Tells the toolkit which CWE classes to test first: path handling, shell or command construction, and memory safety in C. Taken from ar5iv's HTML rendering of the paper because the PDF could not be parsed.
findings.correction: The paper's own numbers match: C had 258 of 513 vulnerable (50.29%) and Python 219 of 571 (38.35%). The paper singles out CWE-22 (100% vulnerable top suggestions), CWE-78 (majority of options vulnerable) and CWE-476 (all three scenarios had vulnerable top suggestions). The only source is the paper itself.

findings.claim: Perry et al. (ACM CCS 2023) found in a user study that participants given a Codex-based assistant wrote significantly less secure code than the control group. They were also more likely to believe their code was secure.
findings.relevance: Developers overestimate the security of AI-assisted code. The harness should rely on tool evidence (scanners, executed tests), not on the developer's or the model's own claims that code is safe.
findings.correction: No correction needed. The assistant was codex-davinci-002 and the venue is CCS '23. Semantic Scholar lists the year as 2022, which is the arXiv preprint date.

findings.claim: Veracode's 2025 GenAI Code Security Report (30 July 2025) tested over 100 LLMs on 80 coding tasks in Java, JavaScript, Python and C#. 45% of samples failed security tests and introduced OWASP Top 10 flaws.
findings.relevance: The main vendor number showing that security has not kept pace with functional correctness. The full report is behind a registration form; these figures come from Veracode's own blog.
findings.correction: No correction needed. The blog date (30 July 2025), "over 100 LLMs", the four languages and the 45% figure are on Veracode's blog. The count of "80 coding tasks" appears in Help Net Security's article, not in the Veracode blog text.

findings.claim: The July 2025 Veracode report gives security failure rates of 72% for Java, 45% for C#, 43% for JavaScript and 38% for Python. It says models failed to defend against XSS (CWE-80) in 86% of relevant samples.
findings.relevance: XSS and output encoding should be a top white-box and black-box test category. Test depth could also be adjusted by language.
findings.correction: The exact per-language figures are on Veracode's blog. Help Net Security independently gives Java >70%, the other three languages at 38–45%, and XSS at 86%.

findings.claim: The report tested four CWEs: SQL injection (CWE-89), XSS (CWE-80), log injection (CWE-117) and insecure crypto (CWE-327). Help Net Security reports an 88% failure rate for log injection. Veracode's 2026 update gives average pass rates of about 82–83% for SQLi, 86–87% for crypto, 15% for XSS and 12–13% for log injection.
findings.relevance: Output encoding and log handling fail far more often than SQL parameterization, so the toolkit should give them extra weight. The 88% log-injection figure is from a secondary article; the 2026 pass rates are from Veracode's own blog.
findings.correction: No correction needed. Spring 2026 (24 March 2026) gives SQLi 82%, crypto 86%, XSS 15% and log injection 13%. The 2026 report (28 July 2026) gives 83%, 87%, 15% and 12%. The 88% log-injection failure rate appears in Help Net Security, not in the Veracode 2025 blog text.

findings.claim: Veracode says newer and larger models improved at functional code but "were no better at writing secure code." Its November 2025 update did find GPT-5 Mini at 72% and GPT-5 at 70% security pass rates, versus Claude Sonnet 4.5 at 50%, Gemini 2.5 Pro at 59% and Grok 4 at 55%.
findings.relevance: Security behaviour differs by model and provider. This supports the user's plan to put different LLMs behind different white-box agents to reduce single-model bias. Even the best model still failed more than a quarter of tasks.
findings.correction: The exact phrase "no better at writing secure code" is on the 2025 blog. The update post is titled October 2025 but dated 18 November 2025, and it confirms all five figures. Wikipedia independently summarizes the October 2025 update as saying security had generally not improved, but it does not give the per-model numbers.

findings.claim: Veracode's 2026 GenAI Code Security Report (blog dated 28 July 2026) gives an average security pass rate of 56% across models. The best listed model, GPT-5.5, reached 68%.
findings.relevance: The problem persisted into 2026. The findings come from a single vendor using its own proprietary benchmark.
findings.correction: Veracode's own blog, dated 28 July 2026, confirms both figures: "GPT-5.5 leads the current snapshot at 68%" and an average of 56%. I found no independent coverage because the web-search budget ran out, so this rests on the vendor source only.

findings.claim: The widely repeated "AI code has 2.74x more vulnerabilities" figure is not in Veracode's report. It comes from CodeRabbit's December 2025 analysis of 470 open-source PRs (320 AI co-authored, 150 human-only), which found about 1.7x more issues overall and security issues "up to 2.74x higher."
findings.relevance: A citation-hygiene warning for the plan: several secondary sites misattribute this number to Veracode. CodeRabbit notes that PRs without an AI signal were assumed to be human-written, so the ratio is approximate.
findings.correction: CodeRabbit's post (17 Dec 2025) confirms the 470/320/150 split and 10.83 vs 6.45 issues per PR (~1.7x). Note that 2.74x is a category maximum: The Register says AI code was "2.74x more likely to add XSS vulnerabilities", so it is XSS-specific, not all security issues. The Veracode 2026 blog does not mention 2.74x or CodeRabbit; I did not check the full report PDF.

findings.claim: Spracklen et al. (USENIX Security 2025, Distinguished Paper) generated 576,000 code samples from 16 LLMs in Python and JavaScript. Of 2.23 million package references, 440,445 (19.7%) were hallucinated, covering 205,474 unique non-existent package names.
findings.relevance: Supports a mandatory dependency-existence and provenance check in the white-box phase. Some secondary sources wrongly say "2.23 million code samples"; 2.23 million is the count of package references.
findings.correction: No correction needed. The USENIX page shows "Distinguished Paper Award Winner." The ;login: summary rounds the overall rate to 19.6%. The repo is MIT-licensed, and the full list of hallucinated names is withheld for security reasons.

findings.claim: The paper reports average hallucination rates of at least 5.2% for commercial models and 21.7% for open-source models, with GPT-4 Turbo lowest at 3.59%. Python averaged 15.8% and JavaScript 21.3%.
findings.relevance: Model choice affects supply-chain risk. The harness should verify every dependency against the registry no matter which LLM produced the code.
findings.correction: No correction needed. The USENIX abstract independently confirms 5.2% and 21.7%. The 3.59%, 15.8% and 21.3% figures come from arXiv v3 only.

findings.claim: Hallucinated package names repeat: 43% came back in all 10 repeated queries, 58% came back more than once, and 39% never repeated. The USENIX ;login: summary rounds these to about 45% and 60%.
findings.relevance: Because names repeat predictably, someone could register them ahead of time. Checking that a package exists is therefore not enough; the toolkit also needs to check package age, popularity and publisher.
findings.correction: No correction needed.

findings.claim: The term "slopsquatting" for registering LLM-hallucinated package names was coined by PSF Developer-in-Residence Seth Larson and popularized by Andrew Nesbitt in April 2025.
findings.relevance: Gives the risk a standard name for the threat-model catalogue. I could not retrieve Larson's original post text; attribution relies on Socket and the title of his Fosstodon post.
findings.correction: No correction needed. Socket's post (8 April 2025) credits Larson with coining the term and Nesbitt with popularizing it. Larson's own post on 13 April 2025 ("Do I have to add 'coined slopsquatting' to my resume now?") is consistent with this. I could not find the exact post where the word was first used.

findings.claim: In March 2024 Lasso Security reported that it uploaded an empty package under the repeatedly hallucinated name "huggingface-cli" to PyPI, and it received more than 30,000 downloads in three months. Lasso also found an Alibaba research repo README recommending it.
findings.relevance: Real-world evidence that hallucinated dependencies get installed. The download count is the researcher's own measurement and was not independently audited.
